patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Severe central chest pain for 45 minutes, not relieved by GTN spray
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Mr Mitchell presents to the Emergency Department with severe central chest pain that started 45 minutes ago while he was watching television at home. The pain is described as crushing pressure, 9/10 severity, radiating to his left arm and jaw. He feels nauseated and has vomited twice. He is sweating profusely and feels short of breath. The pain is not relieved by sitting forward or deep breathing. He used his wife's GTN spray three times without relief. He has never experienced pain like this before. His wife called the ambulance when he became pale and clammy. The paramedics gave him 300mg aspirin en route and commenced oxygen therapy at 4L/min via nasal prongs. He denies any recent exertion, fever, or trauma. He has been feeling more fatigued than usual over the past week and experienced mild chest discomfort yesterday after climbing stairs, which resolved with rest after 5 minutes. He is a current smoker with a 40 pack-year history and admits to poor medication compliance with his diabetes and hypertension medications.

The pain is described as a heavy, crushing sensation across his chest that radiates to his left shoulder and occasionally to his jaw. Symptoms consistently occur when walking uphill or after walking about 200 meters on flat ground, particularly in cold weather or after meals. The pain forces him to stop and rest, typically resolving within 2-3 minutes. He has been using his wife's GTN spray occasionally with good effect, obtaining relief within 1-2 minutes. He quit smoking 5 years ago after a 40 pack-year history. His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 72, and his older brother had coronary bypass surgery at age 65. He's been compliant with his medications but admits his diet could be better, and he's gained 5kg over the past year. Medical therapy does not alter natural history - definitive treatment is valve replacement

osces.title: Acute Pericarditis - Anti-inflammatory Management

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Sharp chest pain for 3 days, worse when lying flat
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Ms Chen presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of sharp, stabbing central chest pain. The pain started gradually after recovering from what she thought was a 'bad cold' two weeks ago with fever, cough, and muscle aches. The pain is located retrosternally, rated 7/10 in severity, and has a pleuritic quality - worsening with deep inspiration and coughing. She notices significant relief when sitting forward and leaning on her knees, but the pain becomes unbearable when lying flat, forcing her to sleep propped up on pillows. The pain does not radiate to her arms or jaw. She feels slightly short of breath but attributes this to avoiding deep breaths due to pain. No associated palpitations, syncope, or leg swelling. She has been taking paracetamol 1g QID with minimal relief. She tried ibuprofen 400mg once yesterday which seemed more helpful but was concerned about taking more without medical advice. No recent travel, no sick contacts apart from her students. She received her influenza vaccine 3 months ago and COVID-19 booster 6 months ago. She is otherwise healthy with no significant medical history.
past_medical_history: Recent viral upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago - self-resolved
Up to date with immunisations including influenza and COVID-19
Non-smoker, occasional social alcohol (2-3 standard drinks per week)
Active lifestyle - regular yoga and swimming

examination_findings.general: Alert, appears uncomfortable, sitting forward with tripod positioning, no acute distress
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Pericardial friction rub audible at left sternal edge, best heard with patient leaning forward in expiration - high-pitched, scratchy, triphasic sound. Heart sounds dual rhythm, no murmurs. JVP not elevated at 2cm. No peripheral oedema. Peripheral pulses equal and palpable.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear lung fields bilaterally, reduced air entry at bases due to shallow breathing, no crackles or wheeze
examination_findings.other: No pulsus paradoxus (BP difference <10mmHg with respiration). No signs of cardiac tamponade.

investigations.ecg: Widespread concave-upward ST elevation in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, and V3-V6 (1-2mm). PR segment depression in leads II, aVF, and V4-V6. PR elevation in aVR. No reciprocal ST depression. Normal QRS complexes. Sinus rhythm at 88 bpm.
investigations.troponin: High-sensitivity troponin I: 45 ng/L (normal <26 ng/L) - mild elevation consistent with myopericarditis
investigations.other: CRP: 68 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L). ESR: 45 mm/hr (normal <20 mm/hr). FBC: WCC 11.8 x10⁹/L with lymphocyte predominance, Hb 128 g/L, Platelets 310 x10⁹/L. UEC: Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, Cr 65 μmol/L, eGFR >90. CXR: Normal heart size, clear lung fields, no pleural effusion. Echocardiogram: Small pericardial effusion (4mm) without haemodynamic compromise, normal LV function (EF 60%), no regional wall motion abnormalities.

immediate: Ibuprofen 600mg PO TDS with food for 1-2 weeks - PBS 1896P
Colchicine 500 micrograms PO BD for 3 months (0.5mg daily if <70kg) - PBS 1842R
Pantoprazole 40mg PO daily for gastric protection while on NSAIDs - PBS 8499T
Paracetamol 1g PO QID can continue as adjunct analgesia - PBS 1823Y
Rest and avoid strenuous activity until symptoms resolve
Monitor for signs of cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis
important_cautions: AVOID corticosteroids in first-line treatment (increases recurrence risk)
AVOID anticoagulation unless compelling indication (risk of haemorrhagic conversion)
AVOID aspirin as sole therapy (less effective than ibuprofen for pericarditis)
Monitor for NSAID side effects (renal function, GI symptoms)
follow_up: Review in 1 week to assess response to treatment
Repeat ECG in 1 week to monitor evolution
Repeat inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) in 2 weeks
Echocardiogram in 1-2 weeks if effusion present or symptoms persist
Taper ibuprofen after 1-2 weeks based on symptom resolution and CRP normalisation
Continue colchicine for full 3 months to prevent recurrence
Advise return if worsening dyspnoea, fever >38.5°C, or symptoms suggesting tamponade
patient_education: Explain benign nature of acute pericarditis with good prognosis
Emphasise importance of completing 3-month colchicine course
Advise to take NSAIDs with food to minimise GI upset
Warn about potential colchicine side effects (diarrhoea, nausea)
Return immediately if severe dyspnoea, dizziness, or chest pressure

marking_criteria.item: Recognises clinical triad: pleuritic chest pain, positional (better sitting forward), pericardial rub

Prescribes colchicine 500mcg BD for 3 months

red_flags: Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg
Large pericardial effusion (>20mm) on echocardiogram
Evidence of myocardial involvement with significant troponin elevation or wall motion abnormalities
Fever >38.5°C suggesting bacterial pericarditis

Failure to respond to NSAIDs within 1 week
Recurrent pericarditis (>1 episode) requiring specialist referral

differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_features: Crushing pain, not positional, ST elevation in vascular territory, significant troponin rise
Sudden onset dyspnoea, risk factors for VTE, elevated D-dimer, CTPA findings

Tearing pain, pulse deficit, widened mediastinum, CT aortogram findings
Lateral chest pain, pleural rub different quality, no ECG changes

key_decision_points: Positional nature of pain (worse lying flat, better leaning forward) strongly suggests pericarditis
Pericardial friction rub is pathognomonic but present in only 30-60% of cases
Widespread ST elevation distinguishes from STEMI (which has territorial changes)
Colchicine for 3 months reduces recurrence from 30% to 10-15%
NSAIDs should be tapered based on CRP normalisation, not just symptoms
Avoid steroids unless contraindication to NSAIDs or recurrent disease

ICAP trial: Colchicine reduced incessant/recurrent pericarditis (Imazio et al, 2013)
Australian therapeutic guidelines align with international recommendations

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Sudden onset shortness of breath and sharp chest pain for 4 hours
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Mr Wilson presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain that started 4 hours ago while walking to his car after a 14-hour flight from London to Sydney yesterday. The chest pain is sharp, 7/10 severity, worse on deep inspiration, localised to the right side of his chest. He feels breathless at rest and cannot complete sentences without pausing. He has noticed his right calf feels tight and swollen since the flight. He denies coughing up blood but feels light-headed when standing. No fever or productive cough. He took paracetamol 1g two hours ago with no relief. He flew economy class and did not move much during the flight due to turbulence. past_medical_history: Previous DVT right leg 5 years ago (3 months anticoagulation completed)
Factor V Leiden heterozygous (diagnosed after previous DVT)

vital_signs.spo2: 92% on room air, 96% on 2L nasal prongs

examination_findings.general: Anxious, tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles, able to speak in short phrases
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardic regular rhythm, loud P2, no murmurs, JVP 4cm, no parasternal heave, peripheral pulses intact

investigations.troponin: High sensitivity troponin I: 45 ng/L (normal <26 ng/L) - mild elevation suggesting RV strain

investigations.bnp: BNP 285 pg/mL (normal <100 pg/mL) - suggests RV strain
investigations.other: FBC: Hb 145 g/L, WCC 9.8 x10⁹/L, Platelets 285 x10⁹/L. UEC: Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, Cr 88 μmol/L, eGFR >90. LFTs normal. Coags: INR 1.1, APTT 32 seconds

IV access and continuous cardiac monitoring
Analgesia with paracetamol 1g PO/IV QID - PBS 1721R
Consider oxycodone 5mg PO for severe pleuritic pain - PBS 2622M
management_plan.risk_stratification: PESI Score: 48 points (Age 48, male +0, no comorbidities, HR >110 +20, RR >30 +20, temp normal +0, no altered mental status, SpO2 <90% +20, BP normal +0). Class II - Low-intermediate risk (1.7-3.5% 30-day mortality). Intermediate-low risk PE with RV dysfunction on imaging but no hypotension. Suitable for early discharge after 24-48 hours observation if stable
anticoagulation: Apixaban 10mg PO BD for 7 days (loading) - PBS 3467K
Then Apixaban 5mg PO BD ongoing - PBS 10234L
Alternative: Rivaroxaban 15mg PO BD x 21 days then 20mg daily - PBS 3465H
Alternative if DOAC contraindicated: Enoxaparin 1mg/kg (90mg) SC BD bridge to warfarin target INR 2-3 - PBS 8393N
Duration: Minimum 3 months (provoked PE with transient risk factor - long haul flight)
Consider extended anticoagulation given Factor V Leiden and recurrent VTE
monitoring: Vital signs hourly x 6 hours then 4-hourly
Daily FBC, UEC, LFTs while inpatient
Echo within 24-48 hours to assess RV function
discharge_planning: Oral anticoagulation education - bleeding risks, drug interactions
Compression stockings for post-thrombotic syndrome prevention - not PBS
Travel advice - mobilisation during flights, consider prophylaxis
Follow-up in 1 week with GP for anticoagulation monitoring
Respiratory clinic in 3 months for repeat CTPA if ongoing symptoms
Haematology referral for thrombophilia given recurrent VTE and Factor V Leiden
Consider IVC filter only if absolute contraindication to anticoagulation

marking_criteria.item: Calculates Wells Score correctly (>4 points = PE likely)
Orders appropriate initial investigations (D-dimer, ECG, CXR, ABG)
Recognises high D-dimer and proceeds to CTPA
Interprets CTPA findings (bilateral PE with RV strain)
Risk stratifies using PESI or sPESI score
Identifies intermediate-low risk PE (RV dysfunction, no hypotension)
Initiates appropriate DOAC (apixaban 10mg BD loading dose)
Specifies correct duration (minimum 3 months for provoked PE)
Provides oxygen therapy to maintain SpO2 >94%
Orders duplex ultrasound to confirm DVT
Arranges appropriate monitoring (cardiac, echo for RV function)
Considers extended anticoagulation given Factor V Leiden
Plans appropriate follow-up (GP, respiratory, haematology)
Educates about anticoagulation and travel precautions
Recognises thrombolysis indications if deteriorates

Interpret CTPA findings including RV strain indicators

Select appropriate anticoagulation with correct loading doses
Determine anticoagulation duration based on provoked vs unprovoked PE

Thrombolysis only for high-risk PE with haemodynamic instability

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Severe shortness of breath and chest pain 12 hours after confirmed anterior STEMI
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Mrs Chen is a 68-year-old woman who presented 12 hours ago with an anterior STEMI and underwent primary PCI to the LAD with drug-eluting stent insertion. She initially improved post-procedure but has deteriorated over the past 3 hours. She is now severely short of breath, unable to lie flat, and has developed recurrent central chest pain (6/10 severity). She feels lightheaded and confused, with her daughter noting she seems less responsive than earlier. She has passed only 50mL of urine in the past 4 hours despite IV fluids. She denies any bleeding symptoms but reports feeling extremely cold and weak. The nursing staff report progressive hypotension not responding to fluid boluses (received 1L normal saline). She is becoming increasingly agitated and confused, repeatedly asking where she is. Her skin is cold and clammy to touch with mottled appearance over her knees. She has frothy pink sputum when coughing.
past_medical_history: Anterior STEMI 12 hours ago - LAD occlusion, door-to-balloon time 82 minutes
Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 12 years (HbA1c 8.2% last month)
Chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 110 μmol/L)
Family history: Brother had CABG at age 65

vital_signs.gcs: 14/15 (E4 V4 M6) - confused to time and place

examination_findings.general: Acutely unwell, confused, restless, using accessory muscles for breathing, cold and clammy skin with mottling over knees and elbows, capillary refill time 5 seconds
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated at 10cm above sternal angle, apex beat displaced to 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line, dual heart sounds with gallop rhythm (S3 present), no murmurs audible, bilateral pedal oedema to mid-shin, weak peripheral pulses, liver enlarged 3cm below costal margin and tender
examination_findings.respiratory: Bilateral coarse crackles to mid-zones, wheeze present, pink frothy sputum, decreased air entry at bases bilaterally, dullness to percussion at both bases
examination_findings.neurological: GCS 14/15, confused and agitated, no focal neurological deficits, pupils equal and reactive
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, hepatomegaly 3cm below costal margin, tender right upper quadrant, no ascites

investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 115 bpm, Q waves in V1-V4 (evolved anterior MI), ST elevation 1-2mm persisting in V2-V4, poor R wave progression
investigations.troponin: High sensitivity troponin I: 45,000 ng/L (peak, now trending down to 38,000 ng/L)
investigations.chest_xray: Cardiomegaly with cardiothoracic ratio 0.65, bilateral pulmonary oedema with bat-wing appearance, upper lobe blood diversion, Kerley B lines, bilateral pleural effusions
investigations.echo: Severe LV systolic dysfunction with LVEF 20%, anterior and anteroseptal wall akinesis, apical akinesis with possible early thrombus formation, moderate mitral regurgitation, TAPSE 14mm suggesting RV dysfunction, no pericardial effusion, dilated LV with end-diastolic diameter 65mm
investigations.blood_gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 32 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L (metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation), SaO2 91%
investigations.bloods: FBC: Hb 125 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10⁹/L, platelets 189 x10⁹/L. UEC: Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, Cr 165 μmol/L (baseline 110), eGFR 32, urea 14.2 mmol/L. LFTs: ALT 185 U/L, AST 210 U/L, ALP 95 U/L, bilirubin 28 μmol/L (shock liver pattern). Coags: INR 1.4, APTT 38 seconds
investigations.cardiac_index: Estimated cardiac index 1.8 L/min/m² (normal 2.5-4.0), SVR 1800 dynes·sec/cm⁵ (elevated)

immediate: ICU admission urgently - patient requires intensive monitoring and support
Insert arterial line for continuous BP monitoring and frequent ABG sampling
Insert central venous catheter (internal jugular or subclavian) for CVP monitoring and vasopressor administration
Consider pulmonary artery catheter for cardiac output monitoring if not responding to initial therapy
Commence dobutamine infusion 2.5-5 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP >65mmHg and improved perfusion (PBS 8234T)
If hypotension persists (MAP <65), add noradrenaline 0.05-0.5 mcg/kg/min via central line (PBS 2894M)
Continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator pads attached
Insert indwelling catheter with hourly urine output monitoring (target >0.5mL/kg/hr)
Increase oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94% - consider BiPAP if deteriorating
Cautious diuresis with frusemide 40mg IV if BP stabilises (avoid excessive preload reduction)
Correct metabolic acidosis if pH <7.2 with sodium bicarbonate
DVT prophylaxis with pneumatic compression devices (hold anticoagulation given shock state)
management_plan.haemodynamic_targets: MAP >65mmHg, cardiac index >2.2 L/min/m², ScvO2 >70%, urine output >0.5mL/kg/hr, lactate clearance >10% per 2 hours, mental status improvement. Monitor for signs of adequate perfusion: warming of extremities, improved capillary refill, resolution of mottling, improved mentation
management_plan.inotrope_selection: First line: Dobutamine 2.5-20 mcg/kg/min for inotropic support without significant vasoconstriction. Add noradrenaline 0.05-2.0 mcg/kg/min if MAP remains <65mmHg despite dobutamine. Consider milrinone 0.25-0.75 mcg/kg/min if inadequate response to dobutamine (phosphodiesterase inhibitor - vasodilator and inotrope). Avoid high-dose vasopressors which increase afterload and myocardial oxygen demand
mechanical_support: Consider intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) if not responding to medical therapy within 2 hours
Assess for candidacy for mechanical circulatory support (Impella, ECMO) if refractory shock
Early cardiology and cardiac surgery consultation for advanced support options
Consider urgent coronary angiography to assess stent patency if clinical deterioration
monitoring: Continuous ECG monitoring for arrhythmias (high risk of VT/VF)
Arterial line for continuous BP and frequent ABG (every 2-4 hours initially)
Serial lactate levels every 2-4 hours to assess tissue perfusion
Daily echo to assess LV function and exclude mechanical complications
Monitor for complications: reinfarction, mechanical complications (VSD, papillary muscle rupture), arrhythmias
Monitor liver function (shock liver) and renal function
medication_adjustments: Withhold ACE inhibitor/ARB until haemodynamically stable
Withhold beta-blocker until cardiogenic shock resolved
Continue dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 100mg + ticagrelor 90mg BD)
Anticoagulation for LV thrombus prevention once stable (enoxaparin 1mg/kg BD)
Consider amiodarone 200mg TDS if ventricular arrhythmias
Stress ulcer prophylaxis with pantoprazole 40mg IV daily
Insulin infusion for tight glycaemic control in ICU
complications_watch: Mechanical complications: ventricular septal defect, free wall rupture, papillary muscle rupture with acute MR
Arrhythmias: VT/VF (most common cause of death), complete heart block, atrial fibrillation
LV thrombus formation with risk of systemic embolisation
Progressive multi-organ failure: acute kidney injury, shock liver, ARDS
Bleeding complications from dual antiplatelet therapy
management_plan.prognosis_discussion: Cardiogenic shock post-MI carries 40-50% in-hospital mortality despite optimal therapy. Early revascularisation and mechanical support improve outcomes. Need to discuss prognosis with family, consider advance care directives if deteriorating despite maximal therapy. Survivors require long-term heart failure management and consideration for ICD/CRT

marking_criteria.item: Recognises cardiogenic shock (hypotension, pulmonary oedema, poor perfusion)
Orders immediate ICU admission for intensive monitoring
Establishes invasive monitoring (arterial line and central line)
Initiates appropriate inotrope (dobutamine 2.5-20 mcg/kg/min)
Adds vasopressor if needed (noradrenaline for MAP <65)
Sets appropriate haemodynamic targets (MAP >65, CI >2.2)
Monitors tissue perfusion (lactate, ScvO2, urine output)
Considers mechanical support (IABP, Impella, ECMO)
Manages pulmonary oedema appropriately (oxygen, cautious diuresis)
Withholds beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor during shock
Continues antiplatelet therapy and statin
Monitors for mechanical complications (echo surveillance)
Provides organ support (renal replacement therapy if needed)
Discusses prognosis with family appropriately
Coordinates multidisciplinary care (cardiology, ICU, cardiac surgery)

learning_objectives: Recognise clinical features of cardiogenic shock post-MI including hypotension, pulmonary oedema, and end-organ hypoperfusion
Understand haemodynamic monitoring requirements including arterial line, central venous catheter, and cardiac output monitoring
Select appropriate inotropic support with dobutamine as first-line agent for cardiogenic shock
Know when to add vasopressor support (noradrenaline) for refractory hypotension
Identify indications for mechanical circulatory support including IABP, Impella, and ECMO
Manage complications of cardiogenic shock including pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, and arrhythmias
Understand the importance of avoiding excessive preload reduction in RV involvement
Monitor tissue perfusion using lactate clearance, ScvO2, and urine output
Coordinate multidisciplinary ICU care for critically ill cardiac patients
Recognise mechanical complications of MI requiring urgent surgical intervention

references.title: eTG Complete - Cardiogenic Shock Management
CSANZ Guidelines - Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes
references.key_points: Cardiogenic shock complicates 5-10% of STEMI cases with 40-50% mortality

references.title: Australian Resuscitation Council - Post-Cardiac Arrest Care
National Heart Foundation - Acute Heart Failure Guidelines
references.key_points: Early recognition and aggressive management of cardiogenic shock improves outcomes

references.title: Talley & O'Connor Clinical Examination 9th Edition
references.key_points: Clinical signs of cardiogenic shock: cool peripheries, oliguria, altered mental state

clinical_pearls: Cardiogenic shock has high mortality (40-50%) despite optimal therapy - early recognition is crucial
Avoid excessive fluid administration which worsens pulmonary oedema - use invasive monitoring to guide therapy
Dobutamine is preferred first-line inotrope; add noradrenaline only if MAP <65mmHg persists
Consider mechanical support early (within 2-6 hours) if not responding to medical therapy
Monitor for mechanical complications with daily echo - papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture
Lactate clearance >10% per 2 hours indicates adequate resuscitation
ScvO2 <70% suggests inadequate oxygen delivery requiring escalation of support
Withhold beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors until haemodynamically stable (usually 24-48 hours)
IABP reduces afterload and improves coronary perfusion but mortality benefit unclear
Early revascularisation is the most important intervention to improve survival
differential_diagnosis: Mechanical complications of MI (acute MR from papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture)
Acute decompensated heart failure without true cardiogenic shock

osces.title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy - Sudden Cardiac Death Risk Stratification in Young Athlete

demographics.name: Joshua Anderson
demographics.occupation: Elite Australian Rules Football player (VFL level)

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Recurrent pre-syncope during training sessions over past 3 months, father died suddenly at age 38
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Joshua is a 22-year-old semi-professional footballer who presents for cardiac assessment after experiencing three episodes of near-fainting during intense training sessions over the past three months. The episodes occur specifically during sprint drills, characterized by sudden lightheadedness, tunnel vision, and chest tightness lasting 30-60 seconds. He has never lost consciousness but has had to stop and crouch down during each episode. He denies palpitations during these events but notes occasional 'heart racing' at rest over the past year, which he attributed to pre-game anxiety. His father died suddenly during recreational tennis at age 38, with autopsy reportedly showing 'enlarged heart'. His paternal uncle has an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator but Joshua doesn't know the indication. He has no history of rheumatic fever, recent viral illness, or illicit drug use. He's concerned about his football career and whether he can continue playing. He's never had formal cardiac screening despite family history. His coach referred him after witnessing the most recent episode during a practice match. He reports excellent exercise tolerance otherwise, regularly completing 10km runs and high-intensity interval training without symptoms when not doing maximal sprints. No chest pain at rest or with exertion outside these episodes. No orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. He takes no regular medications and has never been hospitalized.

examination_findings.general: Athletic build, well-appearing young man, no acute distress
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated. Double apical impulse palpable (sustained forceful apical beat with presystolic impulse). Harsh grade 3/6 late systolic ejection murmur at left sternal edge, increases with Valsalva manoeuvre and standing, decreases with squatting. Fourth heart sound audible. No radiation to carotids. Carotid upstroke rapid and jerky (bisferiens pulse). Peripheral pulses normal and symmetrical.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no crackles or wheeze
examination_findings.other: No signs of Marfan syndrome (arm span equals height, no arachnodactyly, no lens dislocation)

investigations.ecg: Sinus rhythm 58 bpm. Deep septal Q waves in leads I, aVL, V5-V6 (depth 5mm in V5). Deep T wave inversions in leads I, aVL, V4-V6 (12mm inversion V5). Left ventricular hypertrophy voltage criteria met (SV1 + RV5 = 52mm). Left atrial enlargement (P wave duration 130ms, biphasic in V1). No delta waves or short PR interval.
investigations.troponin: High-sensitivity troponin I: 8 ng/L (reference <14 ng/L) - not elevated

other.echocardiogram: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with maximal wall thickness 22mm (basal septum), posterior wall 11mm. Systolic anterior motion of anterior mitral valve leaflet with mitral-septal contact. Left ventricular outflow tract gradient 68 mmHg at rest, 112 mmHg post-Valsalva. Mitral regurgitation mild-moderate (posteriorly directed jet). Left ventricular ejection fraction 75% with hyperdynamic function. Left atrium dilated (volume index 38 mL/m²).
other.holter_monitor: Three episodes non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT): longest run 8 beats at 180 bpm during daytime activity. Frequent ventricular ectopics (1,247 in 24 hours). No atrial fibrillation.
other.exercise_stress_test: Terminated at Stage 4 Bruce protocol due to pre-syncope. Blood pressure failed to rise appropriately (baseline 128/76, peak 132/78 at peak exercise). Achieved 14 METs. NSVT induced (6 beats at 190 bpm).
other.cardiac_mri: Maximal wall thickness 23mm. Late gadolinium enhancement present in 8% of left ventricular mass (mid-wall and RV insertion points). No apical aneurysm.

immediate: Immediate cessation of all competitive and high-intensity recreational sport
Urgent cardiology specialist referral for risk stratification within 7 days
Family cascade screening - arrange echocardiogram and ECG for first-degree relatives
Provide written documentation for sports club regarding medical restriction from training and competition
Genetic counselling referral
Education regarding warning symptoms (syncope, sustained palpitations, chest pain) and need for immediate medical review
management_plan.sudden_cardiac_death_risk_stratification: High-risk features present: (1) NSVT on Holter monitoring, (2) Abnormal blood pressure response to exercise, (3) Maximal wall thickness ≥30mm not met but 22-23mm is intermediate risk, (4) Family history of sudden cardiac death <40 years, (5) Unexplained syncope - patient has pre-syncope with exercise BP response issue. Late gadolinium enhancement 8% adds additional risk. ESC Risk-SCD score calculation required - likely >6% 5-year risk based on major risk factors.
management_plan.icd_consideration: Likely indication for primary prevention ICD based on: (1) NSVT, (2) Abnormal exercise BP, (3) Strong family history SCD, (4) Extensive LGE on MRI (≥15% is high risk, 8% intermediate but combined with other factors increases risk), (5) Pre-syncope with haemodynamic evidence. Shared decision-making discussion required regarding ICD vs medical management.

medical_therapy.name: Bisoprolol
medical_therapy.indication: Negative inotrope to reduce LVOT gradient, reduce arrhythmia burden, symptom control

medical_therapy.name: Disopyramide (if beta-blocker insufficient)
medical_therapy.indication: Negative inotrope for refractory LVOT obstruction symptoms

lifestyle_modifications: Permanent restriction from competitive sports and high-intensity exercise (ESC/ACC guidelines)
Moderate-intensity exercise permitted if symptoms controlled and no high-risk features post-ICD (if inserted)
Annual cardiology review with echocardiogram and Holter monitoring
follow_up: Cardiology review within 1 week for ICD discussion
Cardiac MRI and exercise testing results to guide ICD decision
Electrophysiology referral if ICD decision made
Genetic testing (MYBPC3, MYH7, TNNT2 genes) - may take 3-6 months
Psychology referral for adjustment to diagnosis and career impact
6-monthly echocardiogram to assess progression
Family screening results review

marking_criteria.item: Recognizes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from history, examination (dynamic murmur, bisferiens pulse, double apical impulse)
Identifies sudden cardiac death risk factors: family history SCD <40 years, NSVT on Holter, abnormal BP response to exercise, pre-syncope
Interprets ECG correctly: LVH voltage criteria, deep T inversions, septal Q waves consistent with HCM
Recognizes dynamic LVOT obstruction from echocardiogram (gradient >30mmHg, SAM, increase with Valsalva)
Immediate management: cessation of competitive sport, urgent cardiology referral within days (not weeks)
Initiates family cascade screening (first-degree relatives - ECG and echo)
Discusses ICD consideration based on risk stratification (ESC Risk-SCD score, major risk factors present)
Prescribes beta-blocker (bisoprolol or equivalent) for symptom control and negative inotropy
Addresses psychological impact of career-ending diagnosis, offers psychology support
Provides clear documentation for sports club regarding medical restriction (medicolegal)

learning_objectives: Recognize classic clinical features of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy including dynamic murmur, bisferiens pulse, and double apical impulse
Interpret ECG findings in HCM: LVH voltage criteria, deep T wave inversions, and septal Q waves
Perform sudden cardiac death risk stratification using ESC Risk-SCD score and identify major risk factors (NSVT, abnormal exercise BP, family history SCD, extensive LGE)
Understand indications for primary prevention ICD in HCM according to Australian/ESC guidelines
Recognize immediate need for sports restriction in competitive athletes with HCM (ESC/ACC consensus)
Initiate family cascade screening for first-degree relatives of HCM patients
Understand role of beta-blockers and disopyramide in managing LVOT obstruction symptoms

osces.title: Complete Heart Block - Temporary Pacing in Acute Inferior STEMI

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Severe central chest pain for 90 minutes, now becoming drowsy and feeling faint
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Margaret is a 68-year-old woman who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance with severe central chest pain that started 90 minutes ago while gardening. The pain is 9/10 in severity, described as crushing and heavy, radiating to her left arm and jaw. She became diaphoretic and nauseated, vomiting once. Paramedics gave her aspirin 300mg and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate with minimal relief. En route to hospital, she developed progressive bradycardia from initial heart rate of 88 bpm to current 38 bpm over 15 minutes. She now complains of severe lightheadedness, near-syncope when sitting up, and feels increasingly drowsy. She denies loss of consciousness but states 'everything is going dark'. She has never had chest pain like this before. No recent fever, no cough, no leg swelling. Her husband reports she has been completely well until today. Risk factors include type 2 diabetes for 12 years (HbA1c last month 7.8%), hypertension for 8 years, dyslipidaemia, and former smoker (quit 15 years ago, 25 pack-year history). No family history of premature coronary disease. She takes metformin, ramipril, atorvastatin, and aspirin regularly. No known drug allergies. She lives independently with her husband, mobilizes well normally, and was gardening vigorously when symptoms started. No recent overseas travel, no leg pain or swelling to suggest DVT/PE.
past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (12 years, HbA1c 7.8%, no microvascular complications documented)
Dyslipidaemia (LDL 2.8 mmol/L on last test 3 months ago on atorvastatin)
Former smoker (quit 15 years ago, 25 pack-year history)

vital_signs.spo2: 94% on room air, 98% on 4L O2 via Hudson mask

examination_findings.general: Pale, diaphoretic, appears drowsy but rousable to voice. In moderate distress. GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6).
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated 6cm with cannon A waves visible. Apex beat not displaced. Heart sounds bradycardic at 38 bpm, normal S1 and S2, no murmurs audible. Slow-rising carotid pulses, equal bilaterally. Peripheral pulses all palpable but weak. Cold peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds. No peripheral oedema.
examination_findings.respiratory: Bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, right worse than left. No wheeze. Dullness to percussion at right base.
examination_findings.neurological: Drowsy but oriented to person and place. Moving all limbs. Pupils equal and reactive.

investigations.ecg: Complete atrioventricular dissociation - atrial rate 78 bpm (regular P waves), ventricular rate 38 bpm (regular wide QRS complexes at 148ms duration). No relationship between P waves and QRS complexes (P waves march through QRS at varying PR intervals). ST elevation 4mm in leads II, III, aVF. ST depression 2mm in leads I and aVL (reciprocal changes). Right-sided ECG: ST elevation 3mm in V4R. QRS axis +110 degrees.
investigations.troponin: High-sensitivity troponin I: 3,847 ng/L (reference <14 ng/L) - markedly elevated. Initial troponin (on arrival) was 487 ng/L - rising trend confirming acute MI.

other.fbc: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 11.8), platelets 289 x10^9/L
other.uec: Sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L (eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73m²), urea 7.2 mmol/L
other.chest_xray: Mild cardiomegaly. Interstitial oedema pattern with bilateral perihilar haziness. Small right pleural effusion. Upper lobe blood diversion.
other.portable_echocardiogram: Inferior and inferolateral wall akinesis. Basal inferior wall shows paradoxical motion. Right ventricular dilatation and dysfunction (TAPSE 12mm). Estimated LVEF 35%. No pericardial effusion.

immediate_critical_actions: High-flow oxygen via Hudson mask at 8L/min to maintain SpO2 >94%
Establish large-bore IV access (14G or 16G) x2
Continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator pads attached (transcutaneous pacing standby)
Urgent cardiology and interventional cardiology consultation - activate cath lab
Atropine 600 micrograms IV bolus (may give up to 3mg total) - often ineffective in inferior STEMI with CHB but trial justified
Prepare for temporary transvenous pacing wire insertion - alert ICU/CCU
Fluid resuscitate cautiously: 250mL 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus, reassess (RV infarction - preload dependent but risk pulmonary oedema)
management_plan.temporary_pacing_indication: Absolute indication: Complete heart block (third-degree AV block) in setting of acute inferior STEMI with haemodynamic compromise (systolic BP <90 mmHg, GCS 14, near-syncope). Right ventricular infarction present (ST elevation V4R, RV dysfunction on echo) makes patient preload-dependent and poorly tolerant of bradycardia. Transcutaneous pacing as bridge if deteriorates before transvenous wire inserted.

dual_antiplatelet_loading.name: Aspirin
dual_antiplatelet_loading.frequency: Stat PO (already given by paramedics - do not repeat)

dual_antiplatelet_loading.name: Ticagrelor
dual_antiplatelet_loading.indication: STEMI - P2Y12 inhibitor loading (preferred over clopidogrel in STEMI)

primary_pci_preparation: Activate cath lab for primary PCI to right coronary artery (RCA) - likely proximal occlusion given inferior + RV infarction
Heparin 70 units/kg IV bolus (approximately 5,000 units for 70kg patient) - check aPTT
Withhold glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors until angiography (high bleeding risk, operator decision)
Cross-match 2 units packed red cells (PCI bleeding risk)
Consent for PCI and temporary pacing wire (if patient capacity permits, otherwise emergency waiver)
NBM (nil by mouth) - procedural sedation required
temporary_pacing_wire_insertion: Right internal jugular vein access (preferred over femoral - lower infection risk, easier to manage post-PCI with ambulation)
5F or 6F pacing catheter to right ventricular apex under fluoroscopy guidance
Settings: VVI mode, rate 60-70 bpm, output 5mA (threshold usually 0.5-1.5mA, set at 3x threshold), sensitivity 2mV
Confirm capture: 1:1 pacing on ECG, palpable pulse corresponds to paced rate
Chest X-ray post-insertion to confirm position and exclude pneumothorax
Temporary wire typically required for 5-7 days (CHB in inferior STEMI often resolves as oedema settles)

post_pci_management.name: Metoprolol
post_pci_management.frequency: BD (start low dose given bradycardia, uptitrate once pacing wire removed)
post_pci_management.indication: Beta-blocker post-MI (mortality benefit). Withhold initially due to CHB, start once intrinsic rate recovers.

post_pci_management.name: Ramipril (restart after acute phase)
post_pci_management.frequency: Daily (reduce from 10mg, titrate up over weeks)
post_pci_management.indication: ACE inhibitor post-MI with LV dysfunction (LVEF 35%). Restart once BP stable and off inotropes.

monitoring_and_follow_up: CCU admission with continuous telemetry monitoring
Daily ECG to assess for resolution of CHB (check native ventricular rate by temporarily turning off pacemaker)
Monitor for: pacemaker malfunction (failure to capture/sense), infection at wire site, pneumothorax
Temporary wire removal once: (1) Native heart rate >50 bpm for 24 hours, (2) No high-grade AV block for 48 hours, (3) Haemodynamically stable
Permanent pacemaker indication assessment: If CHB persists >14 days post-MI despite revascularization, consider permanent PPM (Class IIa indication)
Echocardiogram at 6 weeks to reassess LVEF (may improve with revascularization and stunning resolution)
ICD consideration if LVEF remains ≤35% at 3 months post-MI (primary prevention sudden cardiac death)

marking_criteria.item: Recognizes complete heart block (third-degree AV block) on ECG: AV dissociation with independent atrial and ventricular rates
Identifies acute inferior STEMI: ST elevation leads II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes I, aVL
Recognizes right ventricular infarction: ST elevation V4R, RV dysfunction on echo, JVP elevated with hypotension
Immediate haemodynamic support: oxygen, IV access, atropine trial, cautious fluid bolus (avoid overload in RV infarction)
Identifies absolute indication for temporary transvenous pacing: CHB with haemodynamic compromise in acute STEMI
Activates primary PCI pathway urgently (door-to-balloon <90 minutes) and contacts interventional cardiology
Administers dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin already given, adds ticagrelor 180mg loading dose
Describes temporary pacing wire insertion: RIJ access, VVI mode, appropriate settings (rate 60-70, output 3x threshold)
Discusses monitoring plan for CHB resolution and criteria for temporary wire removal vs permanent pacemaker consideration
Withholds beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor acutely (bradycardia + hypotension), plans reintroduction when appropriate

learning_objectives: Diagnose complete heart block (third-degree AV block) on ECG by identifying AV dissociation with independent atrial and ventricular rhythms
Recognize right ventricular infarction in acute inferior STEMI (ST elevation V4R, hypotension with elevated JVP, echo findings)
Understand absolute indications for temporary transvenous pacing in acute MI: high-grade AV block with haemodynamic compromise
Manage haemodynamic instability in RV infarction: preload maintenance with cautious fluid resuscitation, avoid excessive vasodilators
Describe temporary pacing wire insertion technique, settings (VVI mode, rate, output, sensitivity), and post-insertion care
Differentiate transient CHB in acute inferior STEMI (usually resolves in 5-7 days) from indications for permanent pacemaker (persistent >14 days)
Apply primary PCI guidelines in STEMI with complete heart block: urgent revascularization may resolve conduction abnormality

osces.title: Acute Myocarditis - Distinguishing Viral from Immune-Mediated in Young Adult

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Sharp central chest pain for 2 days, worse lying flat, preceded by flu-like illness 1 week ago
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Emily is a 28-year-old woman presenting with 2 days of sharp, central chest pain that started suddenly while working at her desk. The pain is constant, sharp in quality, 6/10 severity, worse when lying flat and taking deep breaths, slightly improved when sitting forward. Unlike typical cardiac pain, movement and position changes affect the pain intensity. She has no radiation of pain to arms or jaw. One week ago, she had a flu-like illness with fever to 38.9°C, myalgia, headache, and dry cough lasting 4 days. She recovered from the febrile illness but then developed this chest pain. She also reports mild dyspnoea on exertion over the past 2 days - normally runs 5km easily but now becomes breathless walking up one flight of stairs. She denies palpitations, syncope, or leg swelling. No orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. She has never had chest pain before. No recent overseas travel but her housemate had a similar flu-like illness 2 weeks ago. She received her second dose of Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine 3 weeks ago. No other recent vaccinations. She takes only the combined oral contraceptive pill and occasional paracetamol. No illicit drug use, social alcohol only (2-3 standard drinks per week), non-smoker. No autoimmune disease history. No family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death. Lives with two housemates, works in an office. Presented to GP yesterday who was concerned about cardiac cause and referred urgently to emergency department.
past_medical_history: Combined oral contraceptive pill for 8 years (Microgynon 30)
Nil other medical history - previously fit and well

examination_findings.general: Young woman, appears well but uncomfortable with chest pain. No acute distress at rest. Able to speak in full sentences.
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated. Apex beat not displaced. Tachycardic at 102 bpm, regular rhythm. Friction rub audible at left sternal edge (triphasic scratching sound, heard best with patient leaning forward). Heart sounds normal, no murmurs. Peripheral pulses normal and equal. No peripheral oedema.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no crackles or wheeze. Pain on deep inspiration (pleuritic component).
examination_findings.skin: No rash, no stigmata of endocarditis

investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 102 bpm. Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation in leads I, II, III, aVF, V2-V6 (1-2mm elevation). PR segment depression in leads II, aVF, V4-V6. No reciprocal ST depression. T waves upright. No Q waves.
investigations.troponin: High-sensitivity troponin I: 1,248 ng/L at presentation (reference <14 ng/L), repeat 4 hours later: 1,892 ng/L - rising but lower than typical STEMI levels. CK-MB also elevated at 68 micrograms/L (reference <5).

other.fbc: Hb 132 g/L, WCC 11.8 x10^9/L (lymphocytes 4.2, neutrophils 6.4, eosinophils 0.8 - mild lymphocytosis), platelets 267 x10^9/L
other.uec: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L (eGFR >90), urea 4.8 mmol/L - all normal
other.bnp: 587 pg/mL (reference <100 pg/mL) - elevated suggesting cardiac dysfunction
other.tft: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, free T4 14 pmol/L - normal (exclude thyrotoxicosis)
other.autoimmune_screen: ANA negative, ENA negative, ANCA negative, RF negative - no evidence of systemic autoimmune disease
other.viral_serology: COVID-19 PCR negative. Coxsackie B IgM positive (titre 1:160), IgG negative (acute infection). Echovirus, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, CMV, EBV serology negative.
other.chest_xray: Cardiac silhouette mildly enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio 0.52, upper limit normal 0.50). No pulmonary oedema. No pleural effusions. Clear lung fields.
other.echocardiogram: Global hypokinesis of left ventricle with diffuse wall motion abnormality (all segments affected equally, unlike regional pattern in CAD). LVEF 42% (moderately impaired). Left ventricle not dilated. No regional wall motion abnormalities. No pericardial effusion. No valvular abnormalities. Right ventricle normal size and function.
other.cardiac_mri: Subepicardial and mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement in inferolateral wall and anterior wall (non-ischaemic pattern). Myocardial oedema on T2-weighted sequences (bright signal in lateral wall). No pericardial effusion. LVEF 40% on cine imaging. Findings consistent with acute myocarditis (Lake Louise criteria met: 2/2 T2 criteria + 2/2 T1 criteria).

immediate_acute_management: Admit to coronary care unit for cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia risk in myocarditis)
Continuous telemetry monitoring for arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia risk)
Bed rest and activity restriction - avoid exercise for 3-6 months (risk of arrhythmias and fulminant deterioration with exertion)
Stop combined oral contraceptive pill (prothrombotic, theoretical risk in acute cardiac inflammation)
Serial troponin monitoring every 6-12 hours to assess for peak and trend
Daily ECG to monitor for evolving changes and arrhythmias

supportive_cardiac_therapy.name: Ibuprofen
supportive_cardiac_therapy.indication: NSAID for pericarditis/myopericarditis - reduces inflammation and chest pain. NOTE: Traditionally avoided in pure myocarditis but permitted for myopericarditis.

supportive_cardiac_therapy.name: Colchicine
supportive_cardiac_therapy.indication: Reduces recurrence of pericarditis component (COPE, ICAP trials)

supportive_cardiac_therapy.name: Pantoprazole
supportive_cardiac_therapy.indication: Gastric protection while on NSAID (>2 weeks use)

supportive_cardiac_therapy.name: Ramipril
supportive_cardiac_therapy.indication: ACE inhibitor for LV dysfunction (LVEF 42%) - cardiac remodelling prevention

supportive_cardiac_therapy.name: Bisoprolol
supportive_cardiac_therapy.indication: Beta-blocker for LV dysfunction and to reduce arrhythmia risk. Also reduces myocardial oxygen demand.

avoid_harmful_interventions: Do NOT give immunosuppression (corticosteroids, azathioprine) in acute viral myocarditis - worsens outcomes by impairing viral clearance
Do NOT perform endomyocardial biopsy unless fulminant myocarditis with haemodynamic compromise (not indicated in stable patient)
Do NOT use inotropes (dobutamine, adrenaline) unless cardiogenic shock - increase myocardial oxygen demand
Strict exercise restriction: NO exercise for minimum 3 months, then gradual return only if LVEF normalized and no arrhythmias on Holter
diagnostic_workup_complete: Viral serology confirms Coxsackie B acute infection (IgM positive, IgG negative) - most common cause of viral myocarditis in Australia
Cardiac MRI confirms acute myocarditis (Lake Louise criteria met): myocardial oedema + LGE in non-ischaemic pattern
Exclude autoimmune causes: ANA, ENA, ANCA all negative - not lupus myocarditis or vasculitis
Exclude giant cell myocarditis (would be fulminant), sarcoidosis (no systemic features), eosinophilic myocarditis (eosinophils normal)

COVID-19 vaccine temporal relationship noted (3 weeks post-Pfizer dose 2) but Coxsackie B serology suggests viral trigger more likely. Vaccine-associated myocarditis typically occurs within 1 week of dose 2 in young males.
monitoring_and_follow_up: Daily ECG and troponin until troponin trending down and ECG stabilizing
Holter monitor at discharge to screen for ventricular arrhythmias (24-48 hour recording)
Repeat echocardiogram at 1 month, 3 months, 6 months to assess LVEF recovery (most patients recover fully within 3-6 months)
Cardiology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks with results of Holter and repeat echo
Strict exercise restriction: no competitive sport or vigorous exercise for 3-6 months minimum
Return to exercise protocol: Only if LVEF normalized (>50%), no arrhythmias on Holter, normal BNP, asymptomatic. Gradual return starting with light walking, increase by 10% per week.
Genetic counselling not required (viral myocarditis, not familial cardiomyopathy)
Influenza vaccination annually (reduce future viral infections)
If LVEF remains <40% at 6 months: consider cardiac MRI to distinguish chronic viral myocarditis from dilated cardiomyopathy. May require endomyocardial biopsy at that stage.
ICD consideration if: (1) LVEF remains ≤35% despite medical therapy, (2) Ventricular arrhythmias on monitoring, (3) Failure to recover after 6 months

marking_criteria.item: Recognizes clinical presentation of acute myocarditis: chest pain post-viral illness, pleuritic pain, friction rub, tachycardia
Interprets ECG correctly: widespread ST elevation (saddle-shaped) + PR depression = myopericarditis, NOT STEMI (no reciprocal changes, widespread distribution)
Identifies viral aetiology: Coxsackie B IgM positive = acute viral infection. Recognizes Coxsackie as commonest cause viral myocarditis.
Applies Lake Louise criteria for cardiac MRI diagnosis: myocardial oedema (T2) + LGE in non-ischaemic pattern confirms myocarditis
Differentiates from STEMI: young age, post-viral, widespread ST elevation, normal coronary arteries (implied by MRI non-ischaemic pattern)
Immediate management: CCU admission, telemetry monitoring, strict bed rest and exercise restriction for 3-6 months (critical for arrhythmia prevention)
Appropriate pharmacotherapy: NSAID + colchicine for pericarditic component, ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker for LV dysfunction (LVEF 42%)
Avoids harmful interventions: NO immunosuppression in acute viral myocarditis (worsens outcomes), NO biopsy unless fulminant
Discusses prognosis: most recover fully in 3-6 months, serial echo to confirm LVEF normalization before return to exercise
Addresses COVID vaccine temporal relationship appropriately: notes 3-week timeframe but Coxsackie serology suggests viral cause. Vaccine myocarditis typically <1 week post-dose 2.

learning_objectives: Diagnose acute myocarditis from clinical triad: chest pain post-viral illness, elevated troponin, LV dysfunction on echo
Differentiate myopericarditis from STEMI on ECG: widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation + PR depression vs regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes
Apply Lake Louise criteria for cardiac MRI diagnosis of myocarditis (T2 oedema + T1 LGE in non-ischaemic pattern)
Identify Coxsackie B virus as commonest cause of viral myocarditis in Australia (IgM positive = acute infection)
Understand strict exercise restriction in myocarditis: 3-6 months minimum, NO return until LVEF normalized and no arrhythmias
Differentiate management of viral myocarditis (supportive, NO immunosuppression) vs immune-mediated myocarditis (may require steroids)
Recognize role of ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers in myocarditis with LV dysfunction (prevent adverse remodelling, reduce arrhythmias)

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Sudden-onset severe breathlessness 4 hours ago, following mild chest discomfort yesterday
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Frank is a 72-year-old man brought to the emergency department by ambulance with severe breathlessness that started suddenly 4 hours ago while watching television. He describes acute dyspnoea 'like drowning', requiring him to sit bolt upright, unable to lie flat at all. He is using 3-4 pillows even when sitting. Yesterday afternoon, he had 20 minutes of mild central chest heaviness (3/10 severity) while mowing the lawn, which he attributed to indigestion and took antacids. The chest discomfort resolved spontaneously and he felt well until this acute breathlessness started this afternoon. He now has pink frothy sputum when coughing. He denies current chest pain but feels 'pressure' in his chest. He is extremely anxious and feels like he's 'suffocating'. His wife reports he has never been breathless like this before - usually independent with activities of daily living, walks 2km daily without breathlessness. Over the past 6 months, he has noticed reduced exercise tolerance - previously walked 5km easily, now stops at 2km due to mild breathlessness, which he attributed to 'getting old'. No fever, no recent illness, no leg pain or swelling. He has hypertension for 15 years, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes for 8 years, and had a 'small heart attack' 6 years ago (inferior STEMI, managed medically, did not have stenting). He takes aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril, metoprolol, and metformin regularly. Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (40 pack-year history). Lives with wife in single-storey home. Wife is very concerned as he has deteriorated dramatically over 4 hours.
past_medical_history: Inferior STEMI 6 years ago (right coronary artery territory, managed conservatively, no PCI performed at the time)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 8 years (HbA1c 7.2% last month)
Former smoker (quit 10 years ago, 40 pack-year history)

vital_signs.spo2: 88% on room air, 93% on 15L O2 via non-rebreather mask

examination_findings.general: Elderly man in severe respiratory distress, sitting bolt upright, visibly anxious, coughing pink frothy sputum. Diaphoretic, pale. GCS 15.
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated 8cm above sternal angle with prominent V waves visible (giant V waves). Apex beat displaced laterally to anterior axillary line (6th intercostal space). Hyperdynamic, diffuse apex impulse. Tachycardic at 118 bpm, irregularly irregular rhythm (new-onset atrial fibrillation). Loud apical pansystolic murmur grade 4/6, radiating to axilla and back (left infrascapular area). Third heart sound (S3 gallop) audible. No diastolic murmur. Carotid pulses weak, no bruits. Bilateral crackles throughout lung fields to apices. Peripheral pulses present but weak. Peripheral oedema 2+ to mid-shins bilaterally.
examination_findings.respiratory: Tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles. Widespread coarse crackles and wheeze throughout both lung fields, heard to apices. Dullness to percussion at both bases. Reduced air entry bilaterally.
examination_findings.abdominal: Soft, mild hepatomegaly (liver edge 3cm below costal margin, smooth, tender). No ascites detected on examination but limited by patient unable to lie flat.

investigations.ecg: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, rate 118 bpm. No P waves visible, irregularly irregular QRS rhythm. Pathological Q waves in leads II, III, aVF (old inferior MI). No acute ST elevation or depression. Left atrial enlargement pattern (biphasic P waves in V1 would be seen if in sinus rhythm - suggested by left atrial dilatation on echo). QRS duration 106ms.
investigations.troponin: High-sensitivity troponin I: 287 ng/L at presentation (reference <14 ng/L), repeat 3 hours later: 412 ng/L - elevated and rising trend suggesting acute myocardial injury (likely small re-infarct with papillary muscle rupture, or ischaemia related to severe MR and pulmonary oedema).

other.fbc: Hb 118 g/L (mild anaemia), WCC 13.4 x10^9/L (stress leucocytosis), platelets 243 x10^9/L
other.uec: Sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 95 micromol/L - acute rise suggesting cardiorenal syndrome), eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m² (was 68 last month), urea 9.8 mmol/L
other.bnp: 3,847 pg/mL (reference <100 pg/mL) - markedly elevated indicating severe heart failure
other.chest_xray: Marked cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.64). Bilateral perihilar alveolar infiltrates ('bat wing' appearance). Kerley B lines visible peripherally. Bilateral pleural effusions (right larger than left, blunting of costophrenic angles). Upper lobe blood diversion. Findings consistent with acute pulmonary oedema.
other.transthoracic_echocardiogram: Severe mitral regurgitation with broad, eccentric posteriorly directed jet (reaching posterior wall of left atrium). Flail posterior mitral leaflet - P2 scallop with ruptured chordae tendineae, prolapsing into left atrium during systole. Effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA) 0.52 cm² (severe MR defined as ≥0.40 cm²). Regurgitant volume 78 mL per beat. Left atrium severely dilated (volume index 52 mL/m²). Left ventricle dilated (LVEDD 6.2cm) with moderate LV dysfunction (LVEF 38%). Inferior and inferolateral wall hypokinesis (old infarct territory). Moderate-severe pulmonary hypertension (estimated PA systolic pressure 58 mmHg based on TR jet velocity). Right ventricle mildly dilated with borderline function. No pericardial effusion.
other.transoesophageal_echocardiogram: Confirms flail P2 scallop of posterior mitral leaflet with complete rupture of chordae tendineae to posteromedial papillary muscle. Torrential mitral regurgitation. Left atrial thrombus excluded (important pre-cardioversion if AF to be acutely treated). Mitral valve annulus dilated (4.2cm). Anterior leaflet normal.
other.coronary_angiography: Right coronary artery (RCA) 100% occluded proximally (chronic total occlusion from previous MI 6 years ago, extensive collaterals from LAD). Left anterior descending artery mild diffuse disease (30-40% stenoses, non-obstructive). Left circumflex 60% stenosis mid-vessel (likely culprit for recent ischaemia causing papillary muscle rupture). Dominant right coronary system. Posteromedial papillary muscle supplied by RCA territory (chronic occlusion) likely rendered vulnerable to ischaemia.

immediate_life_saving_management: High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask at 15L/min to target SpO2 >94% (acute pulmonary oedema)
Sit patient upright at 90 degrees (reduces venous return, improves dyspnoea)
Continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator pads attached (AF with RVR, risk of deterioration)
Frusemide 80mg IV bolus stat (double usual oral dose for acute pulmonary oedema), repeat 80mg IV in 30 minutes if no response, prepare for IV infusion if refractory
Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) infusion 10 micrograms/min IV titrated up by 10-20 micrograms/min every 5 minutes (reduce preload and afterload, target systolic BP >100 mmHg). MAX 200 micrograms/min.
Morphine 2.5-5mg IV (reduces anxiety, venodilation, respiratory distress)
URGENT cardiothoracic surgery consult - acute severe MR with haemodynamic compromise requires emergency surgical assessment

rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.name: Metoprolol IV (already on oral metoprolol)
rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.frequency: Can repeat every 5 minutes up to total 15mg
rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.indication: Rate control in AF with RVR (target HR <110 bpm acutely). Caution with severe MR and pulmonary oedema - may worsen haemodynamics.

rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.name: Digoxin IV (alternative if beta-blocker contraindicated)
rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.dose: 500 micrograms IV loading dose over 30 minutes, then 250 micrograms IV 6 hours later
rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.indication: Rate control AF + heart failure. Less negative inotropy than beta-blocker but slower onset.

rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.name: Amiodarone IV (if haemodynamically unstable)
rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.dose: 300mg IV over 60 minutes, then 900mg IV over 24 hours
rate_control_for_atrial_fibrillation.indication: Rate and rhythm control if patient deteriorating despite initial measures. Consideration for DC cardioversion if remains unstable.

anticoagulation_for_new_af.name: Heparin infusion (unfractionated heparin)
anticoagulation_for_new_af.dose: 80 units/kg IV bolus (approximately 5,600 units for 70kg), then 18 units/kg/hour infusion (approximately 1,260 units/hour)
anticoagulation_for_new_af.indication: Anticoagulation for new-onset AF + planned cardioversion + pre-operative bridging. Target aPTT 60-80 seconds. TOE showed no LA thrombus but new AF <48 hours still requires anticoagulation.

inotropic_support_if_cardiogenic_shock: If systolic BP <90 mmHg despite diuresis and vasodilators, consider ICU transfer for inotropic support
Dobutamine 2.5-5 micrograms/kg/min IV infusion (positive inotropy without excessive vasoconstriction)
Avoid high-dose vasopressors (noradrenaline, adrenaline) as increase afterload and worsen MR
Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) consideration if refractory shock - reduces afterload during systole (augments forward flow), increases diastolic BP (coronary perfusion). Bridge to surgery.
urgent_surgical_intervention: Emergency mitral valve surgery indicated - acute severe MR with pulmonary oedema and haemodynamic compromise (Class I indication, ESC/AHA guidelines)
Timing: Urgent surgery within 24-48 hours (not delayed surgery) - patient in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, medically stabilizing is bridge to surgery

Surgical options: (1) Mitral valve repair preferred if technically feasible (flail leaflet, ruptured chordae - often repairable with chordal replacement and annuloplasty), (2) Mitral valve replacement if repair not possible (mechanical or bioprosthetic valve)

Choice of valve prosthesis: Age 72 - bioprosthetic valve preferred (avoid lifelong warfarin, lower bleeding risk, patient likely has 10-15 year life expectancy, bioprosthetic valve durability 10-15 years suitable). Mechanical valve if patient preference and good anticoagulation control expected.
Concurrent CABG consideration: LCx 60% stenosis may warrant grafting if patient going to surgery anyway (single vessel, intermediate stenosis - likely will graft during MV surgery)

post_operative_management.name: Perindopril
post_operative_management.indication: ACE inhibitor for LV dysfunction (LVEF 38%), cardiac remodelling

post_operative_management.name: Metoprolol
post_operative_management.frequency: BD (restart post-op, may need uptitration for AF rate control)
post_operative_management.indication: Beta-blocker for CAD, LV dysfunction, AF rate control

post_operative_management.name: Frusemide
post_operative_management.indication: Loop diuretic for volume management, prevent pulmonary oedema recurrence

post_operative_management.name: Warfarin OR Apixaban (if AF persists)
post_operative_management.indication: Anticoagulation for AF (CHA2DS2-VASc score 5: age >75, hypertension, diabetes, heart failure = high stroke risk). If bioprosthetic MV: warfarin x3 months post-op, then switch to DOAC if AF persists. If mechanical MV: lifelong warfarin (DOACs contraindicated).

follow_up_and_monitoring: ICU/CCU post-operative care with haemodynamic monitoring
Daily echocardiogram post-surgery to assess valve function, LV function, pericardial effusion
Cardiac rehabilitation referral post-discharge (6-8 weeks post-op)
Repeat echocardiogram at 1 month, 3 months, then annually to assess prosthetic valve function and LV recovery
Anticoagulation clinic if on warfarin (INR monitoring)
Diabetes optimization (HbA1c target <7% for secondary prevention CAD)
If AF persists: rhythm control strategy discussion (amiodarone or DC cardioversion once stable post-op)

marking_criteria.item: Recognizes acute severe mitral regurgitation: sudden pulmonary oedema, loud pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla, giant V waves in JVP
Identifies flail leaflet with ruptured chordae tendineae on echocardiogram - acute mechanical complication post-MI (ischaemic papillary muscle rupture)
Differentiates acute MR (flail leaflet, sudden onset, pulmonary oedema, small LA on echo relative to severity) from chronic MR (gradual onset, dilated LA, compensated)
Immediate management of acute pulmonary oedema: oxygen, upright position, IV frusemide, GTN infusion, morphine
Manages new-onset AF with RVR: rate control (beta-blocker IV or digoxin), anticoagulation (heparin infusion), monitors for haemodynamic instability
Recognizes URGENT surgical indication: acute severe MR with pulmonary oedema and haemodynamic compromise = emergency surgery within 24-48 hours
Discusses surgical options: MV repair preferred (if feasible), MV replacement if not. Bioprosthetic vs mechanical valve choice appropriate for age 72.
Understands pathophysiology: ischaemic papillary muscle rupture (posteromedial PM supplied by RCA - chronic occlusion + acute LCx ischaemia caused critical ischaemia)
Post-operative anticoagulation plan: warfarin x3 months for bioprosthetic MV, then DOAC if AF persists. Warfarin lifelong if mechanical MV.
Avoids harmful interventions: does NOT delay surgery for 'medical optimization' in acute severe MR with pulmonary oedema (surgery is definitive treatment)

learning_objectives: Differentiate acute severe MR (flail leaflet, sudden pulmonary oedema, small LA) from chronic MR (dilated LA, gradual symptoms, compensated haemodynamics)
Recognize ischaemic papillary muscle rupture as mechanical complication of MI (posteromedial PM vulnerable - RCA territory)
Identify echocardiographic features of severe MR: EROA ≥0.4 cm², regurgitant volume >60 mL, flail leaflet, giant V waves on JVP
Manage acute pulmonary oedema: oxygen, diuretics, vasodilators (GTN), morphine, upright positioning
Understand URGENT surgical indications in acute MR: pulmonary oedema, haemodynamic compromise, cardiogenic shock = surgery within 24-48 hours
Differentiate bioprosthetic vs mechanical valve choice based on age, anticoagulation tolerance, life expectancy
Manage new-onset atrial fibrillation: rate control, anticoagulation (heparin bridge), assess for cardioversion vs rate control strategy
