patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Left calf pain and swelling for 3 days, worse today, unable to weight-bear comfortably
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Sandra is a 58-year-old woman presenting with 3 days of progressive left calf pain and swelling. The pain started gradually on Monday morning after a long-haul flight from London to Melbourne (24 hours total travel time including layover in Singapore, landed Sunday night). She was cramped in economy class and 'hardly moved' during the flights due to a middle seat. Initial pain was mild, described as a deep ache in the left calf, which she attributed to 'sitting too long'. Over the past 3 days, the pain has worsened from 3/10 to 7/10 severity, now constant and throbbing. The left calf has become noticeably swollen compared to the right - her shoe feels tight and she can see the swelling. The calf is also warmer to touch and tender when she presses on it. Pain worsens with walking or standing, partially relieved by leg elevation and rest. No pain in the thigh or groin. No shortness of breath, no chest pain, no haemoptysis. No recent trauma to the leg. No fever or rigors. She returned to work on Tuesday (office job, sedentary) but has found it increasingly difficult to walk from car park to office. Today (Thursday) she decided to seek medical attention as the swelling is visibly worse and she is concerned. She has never had leg swelling or clots before. No recent surgery (last surgery was hysterectomy 8 years ago for fibroids). She takes hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms (started 3 months ago after hot flushes became intolerable). No oral contraceptive use. Non-smoker, social alcohol (2-3 glasses wine per week). No family history of clotting disorders - her sister had a DVT after hip replacement surgery age 65, but no unprovoked clots in family. No personal history of cancer. Recent health has been good - went to UK for holiday, felt well throughout trip until leg symptoms started on flight home.
past_medical_history: Hysterectomy for uterine fibroids 8 years ago (ovaries preserved)

current_medications.name: Estradiol (hormone replacement therapy)
current_medications.duration: Started 3 months ago for menopausal symptoms

examination_findings.general: Well-appearing middle-aged woman, walking with slight limp favouring left leg, otherwise no acute distress
examination_findings.left_lower_limb: Left calf visibly swollen compared to right. Skin warm to touch over posterior calf, no erythema or skin changes. Tenderness on palpation over deep posterior calf muscles (medial gastrocnemius). No palpable cord. Left calf circumference 38cm (measured 10cm below tibial tuberosity), right calf 34cm - difference of 4cm. Mild pitting oedema left ankle (1+). Homan's sign positive but non-specific. Peripheral pulses normal and equal bilaterally (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable). No varicosities visible. No skin ulcers.
examination_findings.right_lower_limb: Normal appearance, no swelling, no tenderness, calf circumference 34cm
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Regular rate and rhythm.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no tachypnoea, no signs of pulmonary embolism clinically
examination_findings.wells_score_calculation: Clinical assessment for Wells DVT score: (1) Active cancer (treatment within 6 months or palliative) = NO = 0 points, (2) Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of lower limb = NO = 0 points, (3) Recently bedridden >3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks = NO = 0 points, (4) Localized tenderness along deep venous system = YES = 1 point, (5) Entire leg swollen = NO = 0 points, (6) Calf swelling >3cm compared to asymptomatic leg (measured 10cm below tibial tuberosity) = YES (4cm difference) = 1 point, (7) Pitting oedema (confined to symptomatic leg) = YES = 1 point, (8) Collateral superficial veins (non-varicose) = NO = 0 points, (9) Previously documented DVT = NO = 0 points, (10) Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT = NO = 0 points. TOTAL WELLS SCORE = 3 points (MODERATE PROBABILITY)

investigations.ecg: Sinus rhythm 78 bpm. Normal axis. No evidence of right heart strain (no S1Q3T3 pattern, no RBBB, no RV strain pattern). ECG performed to exclude PE given risk factors.
investigations.d_dimer: D-dimer (ELISA method): 2,847 nanograms/mL (reference <500 nanograms/mL) - markedly elevated, supporting diagnosis of acute thrombosis. D-dimer >4x upper limit of normal correlates with higher clot burden.

other.fbc: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L, platelets 312 x10^9/L - normal, no thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis
other.uec: Sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 72 micromol/L (eGFR >90) - normal renal function
other.coagulation_studies: PT 12.4 seconds (INR 1.0), aPTT 28 seconds - normal baseline coagulation
other.duplex_ultrasound_left_leg: Non-compressible left popliteal vein and posterior tibial vein on ultrasound compression. Echogenic thrombus visible in popliteal vein extending to proximal calf veins (posterior tibial and peroneal veins). Absence of flow on Doppler. Findings diagnostic of acute left lower limb deep vein thrombosis (popliteal + proximal calf DVT - proximal DVT). Common femoral and superficial femoral veins patent with normal compressibility. No Baker's cyst. No superficial thrombophlebitis.
other.chest_xray: Normal cardiac silhouette, clear lung fields, no pleural effusion, no signs of pulmonary infarction (precautionary CXR given risk factors - normal, no PE suggested)
other.thrombophilia_screen_sent: Testing for: Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Protein C, Protein S, Antithrombin III, Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I). NOTE: Acute phase reactants affected by active clot - Protein C/S/AT may be falsely low. Repeat testing in 3-6 months if unprovoked DVT. Results pending (takes 1-2 weeks).

immediate_anticoagulation.name: Apixaban (DOAC - direct oral anticoagulant, first-line in Australia for DVT/PE)
immediate_anticoagulation.dose: 10mg BD for 7 days, then 5mg BD ongoing
immediate_anticoagulation.frequency: Initial: 10mg BD x7 days, then 5mg BD
immediate_anticoagulation.indication: Acute proximal DVT treatment. Apixaban preferred in Australia: no bridging required (unlike warfarin), rapid onset (within hours), predictable pharmacokinetics, no INR monitoring. Alternatives: rivaroxaban 15mg BD x21 days then 20mg daily, OR enoxaparin + warfarin bridge (if DOAC contraindicated).

immediate_anticoagulation.name: Enoxaparin (if DOAC contraindicated - e.g., severe renal impairment eGFR <15, mechanical heart valve, antiphospholipid syndrome)
immediate_anticoagulation.dose: 1.5mg/kg subcutaneous once daily (e.g., 100mg SC daily for 70kg patient), OR 1mg/kg BD
immediate_anticoagulation.frequency: Daily for minimum 5 days AND until INR therapeutic (≥2.0) x2 consecutive days
immediate_anticoagulation.indication: LMWH bridge to warfarin if DOAC unsuitable. Continue enoxaparin overlapping with warfarin until INR 2-3 for 48 hours.

immediate_anticoagulation.name: Warfarin (if DOAC contraindicated)
immediate_anticoagulation.dose: Initial 5mg (elderly or frail: 2.5-3mg), then adjust to INR
immediate_anticoagulation.frequency: Daily (start on day 1 overlapping with enoxaparin)
immediate_anticoagulation.indication: Target INR 2-3. Check INR every 2-3 days during initiation, then weekly, then monthly when stable. Requires dietary vitamin K consistency, multiple drug interactions (avoid NSAIDs).

provoked_vs_unprovoked_dvt_classificatio: This DVT is PROVOKED (secondary DVT) due to: (1) Long-haul flight >6 hours with immobility (strong transient risk factor), (2) Hormone replacement therapy (oestrogen increases VTE risk 2-3 fold - ongoing risk factor). PROVOKED DVT = lower recurrence risk (3-5% per year off anticoagulation) compared to unprovoked (10-15% per year).

Provoking factors identified: Long-haul economy flight (24 hours travel, minimal movement) + HRT (estradiol 1mg daily x3 months). Sister's DVT was provoked (post-hip replacement surgery) - not strong family history of thrombophilia.

STOP hormone replacement therapy immediately - oestrogen-containing HRT contraindicated after VTE. Discuss alternative management for menopausal symptoms (non-hormonal options: venlafaxine, SSRIs, clonidine for hot flushes).
duration_of_anticoagulation: Provoked DVT by major transient risk factor (long-haul flight) + ongoing risk factor (HRT now ceased) = MINIMUM 3 months anticoagulation (standard duration)
ESC/ISTH guidelines: Provoked DVT = 3 months anticoagulation, then STOP if provoking factor removed (HRT ceased, no further long flights planned)

Reassess at 3 months: If HRT ceased, no further risk factors, thrombophilia screen negative → STOP anticoagulation. If thrombophilia found (Factor V Leiden heterozygous, Prothrombin mutation) → consider extended anticoagulation but provoked DVT still allows cessation in many cases.
If unprovoked or recurrent VTE → lifelong anticoagulation recommended (>3 months, often indefinite)

Extended anticoagulation considerations: (1) Extensive clot burden (popliteal + calf veins = moderate burden, not extensive), (2) Thrombophilia (pending), (3) Patient preference and bleeding risk (HAS-BLED score)
additional_acute_management: Leg elevation when sitting/lying (reduce oedema and pain)
Ambulation encouraged (early mobilization does NOT increase PE risk, reduces post-thrombotic syndrome)

Compression stockings (graduated compression 30-40 mmHg) - NOT acutely (wait until swelling reduced), then for 2 years to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome (conflicting evidence - SOX trial showed no benefit, but still recommended in Australian practice)
Adequate analgesia: paracetamol 1g QID regular, avoid NSAIDs (increase bleeding risk on anticoagulation)
No bed rest required - mobilize as tolerated (old teaching was bed rest, now known to be harmful)
monitoring_on_anticoagulation: DOAC (apixaban): No routine monitoring required. Check renal function (eGFR) at baseline, 3 months, then annually (dose adjustment if eGFR <30: apixaban 2.5mg BD). FBC to monitor for bleeding (Hb drop). LFTs at baseline (apixaban hepatically cleared).

Warfarin (if used): INR monitoring every 2-3 days initially, then weekly until stable, then every 4 weeks. Target INR 2-3. More frequent monitoring if intercurrent illness, new medications (many interactions).

Clinical monitoring: Assess for extension of DVT (worsening pain, swelling ascending to thigh), PE symptoms (chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis), bleeding complications (bruising, haematuria, melaena, GI bleeding)
pe_exclusion_and_follow_up: No clinical features of PE currently (no dyspnoea, chest pain, haemoptysis, tachycardia, hypoxia). CXR normal. ECG no RV strain. If PE symptoms develop: CTPA (CT pulmonary angiogram) to diagnose PE.
Safety netting: Advise patient to return immediately if develops: breathlessness, chest pain (especially pleuritic), coughing blood, syncope, severe leg pain/swelling extending to thigh.
Repeat ultrasound at 1 week to assess clot progression vs stability (ensure anticoagulation effective). Some centres do this routinely, others only if symptoms worsen.
Thrombophilia screen results review in 2 weeks (repeat at 3-6 months if done during acute phase as results can be affected by active clot and anticoagulation)
Haematology clinic referral for anticoagulation management and duration decision at 3 months
long_term_management: Cease HRT permanently (absolute contraindication after VTE)

Non-hormonal management menopausal symptoms: Venlafaxine 37.5-75mg daily (PBS 2622K), OR paroxetine 12.5-25mg daily, OR clonidine 25-50 micrograms BD. Lifestyle: cool environment, layered clothing, avoid triggers (caffeine, alcohol, spicy food).

VTE prevention for future travel: (1) Aisle seat, (2) Calf exercises every 30 minutes, (3) Adequate hydration, (4) Avoid alcohol (dehydrating), (5) Compression stockings (knee-high 15-20 mmHg), (6) Consider LMWH prophylaxis if high-risk travel (flight >8 hours + additional risk factors - not needed once therapeutic anticoagulation ceased after 3 months).
Repeat duplex ultrasound at 3-6 months to assess for residual clot (post-thrombotic syndrome risk correlates with residual thrombus)
Annual review: Assess for post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulceration - occurs in 20-50% of DVT patients despite anticoagulation)

marking_criteria.item: Calculates Wells DVT score correctly (3 points = moderate probability): calf tenderness, >3cm swelling, pitting oedema
Interprets investigations appropriately: elevated D-dimer (>4x ULN) + moderate Wells score = proceed to imaging (duplex ultrasound diagnostic)
Identifies proximal DVT (popliteal + proximal calf veins) on ultrasound - requires anticoagulation (vs distal calf DVT which may be monitored)
Classifies DVT as PROVOKED: long-haul flight (major transient risk factor) + HRT (ongoing risk factor now removed)
Immediate anticoagulation: DOAC first-line (apixaban 10mg BD x7 days, then 5mg BD) OR enoxaparin bridging to warfarin if DOAC contraindicated
Stops hormone replacement therapy immediately (absolute contraindication after VTE) and discusses non-hormonal alternatives for menopausal symptoms
Determines anticoagulation duration: 3 months minimum for provoked DVT (transient + ongoing risk factors now removed), reassess at 3 months with thrombophilia results
Safety netting for PE: educates patient on warning symptoms (dyspnoea, chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope) and when to return urgently
Arranges thrombophilia screening appropriately (sent acutely but repeat in 3-6 months if results abnormal - acute phase affects Protein C/S/AT levels)
Long-term VTE prevention counselling: travel advice, compression stockings, hydration, calf exercises for future flights

learning_objectives: Apply Wells DVT score for pre-test probability assessment: <1 point (low), 1-2 points (moderate), ≥3 points (high probability)
Interpret D-dimer appropriately: elevated D-dimer + moderate-high Wells score → imaging (ultrasound). Low Wells + negative D-dimer → DVT excluded (no imaging needed).
Differentiate proximal DVT (requires anticoagulation: popliteal, femoral, iliac veins) from distal calf DVT (may monitor vs anticoagulate based on symptoms and risk factors)
Classify DVT as provoked vs unprovoked: provoked = 3 months anticoagulation, unprovoked = consider extended/lifelong anticoagulation
Prescribe DOAC first-line for DVT/PE in Australia: apixaban or rivaroxaban (no bridging, rapid onset, predictable, no INR monitoring)
Recognize HRT as VTE risk factor (2-3 fold increase) and permanent contraindication after VTE event
Understand thrombophilia testing limitations: acute phase and anticoagulation affect results (Protein C/S/AT falsely low) - repeat testing at 3-6 months if initially abnormal

osces.title: Supraventricular Tachycardia - Adenosine Administration
learningObjectives: Recognize narrow complex tachycardia on 12-lead ECG and differentiate from ventricular tachycardia using QRS duration <120ms
Perform vagal manoeuvres correctly (Valsalva manoeuvre, carotid sinus massage) as first-line therapy for SVT termination
Administer adenosine safely using rapid IV push technique (6mg → 12mg → 12mg escalation protocol)
Monitor for transient AV block and asystole during adenosine administration with continuous ECG recording
Recognize contraindications to adenosine (asthma, second/third-degree AV block, concurrent dipyridamole therapy)
Counsel patient on expected adverse effects (chest tightness, flushing, dyspnoea lasting 10-20 seconds)
Arrange appropriate follow-up with cardiology for ablation if recurrent SVT episodes documented
osces.clinicalScenario: You are the Emergency Registrar at Royal North Shore Hospital. A 32-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations that started 45 minutes ago while exercising at the gym. She describes a rapid, regular heartbeat with associated light-headedness but no chest pain or syncope. She has had 3 similar episodes over the past year, each terminating spontaneously within 2 hours. No known cardiac history. Medications: nil. No drug or alcohol use. Vital signs: HR 184 bpm (regular), BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, afebrile. She appears anxious but comfortable. 12-lead ECG shows narrow complex tachycardia at 184 bpm with regular rhythm, QRS duration 88ms, no visible P waves. The nursing staff have established IV access (18G left ACF) and attached continuous cardiac monitoring. The patient has attempted to hold her breath and bear down without success. Perform the appropriate management for this patient's supraventricular tachycardia.

patientDetails.presentingComplaint: Palpitations for 45 minutes, sudden onset during exercise
patientDetails.relevantHistory: 3 previous episodes of palpitations in past 12 months, all self-terminated within 2 hours. No structural heart disease, no family history of sudden cardiac death. Nulliparous, regular menstrual cycles, not pregnant (LMP 2 weeks ago).
patientDetails.medications: Nil regular medications. No over-the-counter supplements or herbal preparations.

investigations.ecg: 12-lead ECG: narrow complex tachycardia, rate 184 bpm, regular rhythm, QRS duration 88ms, no visible P waves, no ST segment changes, QT interval difficult to measure at this rate. Likely AVNRT (atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia) vs AVRT (atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia). No delta waves visible.
investigations.bloods: Venous blood sample sent: Troponin I, UEC, FBC, TFTs, magnesium pending
investigations.imaging: Portable chest X-ray ordered (not yet performed)

requiredActions.action: Confirm haemodynamic stability and assess for features requiring immediate DC cardioversion
requiredActions.details: Ask about chest pain, dyspnoea, altered consciousness. Assess BP, perfusion, conscious state. Document patient is haemodynamically stable (no shock, no pulmonary oedema, no ongoing chest pain, GCS 15). If unstable features present, synchronized DC cardioversion would be indicated immediately.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Unstable features = systolic BP <90 mmHg, altered mental state, chest pain suggestive of ischaemia, heart failure. This patient has none of these (BP 118/76, GCS 15, no chest pain).

requiredActions.action: Perform vagal manoeuvres as first-line therapy for SVT termination
requiredActions.details: Explain Valsalva manoeuvre to patient: 'I'd like you to take a deep breath and bear down hard, as if straining on the toilet, for 15 seconds while I watch the monitor.' Position patient semi-recumbent (45 degrees). Observe ECG monitor during manoeuvre. If unsuccessful, attempt modified Valsalva (supine positioning with leg raise immediately after strain). If Valsalva fails, consider carotid sinus massage: palpate carotid pulse, auscultate for bruit (contraindicated if bruit present), apply firm pressure to right carotid sinus for 5 seconds while monitoring ECG.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Valsalva manoeuvre success rate 20-40% for SVT termination. Carotid sinus massage contraindications: carotid bruit, previous TIA/CVA, age >65 years (relative). Never perform bilateral carotid massage simultaneously.

requiredActions.action: Prepare adenosine for IV administration if vagal manoeuvres unsuccessful
requiredActions.details: Check contraindications to adenosine: asthma/COPD with active bronchospasm, second or third-degree AV block, concurrent dipyridamole, sick sinus syndrome, long QT syndrome, recent cardiac transplant. Confirm IV access is patent (18G or larger, preferably ACF or more proximal). Draw up adenosine 6mg in 10mL syringe, prepare 20mL normal saline flush in second syringe. Attach both syringes to 3-way tap on IV cannula. Warn patient: 'This medication will cause temporary chest tightness, flushing and a sense of breathlessness for about 10-20 seconds. This is expected and will pass quickly.'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Adenosine half-life <10 seconds. Must use rapid IV push into large proximal vein (ACF or larger) followed immediately by rapid saline flush. Smaller veins (hand, wrist) result in drug metabolism before reaching heart.

requiredActions.action: Administer adenosine 6mg rapid IV push with continuous ECG monitoring
requiredActions.details: Ensure ECG monitor is recording. Inform patient 'I'm giving the medication now.' Inject adenosine 6mg as rapid IV push over 1-2 seconds into ACF cannula. Immediately follow with 20mL normal saline rapid flush (pushed over 2-3 seconds). Elevate arm briefly to speed drug delivery to central circulation. Watch ECG monitor closely for: (1) transient AV block (expected), (2) termination of SVT with return to sinus rhythm, (3) bradycardia or brief asystole (usually <10 seconds). Document ECG rhythm strip during and after adenosine administration.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Adenosine PBS listed: unrestricted benefit. Common adverse effects (90% patients): chest discomfort, dyspnoea, flushing, sense of impending doom - all last 10-20 seconds due to short half-life. Serious adverse effect: transient asystole (usually 3-10 seconds, may require brief CPR if >15 seconds).

requiredActions.action: If 6mg adenosine unsuccessful, administer 12mg dose after 2 minutes
requiredActions.details: If SVT persists after 6mg dose and adverse effects have resolved (wait 1-2 minutes), prepare 12mg adenosine dose. Repeat same rapid IV push technique: 12mg adenosine over 1-2 seconds, immediate 20mL saline flush, elevate arm. Monitor ECG continuously. If 12mg unsuccessful, may give third dose of 12mg after another 2 minutes (total maximum 30mg cumulative dose in guidelines, though most protocols use 6-12-12mg sequence).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Success rate for SVT termination: 60% with 6mg, 90-95% with 12mg dose. If third dose (12mg) fails, consider alternative diagnoses (atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia) or alternative therapy (verapamil 2.5-5mg IV, beta-blocker).

requiredActions.action: Confirm SVT termination and monitor for recurrence
requiredActions.details: After successful cardioversion, obtain immediate 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm. Document rate, rhythm, PR interval, presence of delta waves (Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome). Observe patient on continuous cardiac monitoring for 2 hours post-cardioversion to detect early recurrence. Repeat vital signs: HR, BP, SpO2. Ask about resolution of palpitations. Check for adverse effects from adenosine (prolonged chest pain, sustained bradycardia).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Post-cardioversion 12-lead ECG critical for detecting pre-excitation (short PR <120ms, delta wave) suggesting WPW syndrome. If WPW present, avoid AV nodal blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) in future as they may precipitate VF if atrial fibrillation occurs.

requiredActions.action: Arrange cardiology follow-up and discuss definitive management options
requiredActions.details: Explain to patient: 'You've had an episode of supraventricular tachycardia, a rapid heart rhythm that starts in the upper chambers of your heart. The adenosine stopped this episode, but with 4 episodes in the past year, we should arrange specialist follow-up.' Discuss options: (1) Conservative - manage acute episodes with adenosine in ED, (2) Prophylactic medication (beta-blocker, verapamil, flecainide), (3) Catheter ablation (curative in >95% cases, low risk procedure). Refer to cardiology outpatient clinic for electrophysiology assessment. Provide written advice on vagal manoeuvres to attempt during future episodes before presenting to ED.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Catheter ablation first-line for recurrent symptomatic SVT (Class I recommendation, eTG). Success rate >95% for AVNRT, complication rate <1% (AV block requiring pacemaker 0.5-1%). Advise patient to avoid excessive caffeine, alcohol, other stimulants that may trigger SVT.

markingCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies narrow complex tachycardia on ECG (QRS <120ms) and distinguishes from ventricular tachycardia
Assesses haemodynamic stability (BP, consciousness, chest pain, heart failure) before proceeding with chemical cardioversion
Performs vagal manoeuvres appropriately (Valsalva technique explained correctly, carotid massage with bruit check)
Checks contraindications to adenosine (asthma, AV block, dipyridamole) before administration
Warns patient about expected adverse effects (chest tightness, flushing, dyspnoea lasting 10-20 seconds)
Administers adenosine using correct technique: 6mg rapid IV push into large vein (ACF) followed immediately by 20mL rapid saline flush
Maintains continuous ECG monitoring during adenosine administration and recognizes transient AV block as expected effect
Escalates to 12mg dose if 6mg unsuccessful, using same rapid push technique
Obtains post-cardioversion 12-lead ECG to check for delta waves (WPW syndrome) and documents sinus rhythm
Arranges cardiology follow-up for electrophysiology assessment and discusses ablation as definitive management
Communicates clearly with patient throughout procedure, explaining each step and providing reassurance

commonMistakes: Administering adenosine too slowly (must be rapid 1-2 second push, not slow infusion over 10-20 seconds)
Using small peripheral vein (hand, wrist) instead of large proximal vein (ACF) - drug metabolizes before reaching heart
Forgetting immediate saline flush after adenosine - drug must be flushed rapidly into central circulation
Not warning patient about expected adverse effects (chest tightness, flushing) - causes unnecessary alarm
Attempting DC cardioversion before vagal manoeuvres and adenosine in haemodynamically stable patient
Missing contraindications to adenosine (active asthma with wheeze, concurrent dipyridamole)
Not monitoring ECG continuously during adenosine administration - may miss brief asystole requiring intervention
Failing to obtain post-cardioversion ECG to check for WPW (delta wave, short PR interval)
Not arranging cardiology follow-up for recurrent SVT (4 episodes in 12 months = indication for ablation)
Administering verapamil or diltiazem if WPW present on post-cardioversion ECG (risk of VF if AF occurs)
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability (systolic BP <90 mmHg, altered consciousness, chest pain, pulmonary oedema) - requires immediate synchronized DC cardioversion, not adenosine
Irregular narrow complex tachycardia - suggests atrial fibrillation, NOT SVT; adenosine will not terminate AF (contraindicated in AF with pre-excitation)
Broad complex tachycardia - assume ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise; adenosine may be diagnostic but treatment is different
Active asthma with wheeze or bronchospasm - absolute contraindication to adenosine (may cause severe bronchospasm)
Delta wave on post-cardioversion ECG (WPW syndrome) - avoid AV nodal blockers (digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem) as may precipitate VF
Prolonged asystole >15 seconds after adenosine - may require brief chest compressions until sinus rhythm resumes
Concurrent dipyridamole therapy - potentiates adenosine effect, reduce dose to 3mg initial dose or avoid adenosine
Patient with cardiac transplant - denervated heart, extreme sensitivity to adenosine, reduce dose to 3mg or use alternative
Recurrent SVT immediately after cardioversion - may indicate atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia rather than AVNRT/AVRT
Chest pain persisting >5 minutes after adenosine - consider acute coronary syndrome, check troponin, obtain cardiology consult
safetyConsiderations: Always have resuscitation equipment immediately available (defibrillator, emergency drugs) when administering adenosine
Continuous ECG monitoring mandatory during adenosine administration - transient asystole occurs in 10-15% of patients
Never administer adenosine to patient with active bronchospasm (absolute contraindication) - may cause life-threatening bronchospasm
Use caution in elderly patients (>75 years) - higher risk of prolonged AV block, consider 3mg initial dose
Check drug interactions: dipyridamole (potentiates adenosine 4-fold), theophylline (antagonizes adenosine)
Ensure IV cannula is large bore (18G minimum) and in proximal vein (ACF or more proximal) - hand/wrist veins inadequate
Warn patient about impending sense of doom and chest tightness - prevents panic during expected adverse effects
Do not use adenosine in irregular narrow complex tachycardia (likely AF with rapid ventricular response) - will not cardiovert and may cause diagnostic confusion
Post-cardioversion monitoring for 2 hours minimum - early SVT recurrence occurs in 10-20% of patients
Document adenosine dose, time given, ECG response, and adverse effects in medical record for medico-legal purposes

osces.title: Infective Endocarditis - Modified Duke Criteria Application
learningObjectives: Recognize classic clinical presentation of infective endocarditis (fever, new murmur, embolic phenomena, immunological signs)
Apply Modified Duke Criteria systematically to diagnose definite vs possible vs rejected IE
Obtain appropriate blood cultures (3 sets from different sites, 1 hour apart, BEFORE antibiotics) for microbiological diagnosis
Arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and recognize indications for transoesophageal echo (TOE)
Identify complications requiring urgent cardiac surgical referral (heart failure, abscess, new heart block, large mobile vegetation)
Prescribe appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy (benzylpenicillin + gentamicin for Streptococcus viridans) with correct PBS authority
Recognize indications for early surgery (within 48 hours) in complicated IE vs medical management alone
osces.clinicalScenario: You are the Cardiology Registrar at St Vincent's Hospital Sydney. A 58-year-old man is referred by his GP with 3 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, and weight loss (4 kg). He had a dental extraction 6 weeks ago (no antibiotic prophylaxis given). Two days ago he developed sudden-onset left-sided weakness lasting 30 minutes, which resolved completely (query TIA). Past history: bicuspid aortic valve (known for 10 years, mild aortic regurgitation, not on anticoagulation). He denies IVDU. On examination: temperature 38.4°C, HR 98 bpm, BP 132/58 mmHg (wide pulse pressure), early diastolic murmur loudest at left sternal edge (new compared to previous mild AR murmur). Small painless macules on palms (Janeway lesions). Splinter haemorrhages in 3 fingernails. No Roth spots on fundoscopy. Chest clear, no peripheral oedema. Three blood culture sets taken in ED 1 hour apart have now grown Gram-positive cocci in chains (Streptococcus viridans) in all 6 bottles. Transthoracic echo shows bicuspid aortic valve with 8mm mobile vegetation on non-coronary cusp, moderate-severe aortic regurgitation (vena contracta 6mm, regurgitant volume 45mL). Apply the Modified Duke Criteria and manage this patient's infective endocarditis appropriately.

patientDetails.presentingComplaint: 3 weeks of intermittent fever (38-39°C), night sweats, weight loss 4kg, recent transient left-sided weakness (resolved)
patientDetails.relevantHistory: Bicuspid aortic valve diagnosed 10 years ago (mild AR on previous echo 2 years ago). Dental extraction 6 weeks ago (complex extraction, bleeding controlled, no antibiotic prophylaxis). No IVDU, no recent surgery. Recent transient neurological deficit (left arm weakness 30 min, complete resolution) 2 days ago - likely septic embolus to right MCA territory. Non-smoker, alcohol 10 standard drinks/week.
patientDetails.medications: Nil regular medications prior to admission. No anticoagulation despite AR (not indicated for AR alone).
patientDetails.allergies: Penicillin allergy DENIED. No known drug allergies.

vitalSigns.bloodPressure: 132/58 mmHg (wide pulse pressure - diastolic BP low due to AR)

investigations.bloodCultures: 3 sets (6 bottles total) taken in ED at 0800, 0900, 1000 hrs from different venepuncture sites. All 6 bottles positive for Gram-positive cocci in chains at 18 hours incubation. Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci in chains. Culture: Streptococcus viridans group (likely S. mitis or S. sanguinis - oral flora). Sensitivities pending (expected penicillin-sensitive).
investigations.bloods: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 11.1), Hb 108 g/L (normocytic anaemia of chronic disease), platelets 422 x10^9/L. CRP 142 mg/L, ESR 68 mm/hr. Creatinine 88 micromol/L (eGFR >60), normal UEC. Troponin I <0.01 (negative). LFTs normal. Urinalysis: microscopic haematuria (15 RBC/HPF), no casts.
investigations.ecg: Sinus rhythm 98 bpm, normal axis, normal PR interval 160ms (no heart block), normal QRS 92ms, no ST/T wave changes. QTc 424ms.
investigations.echo: TTE (transthoracic echo): Bicuspid aortic valve (fusion of right and left coronary cusps). Mobile echogenic mass 8mm x 6mm on non-coronary cusp (vegetation). Moderate-severe aortic regurgitation: vena contracta 6mm, regurgitant volume 45mL, PHT 280ms. LV mildly dilated (LVEDD 58mm), LV systolic function preserved (EF 58%). No pericardial effusion. No abscess visualized on TTE (limited sensitivity for abscess - TOE required for definitive assessment).
investigations.imaging: CXR: normal heart size, clear lung fields, no pulmonary oedema. CT brain (non-contrast, performed in ED for TIA): small acute infarct right corona radiata (5mm, consistent with embolic event). No haemorrhage.

requiredActions.action: Apply Modified Duke Criteria systematically to confirm diagnosis of definite infective endocarditis
requiredActions.details: Modified Duke Criteria: MAJOR criteria = (1) Positive blood cultures: typical microorganism (S. viridans) from 2 separate blood cultures, (2) Evidence of endocardial involvement: vegetation on echo (8mm mobile mass on aortic valve). MINOR criteria = (1) Predisposing heart condition (bicuspid aortic valve with AR), (2) Fever ≥38.0°C, (3) Vascular phenomena (embolic stroke - TIA now confirmed as small infarct on CT), (4) Immunological phenomena (Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages). DIAGNOSIS: 2 MAJOR criteria = DEFINITE INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS. Document this clearly in notes.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Definite IE = 2 major criteria OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor. This patient has 2 major (blood cultures + vegetation) + 4 minor (valve disease, fever, vascular phenomena, immunological signs). Possible IE = 1 major + 1-2 minor OR 3 minor. Rejected IE = alternative diagnosis or resolution with <4 days antibiotics.

requiredActions.action: Arrange urgent transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) to exclude perivalvular abscess and assess severity
requiredActions.details: Explain to patient: 'The transthoracic echo confirmed a vegetation on your aortic valve, but we need a more detailed study to check for complications like an abscess around the valve. This requires a probe passed down your oesophagus under light sedation.' Indications for TOE in this case: (1) TTE positive for vegetation but need to exclude abscess (TTE sensitivity 50% for abscess, TOE sensitivity 90%), (2) Prosthetic valve or complex native valve (bicuspid AV), (3) Assess surgical candidacy. Order urgent TOE (within 24 hours). NPO for 6 hours prior. Consent for procedure including risks (oesophageal perforation <0.1%, aspiration, sedation risks).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: TOE superior to TTE for: perivalvular abscess (90% vs 50% sensitivity), valve perforation, fistulae, prosthetic valve IE. Mandatory in: (1) prosthetic valve, (2) TTE non-diagnostic but high IE suspicion, (3) surgical planning. Contraindications: oesophageal pathology, severe cervical spine disease, uncooperative patient.

requiredActions.action: Commence appropriate antibiotic therapy for Streptococcus viridans endocarditis
requiredActions.details: Diagnosis: Native valve endocarditis, S. viridans (pending penicillin sensitivities). First-line therapy (eTG): Benzylpenicillin 2.4g (4 million units) IV 4-hourly PLUS gentamicin 3mg/kg IV daily for synergistic killing. Duration: Benzylpenicillin 4 weeks total, gentamicin 2 weeks only (nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity risk if prolonged). Write prescription: 'Benzylpenicillin 2.4g IV 4-hourly x 28 days (PBS authority required - phone approval 1800-888-333, streamlined authority for endocarditis)' and 'Gentamicin 240mg IV daily x 14 days (weight 80kg x 3mg/kg, adjust for renal function, TDM levels)'. If penicillin MIC ≤0.125 mg/L (likely), can use benzylpenicillin alone 2.4g 4-hourly without gentamicin (4 weeks).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: S. viridans typically penicillin-sensitive (MIC <0.125 mg/L in 90% cases). Benzylpenicillin PBS: authority required (streamlined for endocarditis). Gentamicin TDM: trough <1 mg/L (pre-dose), check Cr and trough every 3 days. Alternative if penicillin-allergic: vancomycin 25-30mg/kg IV BD (target trough 15-20 mg/L) x 4 weeks.

requiredActions.action: Assess for complications requiring urgent cardiac surgery referral
requiredActions.details: Review for surgical indications (ESC/AHA guidelines): (1) Heart failure due to severe AR - PRESENT (moderate-severe AR, but LV function preserved EF 58%, no pulmonary oedema = not acute decompensation yet), (2) Uncontrolled infection (persistent fever >7 days antibiotics, abscess) - not yet (only started antibiotics), (3) Prevention of embolism (vegetation >10mm, mobile, prior embolic event) - PRESENT (8mm vegetation + embolic stroke), (4) New heart block - ABSENT (PR interval normal). Contact cardiothoracic surgery for review. This patient has: (a) embolic event (stroke 2 days ago), (b) 8mm mobile vegetation (borderline size, >10mm = strong indication), (c) moderate-severe AR (not yet causing heart failure). Surgery likely required but timing depends on TOE findings (abscess?) and neurology input (stroke 2 days ago - risk of haemorrhagic transformation if anticoagulated on bypass).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Class I indications for early surgery (<48 hours): severe heart failure, uncontrolled infection (abscess, fistula), large vegetation >15mm with embolic event. Class IIa (reasonable): vegetation >10mm, recurrent emboli despite antibiotics, severe AR/MR with LV dysfunction. This patient has embolic stroke + 8mm vegetation + mod-severe AR = probable surgical candidate, but neurology consult needed (stroke 48 hours ago - bypass risk).

requiredActions.action: Request urgent neurology and neurosurgery consultation for embolic stroke management
requiredActions.details: Document stroke: 'Right corona radiata infarct 5mm on CT brain (embolic source - IE vegetation). Initial presentation TIA with left arm weakness (30 min, complete resolution), now asymptomatic neurologically.' Request neurology review: assess neurological deficits, risk of haemorrhagic transformation if anticoagulated for cardiopulmonary bypass, timing of safe surgery. Request neurosurgery assessment if vegetation size/mobility suggests high re-embolisation risk. Obtain MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging (more sensitive than CT for small embolic infarcts). Repeat neurological examination every 4 hours - monitor for deterioration (haemorrhagic transformation, new embolic event).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Embolic stroke complicates 20-40% of IE cases. Risk of haemorrhagic transformation highest in first 48-72 hours. Cardiac surgery with bypass requires systemic anticoagulation (heparin) - neurosurgery input critical. If surgery urgent (heart failure, abscess), may proceed despite recent stroke if <48 hours and no haemorrhage on imaging. If stroke >48 hours, ideally delay surgery 2-4 weeks unless life-threatening cardiac indication.

requiredActions.action: Arrange therapeutic drug monitoring for gentamicin and monitor renal function
requiredActions.details: Gentamicin once-daily dosing: 3mg/kg IV (patient weight 80kg = 240mg daily). Order TDM: trough level (pre-dose) at 48 hours, then every 3 days. Target trough <1 mg/L (reduce nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity). Check creatinine, urea, electrolytes every 3 days (gentamicin nephrotoxic). If eGFR declines >20% or trough >2 mg/L, withhold dose and recheck levels. Consider audiometry at baseline and week 2 (ototoxicity monitoring). Educate patient: 'The gentamicin antibiotic can affect kidneys and hearing, so we monitor blood tests closely. Report any hearing changes, ringing in ears, or dizziness.'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Gentamicin synergy with penicillin improves S. viridans killing (combination superior to monotherapy). However, ototoxicity (irreversible) and nephrotoxicity risks limit duration to 2 weeks maximum. If penicillin MIC low (≤0.125 mg/L), can omit gentamicin and use benzylpenicillin monotherapy 4 weeks (equally effective, less toxic).

requiredActions.action: Monitor clinical response to antibiotics and arrange weekly inflammatory markers
requiredActions.details: Clinical response expected: (1) Defervescence (fever resolution) within 3-7 days of appropriate antibiotics, (2) Improvement in inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR decline by 50% at 1 week). Order: Temperature chart 4-hourly, daily clinical examination (new murmur, heart failure signs, embolic phenomena), CRP and ESR weekly. Persistent fever >7 days despite antibiotics suggests: (a) wrong antibiotic (check sensitivities), (b) abscess formation (TOE), (c) metastatic infection (splenic abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis - check CT abdomen/pelvis), (d) drug fever. Repeat blood cultures at day 3-5 of antibiotics - should be negative (persistent positive cultures = uncontrolled infection, surgical indication).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Blood culture clearance critical prognostic indicator. Persistent bacteraemia at 48-72 hours despite appropriate antibiotics = uncontrolled infection, consider surgery. S. viridans IE typically responds rapidly (fever resolves 3-5 days). S. aureus IE more aggressive (abscess common, surgery rate 50%).

requiredActions.action: Arrange multidisciplinary team (MDT) review with cardiology, cardiac surgery, infectious diseases, neurology
requiredActions.details: IE management requires MDT input: (1) Cardiology - assess haemodynamics, heart failure, echocardiographic monitoring (repeat TTE at 2 weeks), (2) Cardiac surgery - surgical candidacy, timing of surgery (early vs late), (3) Infectious diseases - antibiotic duration, outpatient IV therapy (OPAT) planning for final 2 weeks, (4) Neurology - stroke management, timing of surgery post-stroke. Document MDT discussion in notes. Key decisions: (a) Medical vs surgical management, (b) Timing of surgery if indicated, (c) Antibiotic duration (4 vs 6 weeks), (d) Post-discharge follow-up (6-monthly echo surveillance, antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: IE MDT improves outcomes (mortality reduction 20% with systematic MDT approach). Weekly MDT meetings typical. Surgical consultation within 48 hours for all IE patients (surgery required in 40-50% of cases). Outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT) allows home IV antibiotics for final 2 weeks if clinically stable.

markingCriteria.criterion: Applies Modified Duke Criteria correctly and classifies as DEFINITE IE (2 major criteria: blood cultures + vegetation)
Identifies both major criteria (S. viridans in blood cultures, vegetation on echo) and at least 3 minor criteria (predisposing valve disease, fever, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena)
Arranges urgent TOE to exclude perivalvular abscess and assess surgical candidacy
Prescribes appropriate first-line antibiotic therapy: benzylpenicillin 2.4g IV 4-hourly x 4 weeks PLUS gentamicin 3mg/kg daily x 2 weeks
Recognizes PBS authority requirement for benzylpenicillin (streamlined authority for endocarditis)
Identifies complications requiring urgent surgical review (embolic stroke, 8mm mobile vegetation, moderate-severe AR)
Requests neurology and neurosurgery consultation for embolic stroke and surgical timing assessment
Arranges gentamicin TDM (trough levels every 3 days, target <1 mg/L) and renal function monitoring
Plans appropriate monitoring (repeat blood cultures day 3-5, weekly CRP/ESR, temperature chart, clinical examination for complications)
Arranges multidisciplinary team review (cardiology, cardiac surgery, infectious diseases, neurology) for management planning
Communicates diagnosis clearly to patient, explains antibiotic duration (4 weeks minimum), potential need for surgery, and embolic stroke complication

commonMistakes: Misclassifying as 'possible IE' when 2 major criteria clearly present (definite IE)
Starting antibiotics before obtaining adequate blood cultures (3 sets, 1 hour apart) - compromises microbiological diagnosis
Using inappropriate antibiotic (e.g., flucloxacillin for S. viridans - only for S. aureus)
Prescribing gentamicin for >2 weeks duration (ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity risk - limit to 14 days)
Not arranging TOE when TTE shows vegetation (TOE mandatory to exclude abscess, assess surgical candidacy)
Missing surgical indications (embolic stroke + mobile vegetation, moderate-severe AR)
Not requesting neurology input for embolic stroke (critical for surgical timing after recent stroke)
Failing to monitor gentamicin levels (trough every 3 days) - risk of toxicity
Not repeating blood cultures at 48-72 hours to confirm clearance (persistent bacteraemia = surgical indication)
Discharging patient on oral antibiotics (IV therapy mandatory for IE, minimum 4 weeks)
Not arranging MDT review (cardiac surgery input required within 48 hours for all IE cases)
Missing PBS authority requirement for high-dose benzylpenicillin (requires streamlined authority approval)
redFlags: Heart failure (dyspnoea, pulmonary oedema, elevated JVP) - indicates severe valve regurgitation, urgent surgical referral required
New heart block (prolonged PR interval >200ms, complete heart block) - suggests perivalvular abscess, requires urgent TOE and surgery
Persistent fever >7 days despite appropriate antibiotics - uncontrolled infection, likely abscess, surgical indication
Persistent positive blood cultures at 48-72 hours - uncontrolled bacteraemia, surgery required
Large vegetation >15mm on echo - high embolic risk (40-60% chance of embolisation), consider early surgery
Recurrent embolic events despite antibiotics - failure of medical therapy, urgent surgery indicated
Severe aortic or mitral regurgitation with LV dysfunction (EF <50%) - hemodynamic instability, urgent surgery within 24-48 hours
S. aureus endocarditis - aggressive organism, abscess rate 40%, surgery rate 50%, high mortality (25-30%)
Prosthetic valve endocarditis - surgery required in 60-80% of cases, medical therapy alone insufficient
Fungal endocarditis (Candida, Aspergillus) - medical therapy failure rate >90%, urgent surgery + prolonged antifungal therapy
Perivalvular abscess on TOE - surgical emergency (abscess rupture risk), surgery within 24 hours
Acute kidney injury (rising creatinine) - may be due to gentamicin toxicity (stop drug, check levels) or immune complex glomerulonephritis (IE complication)
safetyConsiderations: Always obtain blood cultures BEFORE starting antibiotics - delays compromise diagnostic yield by 35-50%
Gentamicin ototoxicity is irreversible - limit duration to 2 weeks, monitor audiometry, warn patient about tinnitus/hearing loss
TOE requires oesophageal intubation - NPO 6 hours, consent for procedure, risk of oesophageal perforation 0.03-0.1%
Cardiac surgery post-stroke requires systemic heparinization on bypass - risk of haemorrhagic transformation (neurosurgery input mandatory)
Empirical antibiotics for IE should cover Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Enterococcus if cultures negative - use vancomycin + gentamicin
Dental procedures require antibiotic prophylaxis AFTER IE episode for life - amoxycillin 2g PO 1 hour pre-procedure (PBS unrestricted)
Monitor for metastatic infections (splenic abscess 30%, vertebral osteomyelitis 10%, mycotic aneurysm 5%) - CT abdomen/pelvis if persistent fever
Outpatient IV antibiotics (OPAT) only suitable for stable patients with negative repeat cultures - requires PICC line, home nursing, weekly review
Post-IE surveillance: echocardiography at 2 weeks, 6 months, 12 months to detect recurrence or progressive valve damage
Educate patient on IE prevention: good dental hygiene, early treatment of infections, avoid IVDU, report fever >38°C for 48 hours post-discharge

osces.title: Cardiac Tamponade - Urgent Pericardiocentesis Indication
learningObjectives: Recognize Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP) and understand pathophysiology
Elicit pulsus paradoxus correctly using manual sphygmomanometer (>10mmHg drop in systolic BP with inspiration)
Interpret echocardiographic signs of tamponade (large pericardial effusion, RA/RV diastolic collapse, IVC plethora)
Differentiate urgent pericardiocentesis indications (haemodynamic compromise) from elective drainage (large asymptomatic effusion)
Perform emergency pericardiocentesis using subxiphoid approach with ECG and echo guidance
Manage complications of pericardiocentesis (coronary artery laceration, pneumothorax, ventricular perforation)
Recognize causes of pericardial effusion requiring specific therapy (malignancy, TB, uraemia, post-MI, autoimmune)
osces.clinicalScenario: You are the Cardiology Registrar at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital. A 62-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (on palliative chemotherapy) presents to ED with 4 days of progressive dyspnoea and chest discomfort. She describes breathlessness worse on lying flat, improved sitting forward. This morning she felt dizzy on standing and nearly fainted. On examination: distressed, sitting upright, unable to lie flat. Temperature 36.9°C, HR 118 bpm (sinus tachycardia), BP 88/64 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 72 mmHg), RR 24/min, SpO2 94% on 4L O2 via Hudson mask. JVP elevated 8cm above sternal angle (non-pulsatile, does not fall with inspiration - Kussmaul's sign absent). Heart sounds very quiet, difficult to auscultate apex beat. Pulsus paradoxus measured: systolic BP drops from 88mmHg in expiration to 68mmHg in inspiration (20mmHg paradox). Lungs: reduced air entry bibasal (small pleural effusions), no crackles. Abdomen: hepatomegaly 4cm below costal margin (pulsatile liver edge - elevated CVP). Peripheral oedema absent. ECG: sinus tachycardia 118 bpm, low voltage QRS complexes (<5mm in limb leads), electrical alternans (beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude). Portable CXR: enlarged cardiac silhouette (cardiothoracic ratio 0.62), globular heart shape ('water bottle' appearance), clear lung fields. Urgent bedside echo shows large circumferential pericardial effusion (2.8cm in diastole), right atrial collapse in diastole (>1/3 of cardiac cycle), right ventricular free wall diastolic collapse, IVC dilated 2.6cm with <50% respiratory variation (plethoric). LV systolic function preserved (EF 60%). Perform emergency management of this patient's cardiac tamponade.

patientDetails.presentingComplaint: 4 days progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, chest discomfort, presyncope this morning
patientDetails.relevantHistory: Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (stage IV) diagnosed 8 months ago. Primary tumour right upper lobe, metastases to liver, bone. Currently on second-line chemotherapy (carboplatin + pemetrexed). Previous echo 3 months ago: small pericardial effusion 0.8cm, no tamponade. No previous cardiac history. Non-smoker (never smoked). ECOG performance status 2 (ambulatory, self-care, but unable to work).
patientDetails.medications: Carboplatin IV every 3 weeks (last dose 10 days ago), pemetrexed 500mg/m2 IV every 3 weeks, dexamethasone 4mg PO BD (chemotherapy-related), metoclopramide 10mg TDS PRN nausea, oxycodone SR 10mg BD (bone pain), paracetamol 1g QID, enoxaparin 40mg SC daily (VTE prophylaxis).

investigations.echo: Urgent bedside TTE: Large circumferential pericardial effusion 2.8cm in diastole (posterior, anterior, lateral). RIGHT ATRIAL COLLAPSE in diastole (occupies >1/3 of cardiac cycle - highly specific for tamponade). RIGHT VENTRICULAR FREE WALL diastolic collapse (early sign of tamponade). IVC diameter 2.6cm, <50% respiratory variation (plethoric IVC - elevated RA pressure). Mitral inflow Doppler: >25% respiratory variation in mitral E velocity (exaggerated ventricular interdependence). LV function preserved (EF 60%). No vegetations. Conclusion: LARGE PERICARDIAL EFFUSION WITH ECHOCARDIOGRAPHIC SIGNS OF TAMPONADE.
investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 118 bpm, normal axis, LOW VOLTAGE QRS complexes in limb leads (QRS amplitude <5mm in all limb leads - suggests large pericardial effusion insulating heart). ELECTRICAL ALTERNANS: beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude (pathognomonic for large pericardial effusion, seen in 10-20% of tamponade cases). No ST elevation, no PR depression (no acute pericarditis). QTc 412ms.
investigations.cxr: PA chest X-ray: Enlarged cardiac silhouette, cardiothoracic ratio 0.62 (normal <0.50). 'Water bottle' or globular heart shape (suggests pericardial effusion). Clear lung fields centrally. Small bilateral pleural effusions (blunted costophrenic angles). No pulmonary oedema. Right upper lobe mass (known primary lung cancer). Bony metastases visible in ribs.
investigations.bloods: WCC 6.8 x10^9/L (chemotherapy-related leucopenia), Hb 98 g/L (anaemia of chronic disease), platelets 142 x10^9/L (mild thrombocytopenia). Na 136, K 4.2, Cr 76 micromol/L (eGFR >60), urea 8.2. Troponin I 0.08 (mildly elevated - ? demand ischaemia from hypotension). CRP 68 mg/L. LDH 420 U/L (elevated - malignant effusion). Albumin 28 g/L (hypoalbuminaemia). INR 1.1, APTT 32 sec (normal coagulation).

requiredActions.action: Recognize cardiac tamponade based on Beck's triad and pulsus paradoxus
requiredActions.details: Beck's triad (classic but only 30% of tamponade cases): (1) Hypotension - PRESENT (BP 88/64, MAP 72 mmHg), (2) Muffled heart sounds - PRESENT (quiet heart sounds, unable to auscultate apex), (3) Elevated JVP - PRESENT (JVP 8cm above sternal angle, non-pulsatile). Pulsus paradoxus: >10mmHg drop in systolic BP during inspiration - PRESENT (88mmHg expiration → 68mmHg inspiration = 20mmHg paradox, diagnostic of tamponade). State clearly: 'This patient has cardiac tamponade based on Beck's triad, pulsus paradoxus 20mmHg, and echocardiographic signs (RA/RV collapse, large effusion).'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Pulsus paradoxus measurement: inflate cuff above systolic BP, deflate slowly, note pressure where Korotkoff sounds first heard ONLY in expiration (systolic BP in expiration), continue deflating until sounds heard in both inspiration and expiration (systolic BP in inspiration). Difference >10mmHg = paradoxical pulse (tamponade, severe asthma, constrictive pericarditis). This patient has 20mmHg paradox (severe tamponade).

requiredActions.action: Initiate immediate resuscitation while preparing for urgent pericardiocentesis
requiredActions.details: This is cardiogenic shock from tamponade - requires URGENT drainage. Temporizing measures while preparing for pericardiocentesis: (1) IV fluid bolus: 500mL normal saline rapid infusion (increases preload, improves cardiac output temporarily - DO NOT give excessive fluid as pericardium cannot stretch), (2) Avoid positive pressure ventilation if possible (increases intrathoracic pressure, worsens tamponade), (3) Avoid vasodilators and diuretics (worsen hypotension), (4) Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%. Call for senior cardiology backup (consultant cardiologist, echocardiography technician). Alert cardiac catheterization lab or cardiothoracic surgery (if pericardiocentesis fails, surgical drainage required). Prepare emergency trolley with resuscitation equipment (defibrillator, intubation equipment, emergency medications).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Tamponade physiology: pericardial pressure = intracardiac pressure → cardiac chambers cannot fill → stroke volume ↓ → cardiac output ↓ → hypotension/shock. Small fluid bolus (250-500mL) increases preload temporarily (improves CO 10-20%), but definitive treatment is drainage. Positive pressure ventilation WORSENS tamponade (↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return).

requiredActions.action: Obtain informed consent for emergency pericardiocentesis and discuss risks
requiredActions.details: Explain to patient (if conscious and able to consent): 'You have a large collection of fluid around your heart causing it to not pump effectively. This is a medical emergency. We need to drain the fluid urgently using a needle inserted below your breastbone, guided by ultrasound. The risks include damage to the heart muscle (1-2%), irregular heartbeat, bleeding, infection, and need for emergency surgery if complications occur (<1%). Without this procedure, your condition is life-threatening.' If patient unable to consent (shock, altered consciousness), proceed under emergency doctrine and document. Obtain verbal consent if possible, written consent if time permits. Notify next of kin.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Pericardiocentesis complications: ventricular perforation 1-2% (most serious), coronary artery laceration 0.5%, arrhythmias (VT/VF 0.5%), pneumothorax 1%, hemothorax, infection. Emergency procedure - consent may be verbal if patient unstable. Echo guidance reduces complication rate 50% vs blind landmark technique.

requiredActions.action: Perform emergency pericardiocentesis using subxiphoid approach with echocardiographic guidance
requiredActions.details: Equipment: Pericardiocentesis kit (16-18G needle, guidewire, dilator, pigtail catheter), sterile drapes, local anaesthetic (lignocaine 1% 10mL), 50mL syringe, ECG monitoring cable with alligator clip (attach to needle), ultrasound machine with echo probe. Patient position: 30-45 degree semi-recumbent (optimizes needle trajectory). Skin preparation: chlorhexidine, sterile drapes. Local anaesthetic: lignocaine 1% infiltration at insertion site (2cm below xiphoid, 1cm left of midline). Echo guidance: identify largest pocket of pericardial fluid (usually anterior or apical). Insertion: advance 16-18G needle at 30-45 degree angle toward left shoulder, aspirating continuously. ECG monitoring: attach alligator clip from V lead to needle hub (if needle touches myocardium → ST elevation on monitor, withdraw needle 2mm). Fluid aspiration: once pericardial space entered (flash of fluid), aspirate 50mL initially (should improve BP and symptoms immediately), then insert guidewire through needle (Seldinger technique), remove needle, advance dilator, insert pigtail drainage catheter over wire. Secure catheter, aspirate remainder of effusion (usually 500-1500mL), send fluid for: (1) cytology (malignant cells?), (2) biochemistry (LDH, protein, glucose), (3) microbiology (TB culture, bacterial culture). Leave pigtail catheter in situ for 24-48 hours (prevents reaccumulation).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Subxiphoid approach: standard technique, avoids pleura and internal mammary artery. Echo guidance MANDATORY (reduces complications 50%). Seldinger technique: guidewire → dilator → catheter (safer than trocar technique). ECG monitoring during procedure: ST elevation = myocardial contact (withdraw needle). Immediate hemodynamic improvement expected after aspirating 50-100mL (tamponade relief).

requiredActions.action: Monitor haemodynamic response to pericardiocentesis and confirm tamponade resolution
requiredActions.details: During drainage: monitor BP, HR, SpO2 continuously. Expected response: BP increases to >100mmHg systolic within 5 minutes, HR decreases to <100 bpm, patient reports improvement in dyspnoea. Repeat bedside echo after draining 200-300mL to confirm effusion reduction and resolution of RA/RV collapse. Pulsus paradoxus should normalize (<10mmHg) after drainage. Continue draining until fluid stops flowing or total 1000-1500mL removed. Post-procedure: repeat echo to confirm residual effusion <1cm (acceptable), no RA/RV collapse, IVC respiratory variation normalized. If BP does not improve after drainage, consider: (1) inadequate drainage (catheter malposition, loculated effusion), (2) ventricular perforation with hemopericardium (worsening effusion on echo), (3) other cause of shock (sepsis, pulmonary embolism, RV infarction).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Tamponade relief: immediate improvement in BP, HR, dyspnoea after draining 50-200mL. If no improvement, catheter may be in wrong space (pleural, peritoneal) or ventricular perforation occurred (bleeding into pericardium). Repeat echo essential to confirm effusion reduction. Leave catheter in situ 24-48 hours (prevents early reaccumulation in malignant effusions).

requiredActions.action: Analyze pericardial fluid and investigate underlying cause of effusion
requiredActions.details: Send pericardial fluid for: (1) Cytology (malignant cells - likely given metastatic lung cancer), (2) Biochemistry: LDH >200 U/L, protein >30 g/L, glucose <60 mg/dL suggests exudate (malignancy, TB, autoimmune), (3) Microbiology: TB culture (Ziehl-Neelsen stain, TB PCR), bacterial culture (aerobic, anaerobic). Fluid appearance: straw-colored = transudate, bloody = malignancy/trauma/post-MI, purulent = bacterial pericarditis, turbid = TB/rheumatologic. In this case, given metastatic lung cancer, expect MALIGNANT EFFUSION (positive cytology for adenocarcinoma cells, elevated LDH, bloody fluid). Other causes to exclude: TB (endemic in some populations, fever, night sweats), uraemia (advanced renal failure, fibrinous pericarditis), autoimmune (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis - check ANA, RF), hypothyroidism (check TSH).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Malignant pericardial effusion: most common in lung cancer (30%), breast cancer (20%), lymphoma, melanoma. Cytology positive in 85% of malignant effusions. Recurrence rate 40-60% after simple drainage. Definitive management: intrapericardial chemotherapy (cisplatin, thiotepa), pericardial window (surgical drainage), or systemic chemotherapy if cancer chemo-responsive.

requiredActions.action: Arrange oncology consultation for management of malignant pericardial effusion
requiredActions.details: Contact medical oncology: 'Patient with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, now complicated by malignant pericardial effusion causing tamponade (drained 1200mL, cytology pending). Request review for: (1) further systemic chemotherapy options, (2) intrapericardial chemotherapy (cisplatin 10mg instilled via pigtail catheter), (3) prognosis discussion (median survival 3-6 months with malignant pericardial effusion).' If effusion recurs (40-60% chance), options: (1) repeat pericardiocentesis, (2) pericardial window (surgical drainage via subxiphoid or thoracoscopic approach), (3) pericardial sclerosis (talc, doxycycline instillation). Discuss goals of care: patient's ECOG 2, metastatic disease, prognosis poor - consider palliative approach if further aggressive intervention not aligned with patient goals.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Malignant pericardial effusion prognosis: median survival 3-6 months (poor prognostic factor). Recurrence rate after drainage: 40-60% within 2-4 weeks. Pericardial window (surgical drainage) more definitive (recurrence rate 10-15%) but requires general anaesthesia. Intrapericardial chemotherapy: cisplatin 10mg or thiotepa 10mg instilled via catheter, dwell 24 hours - reduces recurrence to 20-30%.

requiredActions.action: Monitor for complications post-pericardiocentesis and arrange repeat echocardiography
requiredActions.details: Post-procedure monitoring: continuous cardiac monitoring for 24 hours (arrhythmias), vital signs hourly for 6 hours then 4-hourly, daily CXR to exclude pneumothorax/hemothorax, daily echo while catheter in situ (check for reaccumulation, catheter position). Pigtail catheter care: secure catheter to skin with suture, connect to drainage bag (gravity drainage), record output 6-hourly (expect 50-200mL/day residual drainage). Remove catheter when: (1) drainage <50mL/24 hours, (2) repeat echo shows residual effusion <1cm, (3) no reaccumulation at 48 hours. Complications to monitor: (1) chest pain (myocardial perforation, coronary laceration), (2) sudden hypotension/tachycardia (hemopericardium, ventricular perforation), (3) arrhythmias (catheter irritating myocardium), (4) fever >38°C (infection).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Pigtail catheter removed at 24-48 hours (once drainage minimal and echo confirms no reaccumulation). Early removal (<24 hours) associated with higher recurrence rate. If drainage >200mL/day at 48 hours, consider leaving catheter longer or intrapericardial sclerosis.

markingCriteria.criterion: Recognizes Beck's triad (hypotension 88/64 mmHg, muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP 8cm) and diagnoses cardiac tamponade
Correctly measures pulsus paradoxus (20mmHg drop in systolic BP with inspiration, diagnostic of tamponade)
Identifies echocardiographic signs of tamponade (RA/RV diastolic collapse, large effusion 2.8cm, plethoric IVC)
Initiates appropriate resuscitation (500mL IV fluid bolus, oxygen, avoids positive pressure ventilation and vasodilators)
Obtains informed consent for emergency pericardiocentesis and clearly explains risks (ventricular perforation, coronary laceration, arrhythmias)
Performs pericardiocentesis using correct technique: subxiphoid approach, echo guidance, ECG monitoring (alligator clip to needle)
Uses Seldinger technique safely (needle → guidewire → dilator → pigtail catheter) and aspirates adequate volume (>500mL)
Sends pericardial fluid for appropriate investigations (cytology, biochemistry, microbiology including TB culture)
Monitors haemodynamic response to drainage (BP increases to >100mmHg, HR decreases, pulsus paradoxus resolves) and confirms tamponade relief on repeat echo
Recognizes underlying cause (malignant effusion from metastatic lung cancer) and arranges oncology consultation for definitive management
Plans appropriate post-procedure care (24-48 hour catheter drainage, daily echo, monitor for complications, remove catheter when drainage <50mL/day)

commonMistakes: Delaying pericardiocentesis to obtain CT or formal TTE (bedside echo diagnostic, patient unstable - DO NOT DELAY)
Excessive IV fluid bolus (>1 litre) - pericardium cannot stretch, excessive fluid worsens tamponade
Intubating patient for pericardiocentesis (positive pressure ventilation worsens tamponade physiology - avoid unless respiratory arrest)
Performing blind pericardiocentesis without echo guidance (complication rate 50% higher)
Forgetting ECG monitoring during procedure (ST elevation indicates myocardial contact - withdraw needle)
Not using Seldinger technique (advancing catheter over guidewire safer than trocar method)
Removing drainage catheter immediately after procedure (recurrence rate 40-60% if catheter removed <24 hours)
Missing pulsus paradoxus (not measuring correctly with manual sphygmomanometer)
Attributing hypotension to other causes (sepsis, hypovolemia) and delaying tamponade diagnosis
Not sending pericardial fluid for TB culture (TB pericarditis endemic in some populations, treatable)
Discharging patient without oncology follow-up (malignant effusion recurs in 40-60%, needs definitive management)
Not recognizing electrical alternans on ECG (beat-to-beat QRS variation, pathognomonic for large effusion)
redFlags: Persistent hypotension after draining 500mL pericardial fluid - consider ventricular perforation with hemopericardium (echo shows worsening effusion)
Sudden chest pain during pericardiocentesis - coronary artery laceration (rare <0.5%, requires urgent cardiac surgery)
ST elevation on ECG monitor during needle insertion - myocardial contact (withdraw needle 2mm immediately)
Arrhythmias during procedure (VT, VF) - catheter irritating myocardium (withdraw catheter, give lignocaine/amiodarone if sustained VT)
Bloody pericardial fluid that does not clot (pericardial blood contains fibrinolysins) vs frank blood that clots (ventricular perforation)
Rapidly reaccumulating effusion post-drainage - suggests ongoing bleeding (hemopericardium from perforation) or malignant effusion
Pneumothorax on post-procedure CXR - needle trajectory too lateral, punctured pleura (chest drain required if symptomatic)
Pulsus paradoxus >40mmHg - severe tamponade, high risk of cardiac arrest during procedure (resuscitation equipment immediately available)
Pericardial effusion with pyrexia, pleuritic chest pain - consider purulent pericarditis (Gram stain fluid, IV antibiotics urgently)
Uremic pericarditis (uraemia >30 mmol/L) - fibrinous 'bread-and-butter' pericardium, may require surgical drainage if recurrent
Constrictive physiology after drainage (elevated JVP, Kussmaul's sign persist) - suggests constrictive pericarditis (different pathophysiology, requires pericardiectomy)
safetyConsiderations: Tamponade is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY - pericardiocentesis should be performed within 30-60 minutes of diagnosis if haemodynamically unstable
Echo guidance is MANDATORY for pericardiocentesis (reduces complications by 50%) - never perform blind procedure
ECG monitoring during needle insertion critical - ST elevation indicates myocardial contact (withdraw needle to avoid perforation)
Avoid positive pressure ventilation if possible (increases intrathoracic pressure, worsens tamponade) - maintain spontaneous breathing
Small IV fluid bolus (250-500mL) temporizes tamponade, but definitive treatment is drainage (do not delay drainage for fluid resuscitation)
Ventricular perforation rare (1-2%) but catastrophic - requires immediate cardiac surgery (notify cardiothoracic team before starting procedure)
Pericardial fluid analysis essential: cytology (malignancy), TB culture (TB pericarditis treatable), protein/LDH (exudate vs transudate)
Malignant effusions recur in 40-60% of cases - definitive management (pericardial window, intrapericardial chemo) required
Pigtail catheter left in situ 24-48 hours (prevents early reaccumulation) - remove when drainage <50mL/day and echo confirms no reaccumulation
Post-procedure complications: monitor for arrhythmias (24 hour cardiac monitoring), hemothorax/pneumothorax (daily CXR), infection (fever, leucocytosis)
Anticoagulation relative contraindication for pericardiocentesis (risk of hemopericardium) - this patient on enoxaparin 40mg daily (prophylactic dose, acceptable risk), hold dose on day of procedure

osces.title: Ventricular Tachycardia - Haemodynamic Stability Assessment
learningObjectives: Differentiate ventricular tachycardia (VT) from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy using QRS morphology, duration, AV dissociation
Assess haemodynamic stability in broad complex tachycardia (systolic BP, consciousness, chest pain, heart failure)
Manage haemodynamically stable VT with chemical cardioversion (amiodarone 300mg IV over 20 minutes)
Perform synchronized DC cardioversion correctly for haemodynamically unstable VT (100J → 150J → 200J → 360J)
Recognize Brugada criteria for VT diagnosis (absence of RS complexes, R-S interval >100ms, AV dissociation, QRS morphology)
Investigate underlying causes of VT (acute MI, electrolyte abnormalities, structural heart disease, long QT syndrome)
Arrange appropriate follow-up for VT survivors (ICD assessment, electrophysiology study, exclude ischaemia)
osces.clinicalScenario: You are the Emergency Registrar at Liverpool Hospital. A 68-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with palpitations that started 20 minutes ago while gardening. He describes rapid regular heartbeat with associated chest tightness and light-headedness, but no loss of consciousness. Past history: anterior STEMI 3 years ago (LAD stent), ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 35% on echo 6 months ago), type 2 diabetes. Medications: aspirin 100mg daily, ticagrelor 90mg BD, metoprolol 50mg BD, perindopril 10mg daily, atorvastatin 80mg nocte, metformin 1g BD, empagliflozin 10mg daily. On examination: conscious, alert, appears uncomfortable. HR 164 bpm (regular, monomorphic broad complex rhythm on monitor), BP 102/68 mmHg (systolic BP >90 mmHg), RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air. No acute distress, speaking in full sentences. JVP not elevated. Apex beat displaced laterally (cardiomegaly). Heart sounds normal rhythm at 164 bpm, no murmurs audible. Chest: fine bibasal crackles (mild pulmonary oedema). Peripheral oedema absent. 12-lead ECG: regular broad complex tachycardia, rate 164 bpm, QRS duration 168ms (very broad), northwest axis (-90 degrees), concordant negative QRS complexes in precordial leads V1-V6, no visible P waves, AV dissociation suspected (intermittent capture beats visible). You make a provisional diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia. The patient remains haemodynamically stable (systolic BP 102 mmHg, conscious, GCS 15). Manage this patient's ventricular tachycardia appropriately.

patientDetails.presentingComplaint: Palpitations 20 minutes, rapid regular heartbeat, chest tightness, light-headedness (no syncope)
patientDetails.relevantHistory: Anterior STEMI 3 years ago (LAD stent 2021). Ischaemic cardiomyopathy, LVEF 35% on TTE 6 months ago (moderate LV systolic dysfunction). Type 2 diabetes 15 years (HbA1c 7.2% 3 months ago). No previous VT episodes documented. No ICD (declined in past due to cost, not PBS-subsidized for ischaemic cardiomyopathy unless cardiac arrest survivor or sustained VT). No family history sudden cardiac death.
patientDetails.medications: Aspirin 100mg daily, ticagrelor 90mg BD (post-PCI dual antiplatelet therapy), metoprolol 50mg BD (beta-blocker for ischaemic cardiomyopathy), perindopril 10mg daily (ACE inhibitor for LV dysfunction), atorvastatin 80mg nocte, metformin 1g BD, empagliflozin 10mg daily. Compliance good per patient.

investigations.ecg: 12-lead ECG: Regular broad complex tachycardia. Rate 164 bpm. QRS duration 168ms (very broad, >160ms highly specific for VT). Axis: northwest axis -90 degrees (extreme axis deviation favours VT). Precordial concordance: all QRS complexes negative in V1-V6 (concordant negative pattern, specific for VT). AV dissociation: intermittent capture beats visible (occasional narrow QRS complex at different rate - pathognomonic for VT). No RS complexes in precordial leads V1-V6 (Brugada criteria: absence of RS = VT). QRS morphology in V1: monophasic R wave (favours VT over SVT with aberrancy). DIAGNOSIS: VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA (VT). Fulfills Brugada criteria: (1) absence of RS in all precordial leads, (2) QRS >160ms, (3) AV dissociation, (4) precordial concordance.
investigations.bloods: Pending: Troponin I (rule out acute MI triggering VT), UEC (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ - electrolyte abnormalities can trigger VT), FBC, glucose (diabetes control). Previous: HbA1c 7.2% (3 months ago), Cr 102 micromol/L (eGFR 62 - mild CKD).
investigations.monitoring: Continuous cardiac monitoring: monomorphic VT 164 bpm (same QRS morphology each beat, suggests single focus). No R-on-T phenomena. No degeneration to VF observed. BP stable 102/68 mmHg. Defibrillator pads applied (adhesive pads on anterior chest and back).

requiredActions.action: Differentiate ventricular tachycardia from SVT with aberrancy using Brugada criteria
requiredActions.details: Broad complex tachycardia differential: (1) Ventricular tachycardia (75-80% in patient with previous MI and cardiomyopathy), (2) SVT with aberrant conduction (15-20%), (3) SVT with pre-existing bundle branch block (5%). Apply Brugada criteria systematically: Step 1: Absence of RS complex in all precordial leads (V1-V6)? YES (all precordial leads show concordant negative QRS, no RS) → DIAGNOSIS = VT (98% specificity). If RS present, proceed to Step 2: R-S interval >100ms in any precordial lead? If yes → VT. Step 3: AV dissociation present? If yes → VT (100% specific). Step 4: VT morphology criteria in V1/V2 and V6. This patient fulfills Step 1 (absence of RS) → DEFINITE VT. Additional VT features: QRS >160ms (168ms), extreme axis deviation (-90 degrees), previous MI with scar (substrate for VT).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Broad complex tachycardia in patient with previous MI = VT until proven otherwise (75-80% probability). Brugada criteria: 4-step algorithm, 98.7% sensitivity, 96.5% specificity for VT. AV dissociation pathognomonic for VT but only visible 25% of cases (look for capture beats, fusion beats). Precordial concordance (all QRS positive or all negative) highly specific for VT (95%).

requiredActions.action: Assess haemodynamic stability to determine management strategy (chemical vs electrical cardioversion)
requiredActions.details: Haemodynamic stability assessment (critical decision point): UNSTABLE features = (1) Systolic BP <90 mmHg (shock), (2) Altered consciousness (GCS <15, confusion, loss of consciousness), (3) Chest pain suggesting acute myocardial ischaemia, (4) Heart failure (pulmonary oedema, elevated JVP, hypoxia). This patient: (1) Systolic BP 102 mmHg (>90 mmHg = STABLE), (2) Conscious, alert, GCS 15 (STABLE), (3) Chest tightness but no severe ischaemic pain (STABLE), (4) Mild pulmonary oedema (bibasal crackles) but SpO2 96%, no respiratory distress (STABLE). CONCLUSION: HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE VT. Management: Chemical cardioversion with amiodarone first-line (synchronized DC cardioversion reserved for unstable VT or failed chemical cardioversion).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Haemodynamic instability = IMMEDIATE synchronized DC cardioversion (do not delay for IV drugs). Stable VT = trial of chemical cardioversion (amiodarone, procainamide, sotalol). Caveat: 'Stable' VT can deteriorate to unstable VT or VF within minutes - continuous monitoring mandatory, defibrillator pads applied, resuscitation team on standby.

requiredActions.action: Administer amiodarone 300mg IV over 20 minutes for chemical cardioversion of stable VT
requiredActions.details: First-line chemical cardioversion for stable VT (eTG, AHA guidelines): Amiodarone 300mg IV over 20 minutes, followed by 900mg IV over 24 hours (infusion 37.5mg/hour). Preparation: dilute amiodarone 300mg in 250mL 5% dextrose (amiodarone incompatible with normal saline - precipitates). Administer via volumetric pump over 20 minutes (not bolus - rapid infusion causes hypotension). Continuous cardiac monitoring during infusion. Expected response: VT terminates in 40-60% of patients within 30 minutes. If VT persists after 300mg dose, consider: (1) repeat dose 150mg IV over 10 minutes (maximum 2.2g/24 hours), (2) synchronized DC cardioversion (if patient deteriorates), (3) alternative agent (procainamide, lignocaine). Document: 'Amiodarone 300mg IV over 20 minutes given for stable monomorphic VT. PBS code: unrestricted benefit for VT.'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Amiodarone for VT: class IIa recommendation (AHA), first-line for stable VT. Advantages: effective (40-60% cardioversion rate), does not cause myocardial depression (safe in LV dysfunction EF 35%). Adverse effects: hypotension (slow infusion), bradycardia, phlebitis (use central line if prolonged infusion). Contraindications: severe bradycardia, QT prolongation >500ms (risk of torsades de pointes).

requiredActions.action: Prepare for synchronized DC cardioversion if amiodarone fails or patient becomes unstable
requiredActions.details: Synchronous DC cardioversion procedure for VT (if amiodarone fails or patient unstable): Defibrillator pads already applied. Select 'synchronized' mode on defibrillator (delivers shock on R wave, avoids R-on-T phenomenon causing VF). Energy levels for VT: start 100J biphasic (200J monophasic), escalate to 150J, 200J, then 360J if unsuccessful. Sedation: if patient conscious and stable, give procedural sedation (midazolam 2-5mg IV + fentanyl 25-50mcg IV) before cardioversion.
