If patient unstable (loss of consciousness, BP <90), proceed with unsynchronized DC cardioversion immediately (no sedation). Charge defibrillator to 100J, ensure sync mode active (look for markers on QRS complexes), shout 'Stand clear!', deliver shock. Monitor ECG: successful cardioversion → sinus rhythm resumes. If VT persists, escalate energy to 150J, repeat. If VF develops during cardioversion (rare), switch to unsynchronized mode and defibrillate 200J immediately.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Synchronized vs unsynchronized: Synchronized mode MANDATORY for VT (delivers shock on R wave, prevents VF). Unsynchronized (asynchronous) only for VF, pulseless VT, polymorphic VT. Energy for VT: 100J biphasic sufficient for 80% cardioversion, escalate if unsuccessful. Sedation contraindicated in unstable VT (peri-arrest, do not delay cardioversion for sedation).

requiredActions.action: Investigate underlying triggers for VT (acute MI, electrolytes, QT interval, structural heart disease)
requiredActions.details: VT triggers to investigate urgently: (1) Acute myocardial ischaemia: Order stat troponin I, serial ECGs every 30 min to detect dynamic ST changes (VT may be first presentation of acute STEMI - this patient has previous LAD stent, check for stent thrombosis). (2) Electrolyte abnormalities: Stat UEC (hypokalemia K+ <3.5, hypomagnesemia Mg <0.7 trigger VT - correct aggressively). (3) QT interval prolongation: Measure QTc on baseline ECG if available (QTc >500ms = torsades de pointes risk - amiodarone contraindicated). (4) Drug-induced: Review medications (no QT-prolonging drugs in this patient's list). (5) Structural heart disease: Patient has ischaemic cardiomyopathy LVEF 35% (known VT substrate - scar from previous MI provides re-entry circuit). (6) Acidosis/hypoxia: Check VBG (acidosis lowers VT threshold). Order: Troponin I, UEC, Mg, Ca, VBG, repeat ECG post-cardioversion.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: VT in ischaemic cardiomyopathy: scar tissue from previous MI creates re-entry circuit (substrate for monomorphic VT). Acute MI precipitates VT in 3-5% of STEMI cases. Electrolyte correction CRITICAL: K+ target >4.0 mmol/L (give KCl 20-40 mmol IV), Mg target >1.0 mmol/L (give MgSO4 5-10 mmol IV). Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT in long QT) requires different management (magnesium, temporary pacing, avoid amiodarone).

requiredActions.action: Optimize medical therapy post-cardioversion (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, electrolyte correction)
requiredActions.details: Post-cardioversion management: (1) Increase beta-blocker dose: Patient on metoprolol 50mg BD (low-moderate dose). Increase to metoprolol 100mg BD (maximum tolerated dose for VT prevention). Beta-blockers reduce VT recurrence 30-40% (class I indication post-VT). (2) Ensure ACE inhibitor optimized: Perindopril 10mg daily (maximum dose) - continue. (3) Electrolyte replacement: If K+ <4.0, replace to >4.5 mmol/L (VT threshold higher with hypokalemia). If Mg <1.0, replace to >1.2 mmol/L. (4) Amiodarone infusion continued 24 hours (900mg over 24h = 37.5mg/hour) to prevent VT recurrence. (5) Avoid QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones). Document: 'Post-VT cardioversion. Metoprolol increased to 100mg BD, amiodarone infusion 24h, K+ and Mg replacement as needed.'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Beta-blockers cornerstone of VT prevention (class I indication, reduce mortality 25-30% in ischaemic cardiomyopathy). Amiodarone infusion post-cardioversion prevents early VT recurrence (first 24-48 hours). Electrolyte targets: K+ >4.5, Mg >1.0 (higher thresholds than routine management to suppress VT).

requiredActions.action: Arrange urgent cardiology consultation for ICD assessment and electrophysiology study
requiredActions.details: Contact cardiology registrar: 'Patient with ischaemic cardiomyopathy LVEF 35%, sustained monomorphic VT terminated with amiodarone. Request review for: (1) ICD (implantable cardioverter-defibrillator) assessment - this patient now has secondary prevention indication (sustained VT survivor), (2) Electrophysiology study (EPS) to map VT circuit and consider catheter ablation if recurrent VT, (3) Exclude acute MI (troponin pending, serial ECGs), (4) Optimize heart failure therapy.' ICD indication: Secondary prevention (VT or VF survivor, LVEF ≤35%) = class I indication (PBS-subsidised). Patient previously declined ICD (primary prevention indication weaker), but now has sustained VT = stronger indication. Discuss risks/benefits: ICD prevents sudden cardiac death 50% (absolute risk reduction), but requires device implantation, regular monitoring, shock therapy painful.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: ICD indications: (1) Secondary prevention (cardiac arrest survivor, sustained VT) = class I (PBS-approved, Authority Required code 3119). (2) Primary prevention (ischaemic cardiomyopathy LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II-III) = class I but patient must be >40 days post-MI, on optimal medical therapy 3 months. This patient now has SECONDARY prevention indication (sustained VT). ICD reduces mortality 50% vs amiodarone alone.

requiredActions.action: Monitor for VT recurrence and arrange continuous telemetry for 48 hours
requiredActions.details: Admit to Coronary Care Unit (CCU) or High Dependency Unit (HDU) for continuous cardiac monitoring. VT recurrence risk highest in first 24-48 hours post-cardioversion (20-30% recurrence rate). Continuous telemetry monitoring 48 hours minimum. Defibrillator pads remain applied (in case VT recurs requiring cardioversion). Staff education: 'Patient at high risk VT recurrence - any broad complex tachycardia >30 seconds = call medical emergency team (MET), defibrillator immediately available.' Daily 12-lead ECGs (monitor for dynamic ST changes suggesting ongoing ischaemia). Daily electrolytes (maintain K+ >4.5, Mg >1.0). If VT recurs despite amiodarone infusion, options: (1) repeat cardioversion, (2) add second antiarrhythmic (procainamide, lignocaine), (3) urgent EPS + catheter ablation, (4) emergency ICD implantation.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: VT recurrence rate first 48 hours: 20-30% (high-risk period). Amiodarone infusion reduces recurrence to 10-15%. If VT recurs >2 times despite optimal medical therapy, urgent ICD implantation or catheter ablation indicated (medical therapy failure). CCU/HDU mandatory for post-VT monitoring (staff trained in advanced life support, defibrillator immediately available).

markingCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies ventricular tachycardia using Brugada criteria (absence of RS complexes in V1-V6, QRS >160ms, AV dissociation)
Assesses haemodynamic stability systematically (BP >90 mmHg, GCS 15, no severe chest pain, no pulmonary oedema) and classifies as STABLE VT
Chooses appropriate management for stable VT (chemical cardioversion with amiodarone first-line, NOT immediate DC cardioversion)
Administers amiodarone correctly: 300mg IV over 20 minutes in 5% dextrose (NOT normal saline), followed by 900mg/24h infusion
Prepares for synchronized DC cardioversion as backup (defibrillator pads applied, sync mode selected, energy sequence 100J → 150J → 200J)
Investigates VT triggers appropriately (troponin for acute MI, electrolytes for K+/Mg, ECG for QT interval)
Optimizes post-cardioversion medical therapy (increase beta-blocker to metoprolol 100mg BD, electrolyte correction K+ >4.5, Mg >1.0)
Arranges urgent cardiology review for ICD assessment (secondary prevention indication after sustained VT)
Plans appropriate monitoring (continuous telemetry 48 hours, CCU/HDU admission, defibrillator pads in situ)
Recognizes underlying substrate for VT (ischaemic cardiomyopathy LVEF 35%, previous MI scar) and discusses long-term management (ICD, EPS, catheter ablation)
Communicates clearly with patient about diagnosis (VT), treatment plan (amiodarone, possible ICD), and prognosis

commonMistakes: Assuming broad complex tachycardia is SVT with aberrancy (75-80% are VT in patient with previous MI)
Performing immediate DC cardioversion for haemodynamically STABLE VT (chemical cardioversion with amiodarone first-line)
Using adenosine to 'diagnose' VT vs SVT (dangerous - can precipitate VF in VT, avoid in broad complex tachycardia)
Administering amiodarone in normal saline (precipitates - must use 5% dextrose)
Giving amiodarone as rapid bolus (causes severe hypotension - infuse over 20 minutes)
Using lignocaine first-line for VT (less effective than amiodarone 40% vs 60%, only use if amiodarone contraindicated)
Forgetting to select 'synchronized' mode for DC cardioversion (unsynchronized shock can cause VF)
Not correcting electrolytes (K+ <4.0, Mg <1.0 increase VT recurrence risk)
Missing acute MI as VT trigger (troponin essential, VT may be presenting feature of STEMI)
Discharging patient without ICD assessment (sustained VT = secondary prevention indication, class I for ICD)
Not increasing beta-blocker dose post-VT (beta-blockers reduce VT recurrence 30-40%)
Confusing torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT in long QT) with monomorphic VT (different management - magnesium, pacing)
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability (systolic BP <90 mmHg, altered consciousness, severe chest pain) - requires IMMEDIATE synchronized DC cardioversion, not amiodarone
Polymorphic VT (QRS morphology varies beat-to-beat) - suggests torsades de pointes (check QTc, give magnesium, avoid amiodarone)
Pulseless VT - cardiac arrest, requires immediate unsynchronized defibrillation 200J (CPR, advanced life support protocol)
VT degenerating to ventricular fibrillation during monitoring - immediate unsynchronized defibrillation required
VT in setting of acute STEMI - urgent coronary angiography + PCI (revascularization treats VT substrate)
Recurrent VT despite amiodarone infusion (>2 episodes in 24 hours) - medical therapy failure, requires urgent ICD or catheter ablation
VT with severe LV dysfunction (LVEF <20%, cardiogenic shock) - high risk sudden cardiac death, urgent ICD + inotropic support
QTc >500ms on baseline ECG - risk of torsades de pointes (avoid amiodarone, sotalol, other QT-prolonging drugs)
Brugada syndrome pattern on ECG (RBBB + ST elevation V1-V3) - genetic arrhythmia syndrome, ICD mandatory, avoid sodium channel blockers
VT storm (≥3 VT episodes in 24 hours) - refractory arrhythmia, requires urgent EPS + catheter ablation, deep sedation, sometimes mechanical circulatory support
Hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L - can mimic VT (broad QRS), treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose) before cardioversion
VT in patient with normal LV function and structurally normal heart - consider channelopathies (long QT, CPVT, Brugada), genetic testing required
safetyConsiderations: Broad complex tachycardia in patient with previous MI = VT until proven otherwise (75-80% probability) - do not delay treatment
Haemodynamic stability determines management: STABLE VT = amiodarone first-line, UNSTABLE VT = immediate synchronized DC cardioversion
Adenosine contraindicated in broad complex tachycardia (can precipitate VF if VT, no diagnostic value, risks outweigh benefits)
Amiodarone must be diluted in 5% dextrose (precipitates in normal saline) and infused slowly over 20 minutes (rapid infusion → hypotension)
Synchronized mode MANDATORY for DC cardioversion of VT (delivers shock on R wave, prevents R-on-T phenomenon causing VF)
Defibrillator pads applied prophylactically in all VT patients (if VT recurs or degenerates to VF, immediate defibrillation available)
Electrolyte correction critical for VT prevention: K+ target >4.5 mmol/L, Mg >1.0 mmol/L (higher thresholds than routine care)
Beta-blockers reduce VT recurrence 30-40% and should be up-titrated to maximum tolerated dose (metoprolol 100-200mg BD)
ICD assessment mandatory for all sustained VT survivors (secondary prevention indication, reduces sudden cardiac death 50%)
Continuous telemetry monitoring 48 hours minimum post-VT (recurrence risk highest first 24-48 hours, 20-30% recurrence rate)
Exclude acute MI in all VT patients (troponin, serial ECGs) - revascularization may prevent VT recurrence if ischaemia-triggered
VT storm (≥3 episodes/24h) requires aggressive management: deep sedation, amiodarone infusion, urgent catheter ablation, sometimes mechanical circulatory support

osces.title: Symptomatic Bradycardia - Atropine Administration and Pacing Indications
learningObjectives: Recognize symptomatic bradycardia requiring urgent treatment (dizziness, syncope, chest pain, hypotension, heart failure)
Differentiate physiological bradycardia (athletes, sleep) from pathological bradycardia requiring intervention
Administer atropine correctly for symptomatic bradycardia (600 micrograms IV, repeat to maximum 3mg total dose)
Identify indications for transcutaneous pacing (symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine, high-degree AV block)
Apply external pacing pads correctly and initiate transcutaneous pacing with appropriate current and rate
Arrange urgent temporary transvenous pacing for refractory symptomatic bradycardia or high-degree AV block
Investigate underlying causes of bradycardia (acute MI, medications, electrolytes, hypothyroidism, raised ICP)
osces.clinicalScenario: You are the Medical Registrar at Westmead Hospital. A 72-year-old woman is referred from GP with 3 days of dizziness, near-syncope (2 episodes today, felt faint but did not lose consciousness), and fatigue. She reports intermittent chest pressure lasting 5-10 minutes, worse with exertion. Past history: hypertension, type 2 diabetes. Medications: metoprolol 100mg BD (started 2 weeks ago for hypertension, increased dose from 50mg BD), amlodipine 10mg daily, metformin 1g BD, aspirin 100mg daily. On examination: pale, clammy, appears unwell. HR 38 bpm (regular, bradycardic), BP 94/62 mmHg (hypotension), RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4°C. JVP difficult to assess (low BP). Apex beat palpable, S1 and S2 normal with occasional cannon 'a' waves in JVP (suggests AV dissociation). Chest clear, no peripheral oedema. ECG: sinus bradycardia 38 bpm, normal P waves preceding each QRS (1:1 AV conduction), PR interval 180ms (normal), QRS 96ms (narrow), no ST segment elevation but subtle ST depression 0.5mm in V4-V6 (possible demand ischaemia from bradycardia and hypotension). Troponin I ordered. The patient suddenly becomes more symptomatic, stating 'I feel very faint' and appears pre-syncopal (pale, diaphoretic). HR remains 38 bpm, BP 88/58 mmHg. You diagnose symptomatic sinus bradycardia. Manage this patient appropriately.

patientDetails.presentingComplaint: 3 days dizziness, 2 episodes near-syncope today (presyncope), fatigue, intermittent chest pressure with exertion
patientDetails.relevantHistory: Hypertension 10 years (previously well-controlled on amlodipine 10mg daily). Type 2 diabetes 8 years (HbA1c 6.8% 3 months ago, good control). Metoprolol recently started 2 weeks ago for elevated BP (150/92), dose increased from 50mg BD to 100mg BD one week ago. No previous cardiac history, no previous syncope. Non-smoker, no alcohol. Independent in ADLs, lives alone.
patientDetails.medications: Metoprolol 100mg BD (beta-blocker, started 2 weeks ago, dose doubled 1 week ago - likely cause of symptomatic bradycardia), amlodipine 10mg daily (calcium channel blocker), metformin 1g BD, aspirin 100mg daily. Compliance excellent per patient.

vitalSigns.bloodPressure: 88/58 mmHg initially, then 94/62 mmHg (hypotension, systolic <90 mmHg)

investigations.ecg: 12-lead ECG: Sinus bradycardia 38 bpm. Normal P waves present (upright in II, III, aVF). PR interval 180ms (normal, consistent 1:1 AV conduction). QRS 96ms (narrow, normal intraventricular conduction). ST depression 0.5mm in V4-V6 (lateral leads, ? demand ischaemia from hypotension/bradycardia). No ST elevation, no Q waves. Occasional cannon 'a' waves on JVP examination suggests intermittent AV dissociation (? intermittent complete heart block), but ECG shows consistent P waves before QRS. QTc 480ms (upper limit normal, monitor for QT prolongation if giving atropine).
investigations.bloods: Pending: Troponin I (rule out acute MI causing bradycardia - inferior MI can affect SA/AV node blood supply), UEC (hyperkalaemia can cause bradycardia), TFTs (hypothyroidism), glucose (diabetes control). Bedside glucose 8.2 mmol/L (acceptable).
investigations.monitoring: Continuous cardiac monitoring: sinus bradycardia 38 bpm, occasional sinus pauses up to 3 seconds duration (symptomatic pauses). External pacing pads applied (anterior-posterior position). Defibrillator/pacing unit at bedside, charged and ready.

requiredActions.action: Recognize symptomatic bradycardia requiring urgent intervention and assess severity
requiredActions.details: Symptomatic bradycardia defined as: HR <60 bpm (this patient 38 bpm) PLUS adverse features = (1) Hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg) - PRESENT (88 mmHg), (2) Altered consciousness, syncope, presyncope - PRESENT (near-syncope x2, currently pre-syncopal), (3) Chest pain suggesting myocardial ischaemia - PRESENT (chest pressure, ST depression on ECG), (4) Heart failure (pulmonary oedema, elevated JVP) - ABSENT. This patient has 3/4 adverse features → SEVERE SYMPTOMATIC BRADYCARDIA requiring URGENT treatment. Differentiate from physiological bradycardia (athletes HR 40-50 bpm, asymptomatic) or asymptomatic pathological bradycardia (no treatment needed unless HR <40 bpm or symptoms develop). State clearly: 'This is symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension, presyncope, and ischaemic chest pain - requires immediate atropine and preparation for pacing.'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Symptomatic bradycardia = medical emergency (risk of cardiac arrest from severe bradycardia + hypotension). Adverse features: hypotension, altered consciousness, chest pain, heart failure. Presence of ANY adverse feature = treat immediately. Asymptomatic bradycardia (e.g., athlete with HR 45, BP 120/70, no symptoms) = no treatment, observation only.

requiredActions.action: Withhold metoprolol immediately and identify medication as likely cause of bradycardia
requiredActions.details: Review medication history: Metoprolol 100mg BD started 2 weeks ago, dose doubled 1 week ago (from 50mg BD to 100mg BD). Beta-blockers cause bradycardia (block SA node automaticity, slow AV conduction). Excessive beta-blockade likely cause of symptomatic bradycardia in this patient (timing: dose increase 1 week ago → symptoms started 3 days ago). Document: 'WITHHOLD metoprolol immediately - likely cause of symptomatic bradycardia. Do not administer further doses until reviewed by cardiology.' Consider other bradycardic medications: Amlodipine (CCB, but dihydropyridine class - minimal effect on heart rate, unlikely cause). If patient also on digoxin, diltiazem, or verapamil (non-dihydropyridine CCBs), would also withhold.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Beta-blocker-induced bradycardia: dose-dependent, worse in elderly, renal impairment (metoprolol renally cleared). High-dose metoprolol (100mg BD = 200mg daily) excessive for elderly patient. Symptomatic bradycardia develops 1-2 weeks after dose increase (matches timeline). Withholding beta-blocker may resolve bradycardia within 24-48 hours (metoprolol half-life 3-7 hours), but immediate treatment with atropine required.

requiredActions.action: Administer atropine 600 micrograms IV for acute management of symptomatic bradycardia
requiredActions.details: First-line treatment for symptomatic bradycardia (AHA/ARC guidelines): Atropine 600 micrograms (0.6mg) IV bolus. Atropine is anticholinergic (blocks vagal tone on SA node, increases heart rate). Preparation: Draw up atropine 600 micrograms (600 micrograms = 0.6mL of 1mg/mL ampoule, or use 600 microgram pre-filled syringe if available). Administer rapid IV push via existing IV cannula (fast bolus, not infusion). Monitor ECG continuously: expect HR increase to 50-60 bpm within 2-3 minutes. If insufficient response (HR still <50 bpm or symptoms persist), repeat atropine 600 micrograms every 3-5 minutes. Maximum total dose: 3mg (i.e., five 600 microgram doses). Document: 'Atropine 600 micrograms IV given for symptomatic bradycardia (HR 38, BP 88/58, presyncope). PBS code 1864N (unrestricted benefit).'
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Atropine for bradycardia: first-line (class IIa recommendation AHA). Dose: 600 micrograms (0.6mg) - higher doses (1mg) used in some protocols but 600 micrograms adequate for most patients. Avoid doses <500 micrograms (paradoxical bradycardia can occur with very low doses <0.5mg). Maximum cumulative dose 3mg (further doses ineffective and increase adverse effects).

requiredActions.action: Apply external pacing pads and prepare for transcutaneous pacing if atropine ineffective
requiredActions.details: External pacing pads: Apply adhesive pacing pads in anterior-posterior position (anterior pad: left of sternum below clavicle, posterior pad: left scapula region on back). Connect to defibrillator/pacing unit. Select 'pacing' mode (not defibrillation mode). Settings: Rate 60 bpm (physiological), Current start at 70 mA and titrate upwards. Explain to patient: 'If your heart rate doesn't improve with medication, we may need to use an external pacemaker. You'll feel tapping or twitching sensations on your chest with each paced beat - we'll give you pain relief.' Sedation: If transcutaneous pacing required, give analgesia (fentanyl 25-50 micrograms IV) or procedural sedation (midazolam 1-2mg IV + fentanyl) as pacing is uncomfortable. Initiate pacing if: (1) atropine fails (HR <50 bpm after 3mg total atropine), (2) patient deteriorates (loss of consciousness, systolic BP <80 mmHg), (3) high-degree AV block (Mobitz type II, complete heart block).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP): temporary bridge to transvenous pacing. Uncomfortable (skeletal muscle stimulation), requires sedation. Pacing current: start 70 mA, increase by 10 mA increments until electrical capture seen (pacing spike followed by wide QRS complex on ECG). Then check mechanical capture (palpate pulse, measure BP - should match paced rate). Rate 60-80 bpm typical. TCP duration: maximum 2-4 hours (skin burns risk), arrange transvenous pacing urgently if prolonged pacing needed.

requiredActions.action: Monitor response to atropine and assess need for further interventions
requiredActions.details: After atropine 600 micrograms IV: monitor ECG continuously for HR increase. Expected response: HR increases from 38 bpm to 50-70 bpm within 2-5 minutes. Also monitor: (1) BP improvement (target systolic >100 mmHg), (2) symptom resolution (dizziness, presyncope improved), (3) ECG changes (ST depression should improve if demand ischaemia). If inadequate response after first atropine dose (HR <50 bpm, BP <90 mmHg, ongoing symptoms): Give second dose atropine 600 micrograms IV (3-5 minutes after first dose). If still inadequate after second dose: Consider third dose OR initiate transcutaneous pacing. Maximum 5 doses atropine (3mg total). If atropine effective: HR 50-60 bpm, BP >100 mmHg, symptoms resolved - continue observation, withhold beta-blocker, arrange cardiology review.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Atropine response time-course: peak effect 2-5 minutes after IV bolus, duration 30-60 minutes. If HR improves transiently then drops again, may need repeat doses or pacing. Assess response objectively: HR (target >50 bpm), BP (target systolic >100 mmHg), symptoms (presyncope resolved), ECG (ST depression improved). Inadequate response after 2-3 doses = consider pacing.

requiredActions.action: Arrange urgent temporary transvenous pacing if transcutaneous pacing required or refractory bradycardia
requiredActions.details: Indications for temporary transvenous pacing (TVP): (1) Symptomatic bradycardia refractory to atropine (still HR <50, hypotensive, symptomatic after 3mg atropine), (2) High-degree AV block (Mobitz II, complete heart block) - even if asymptomatic (risk of asystole), (3) Bradycardia requiring prolonged pacing >2-4 hours (TCP causes skin burns, TVP more definitive). Contact cardiology registrar urgently: 'Patient with symptomatic bradycardia, HR 38, BP 88/58, given atropine 600 micrograms with partial response. Request urgent TVP insertion (right internal jugular or subclavian approach).' TVP procedure: central venous access (RIJ or subclavian vein), fluoroscopy-guided pacing wire insertion to RV apex, temporary pacing box settings (VVI mode, rate 60 bpm, output 5-10V). TVP duration: hours to days (bridge to permanent pacemaker if indicated).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: TVP vs TCP: TVP more reliable (100% capture vs 80% for TCP), less painful, can maintain for days. TVP complications: pneumothorax (subclavian approach 1-2%), bleeding, infection, arrhythmias during wire insertion (VT if wire touches RV apex). Indications for PERMANENT pacemaker after TVP: symptomatic sinus node dysfunction, high-degree AV block (Mobitz II, complete heart block), bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome.

requiredActions.action: Investigate underlying causes of bradycardia and exclude acute MI
requiredActions.details: Causes of symptomatic bradycardia to investigate: (1) Medications (MOST COMMON in this case - beta-blocker overdose) - already identified and withheld. (2) Acute MI: Inferior STEMI affects RCA which supplies SA node (60%) and AV node → bradycardia. Order: Troponin I (stat and 3-hour repeat), serial ECGs (look for inferior ST elevation II, III, aVF). This patient has ST depression V4-V6 (demand ischaemia, not STEMI), but troponin needed to exclude NSTEMI. (3) Electrolyte abnormalities: Hyperkalaemia (K+ >6.0 causes bradycardia, wide QRS) - order stat UEC. (4) Hypothyroidism: Severe hypothyroidism → bradycardia - order TFTs. (5) Raised intracranial pressure (Cushing's triad: bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respiration) - unlikely given hypotension. (6) Sick sinus syndrome (elderly, intrinsic SA node disease) - possible but less likely given recent beta-blocker dose increase. (7) High vagal tone (athletes, vomiting) - unlikely given age and symptoms.
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Inferior MI + bradycardia: RCA supplies SA node (55-60% of people) and AV node (90%) → inferior STEMI causes bradycardia (sinus bradycardia, AV block). Look for ST elevation in II, III, aVF on ECG. Treat with atropine + urgent PCI (revascularization resolves bradycardia). This patient has ST depression (demand ischaemia from bradycardia/hypotension), not STEMI, but exclude NSTEMI with troponin.

requiredActions.action: Arrange cardiology consultation for permanent pacemaker assessment if bradycardia persists
requiredActions.details: Contact cardiology for review: 'Patient with symptomatic sinus bradycardia (HR 38, hypotension, presyncope), likely beta-blocker induced (metoprolol 100mg BD, recently increased). Atropine given with partial response. Request assessment for: (1) need for TVP if refractory bradycardia, (2) permanent pacemaker indication if underlying sinus node dysfunction (beyond beta-blocker effect), (3) exclude structural heart disease (echo to assess LVEF, valves).' Permanent pacemaker indications: (1) Symptomatic sinus bradycardia (documented HR <40 bpm with symptoms, not medication-induced) = class I. (2) Mobitz type II or complete heart block (even if asymptomatic) = class I. (3) Sinus pauses >3 seconds while awake + symptoms = class IIa. (4) Chronotropic incompetence (HR <50 bpm with exertion causing symptoms) = class IIa. If bradycardia resolves after stopping beta-blocker, permanent pacemaker NOT needed (medication-induced, reversible).
requiredActions.criticalDetails: Permanent pacemaker (PPM) indications (Class I, PBS Authority 5036B): symptomatic bradycardia <40 bpm (documented on Holter or in-hospital monitoring), high-degree AV block, symptomatic sinus pauses >3 sec. PBS requires: (1) documented symptomatic bradycardia on ECG/Holter, (2) cardiologist assessment, (3) Authority application (phone or written). PPM device: dual-chamber (DDD) preferred over single-chamber (VVI) for sinus node disease. This patient likely medication-induced bradycardia → will resolve when beta-blocker ceased (no PPM needed).

markingCriteria.criterion: Recognizes symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features (HR 38, BP 88/58, presyncope, chest pain) requiring urgent treatment
Identifies metoprolol as likely cause of bradycardia (recent dose increase from 50mg to 100mg BD) and withholds beta-blocker immediately
Administers atropine correctly: 600 micrograms (0.6mg) IV bolus, can repeat every 3-5 minutes up to maximum 3mg total
Applies external pacing pads (anterior-posterior position) and prepares transcutaneous pacing as backup if atropine fails
Monitors response to atropine appropriately (HR, BP, symptom resolution, ECG changes) and recognizes need for further intervention if inadequate response
Arranges urgent temporary transvenous pacing if atropine refractory or high-degree AV block develops
Investigates underlying causes appropriately (troponin for acute MI, UEC for electrolytes, TFTs for hypothyroidism)
Recognizes PBS code for atropine (1864N, unrestricted benefit) and documents dose/indication correctly
Arranges cardiology consultation for permanent pacemaker assessment and further management
Provides analgesia/sedation (fentanyl, midazolam) if transcutaneous pacing required (pacing is painful)
Communicates clearly with patient about diagnosis (symptomatic bradycardia from beta-blocker), treatment plan (atropine, possible pacing), and prognosis (likely reversible when medication ceased)

commonMistakes: Delaying treatment while waiting for investigations (troponin, electrolytes) - symptomatic bradycardia requires immediate atropine
Using atropine dose <500 micrograms (e.g., 300 micrograms) - paradoxical bradycardia can occur with very low doses
Continuing beta-blocker despite symptomatic bradycardia (must withhold metoprolol immediately)
Not applying external pacing pads prophylactically (if atropine fails, delay in initiating pacing can cause cardiac arrest)
Initiating transcutaneous pacing without sedation/analgesia (very painful, patient distress)
Missing adverse features of bradycardia (hypotension, presyncope, chest pain) and treating as asymptomatic bradycardia
Giving excessive IV fluids for hypotension (hypotension due to bradycardia, not hypovolemia - treat HR first)
Not recognizing beta-blocker as causative medication (recent dose increase, timing of symptoms)
Administering atropine beyond maximum 3mg total dose (further doses ineffective, increases adverse effects)
Forgetting to check for inferior STEMI (ST elevation II, III, aVF) as cause of bradycardia
Not arranging cardiology review for permanent pacemaker assessment (if bradycardia persists after stopping beta-blocker, may need PPM)
Using adrenaline/isoprenaline infusion before atropine (atropine is first-line, chronotropes second-line if atropine fails)
redFlags: Complete heart block (AV dissociation, P waves and QRS complexes at different rates) - high risk asystole, requires urgent pacing even if asymptomatic
Mobitz type II second-degree AV block (dropped QRS without PR prolongation) - progresses to complete heart block, urgent pacing required
Sinus pauses >3 seconds - risk of syncope and asystole, may require pacing if symptomatic
Bradycardia with loss of consciousness (syncope) - high-risk, requires immediate intervention (atropine + pacing)
Inferior STEMI with bradycardia (ST elevation II, III, aVF + HR <50) - RCA occlusion affecting SA/AV node, requires urgent PCI + atropine
Hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L with bradycardia - life-threatening, requires urgent calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, not just atropine
Bradycardia post-cardiac arrest - may indicate hypoxic brain injury, check neurological status, consider targeted temperature management
Bradycardia in patient on digoxin (especially if K+ low) - digoxin toxicity causes bradycardia and AV block (check digoxin level, stop drug, consider DigiFab)
Bradycardia with wide QRS escape rhythm (ventricular escape <40 bpm) - unstable, high risk asystole, urgent pacing required
Cushing's triad (bradycardia + hypertension + irregular respiration) - raised ICP, requires urgent neurosurgical assessment and treatment of underlying cause
Hypothermia (<32°C) with bradycardia - atropine ineffective until rewarmed, treat hypothermia first
Bradycardia refractory to atropine 3mg + transcutaneous pacing - consider adrenaline infusion (2-10 micrograms/min) as bridge to transvenous pacing
safetyConsiderations: Symptomatic bradycardia is a medical emergency - do not delay treatment while awaiting investigations (give atropine first, investigate concurrently)
Atropine is first-line for symptomatic bradycardia (600 microgram doses, maximum 3mg total) - simple, rapid, effective in 70-80% of cases
External pacing pads should be applied prophylactically to all patients with symptomatic bradycardia (if atropine fails, transcutaneous pacing can be initiated immediately)
Transcutaneous pacing is painful (skeletal muscle stimulation) - always provide analgesia (fentanyl 25-50 mcg IV) or procedural sedation before initiating pacing
Do not give atropine doses <500 micrograms (risk of paradoxical bradycardia) - use 600 microgram (0.6mg) boluses
Beta-blocker-induced bradycardia is common, especially in elderly with dose escalation - always review medications and withhold if bradycardic
Inferior STEMI commonly causes bradycardia (RCA supplies SA and AV nodes) - check for ST elevation in II, III, aVF, treat with atropine + urgent PCI
High-degree AV block (Mobitz II, complete heart block) requires pacing even if asymptomatic - high risk of progression to asystole
Temporary transvenous pacing is more reliable and comfortable than transcutaneous pacing - arrange urgently if prolonged pacing needed (>2-4 hours)
Permanent pacemaker indications: symptomatic bradycardia <40 bpm (not medication-induced), high-degree AV block, symptomatic sinus pauses >3 seconds
PBS authority required for permanent pacemaker (code 5036B) - requires documented symptomatic bradycardia on ECG/Holter and cardiologist assessment
Monitor patient continuously during treatment (cardiac monitoring, frequent vital signs) - bradycardia can progress to asystole without warning

patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Brought in by ambulance after wife found him collapsed in bathroom 2 hours ago. Brief loss of consciousness, no seizure activity witnessed. Confused on waking, complained of dizziness and nausea. Paramedics documented heart rate 28 bpm. In ED, remains dizzy when sitting up, nauseated, mild central chest heaviness. Wife reports 3 similar but less severe dizzy spells over past week, each lasting seconds. No recent medication changes. Background of inferior STEMI 8 years ago treated with PCI to RCA.
past_medical_history: Inferior STEMI 2018 - PCI to RCA with drug-eluting stent

social_history.occupation_detail: Retired electrician, lives with wife, independent with ADLs

patient_scenario.family_history: Father died MI age 68, mother stroke age 82, no family history of conduction disease

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP visible with cannon A waves. Regular bradycardia, variable intensity S1. No murmurs. Cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds. Peripheral pulses palpable but weak.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear lung fields, no crackles or wheeze
examination_findings.other_systems: Alert but slow to respond, GCS 15. Abdomen soft non-tender. No focal neurology.

investigations.ecg: Complete heart block. Ventricular rate 32 bpm, regular. P waves 75 bpm, regular. Complete AV dissociation with P waves marching through QRS complexes. QRS duration 140ms with RBBB morphology (escape from left bundle). No acute ST changes.
investigations.chest_xray: Normal heart size, clear lungs, permanent pacing lead from previous temporary wire visible in RV apex (fractured)
investigations.bloods: Troponin I 85 ng/L (mildly elevated), K 5.1 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, Cr 125 μmol/L, Urea 7.8 mmol/L, Mg 0.82 mmol/L, Corrected Ca 2.35 mmol/L, TSH 2.1 mU/L
investigations.echocardiogram: Bedside echo: Normal LV function (EF 55%), inferior wall hypokinesis (old), no acute wall motion abnormality, no pericardial effusion
investigations.other: Previous angiogram (2018): RCA stent patent, 30% LAD stenosis, 40% Cx stenosis

immediate: Atropine 600mcg IV - ineffective (expected in complete heart block)
Withhold metoprolol immediately
Urgent temporary pacing wire insertion via right internal jugular approach
Transcutaneous pacing pads as backup while preparing for transvenous wire
short_term: Continuous cardiac monitoring in CCU
Serial troponins to exclude acute ischaemia
Urgent cardiology review for permanent pacemaker
Check pacing thresholds twice daily
long_term: Permanent dual-chamber pacemaker insertion within 24-48 hours
Consider ICD given previous MI and moderate LV dysfunction
Pacemaker clinic follow-up at 1 week, then 3 monthly
May need to restart beta-blocker at lower dose post-PPM
discharge_planning: Discharge day 2 post-permanent pacemaker insertion
Pacemaker identification card and MedicAlert bracelet
Driving restrictions 2 weeks private, 4 weeks commercial license
Wound care instructions and signs of infection education

marking_criteria.item: Correctly identifies complete heart block on ECG
Recognises atropine ineffectiveness in complete heart block
Appropriately withholds beta-blocker
Arranges urgent temporary pacing (transcutaneous or transvenous)
Correctly identifies right internal jugular as preferred access
Plans permanent pacemaker within appropriate timeframe
Chooses dual-chamber over single-chamber pacemaker
Monitors for complications (lead displacement, pneumothorax)
Provides appropriate driving restriction advice
Arranges appropriate follow-up and device monitoring

learning_objectives: Recognise ECG features of complete heart block with AV dissociation
Understand indications for temporary vs permanent cardiac pacing
Apply Australian driving guidelines following pacemaker insertion
Manage haemodynamic compromise from bradyarrhythmias
references: eTG - Cardiovascular: Cardiac arrhythmias and pacing
CSANZ Guidelines on cardiac pacing 2021
Austroads guidelines for fitness to drive - cardiac conditions

osces.title: Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome - Medication Safety in Pre-Excitation

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Recurrent palpitations with near-syncope, ECG shows pre-excitation pattern
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: ED nurse self-presented after episode of rapid palpitations during night shift 3 hours ago. Heart rate felt >200 bpm, associated with chest tightness, dizziness and pre-syncope. Symptoms lasted 20 minutes, terminated spontaneously after vagal manoeuvres. Three similar episodes over past 6 months, each lasting 5-30 minutes. Previous episodes terminated with Valsalva or cold water immersion. No syncope but feels 'about to faint' during episodes. Between episodes completely asymptomatic. Concerned about episodes occurring while caring for critically ill patients.

social_history.exercise: Gym 3 times per week, runs 5km twice weekly
social_history.occupation_detail: Senior ED nurse, rotating shifts, high-stress environment

patient_scenario.family_history: Nil cardiac history, mother has migraines, father hypertensive

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated. Normal apex beat. Normal S1 S2, no murmurs or added sounds. No carotid bruits. Peripheral pulses normal and equal.
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear lung fields bilaterally
examination_findings.other_systems: Alert and oriented. No thyromegaly. Neurologically intact.

investigations.ecg: Sinus rhythm 68 bpm, PR interval 100ms (short), QRS 124ms with delta wave (slurred upstroke) best seen in V4-V6, secondary repolarisation abnormalities. Type B pattern (negative delta V1, positive V2-V6) suggesting right-sided pathway.
investigations.chest_xray: Normal cardiac size and contour, clear lung fields
investigations.bloods: FBC normal, UEC normal, TSH 1.8 mU/L, Troponin I <2 ng/L
investigations.echocardiogram: Structurally normal heart, LVEF 60%, no valvular abnormalities, no evidence of cardiomyopathy or Ebstein's anomaly
investigations.other: 24-hour Holter (arranged urgently): Baseline pre-excitation, one episode of narrow complex tachycardia rate 210 bpm lasting 8 minutes (orthodromic AVRT), self-terminated

immediate: Education on vagal manoeuvres for episode termination
Strict avoidance of AV nodal blockers - document allergy alert
Provide written list of contraindicated medications
If presents with AF: NO digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem (risk of VF)
short_term: Urgent electrophysiology referral for risk stratification
Consider flecainide 100mg BD as bridge to ablation - PBS code 1750N
Workplace risk assessment given patient-care responsibilities
Holter monitoring to document arrhythmia burden
long_term: Catheter ablation of accessory pathway (curative in >95%)
Pre-ablation counselling: 0.5% major complication risk
Return to full duties 48 hours post-successful ablation
No long-term medication required if ablation successful
discharge_planning: MedicAlert bracelet stating WPW - avoid AV nodal blockers
Emergency action plan if prolonged tachycardia
Letter to GP listing contraindicated medications
Electrophysiology appointment within 2-4 weeks

marking_criteria.item: Recognises short PR interval and delta wave on ECG
Correctly identifies WPW syndrome diagnosis
Lists contraindicated medications (digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem)
Explains risk of VF if AV nodal blockers used in AF with WPW
Recommends catheter ablation as definitive treatment
Considers bridging antiarrhythmic (flecainide) if symptomatic
Arranges urgent electrophysiology referral
Provides education on safe vagal manoeuvres
Documents medication contraindications prominently
Addresses occupational risk given healthcare role

learning_objectives: Identify ECG features of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Understand contraindicated medications in pre-excitation syndromes
Recognise catheter ablation as curative treatment for accessory pathways
Apply knowledge of re-entrant tachycardia mechanisms
references: eTG - Cardiovascular: Supraventricular tachycardia and pre-excitation
CSANZ Clinical Practice Update on SVT Management 2020
Emergency Medicine Australasia - WPW and AF management guidelines

osces.title: Pulmonary Embolism with RV Strain - Thrombolysis Decision

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Severe dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain after international flight, hypotensive in ED
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Presented 2 hours after 14-hour flight from Los Angeles. Sudden onset severe dyspnoea while walking through airport, sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain, near-syncope in taxi. Pain worse with deep inspiration, rated 8/10. Mild calf discomfort right leg noticed 2 days ago. On combined oral contraceptive pill for 10 years. No recent surgery or immobilisation apart from long flight. No haemoptysis. Sister had DVT age 35 during pregnancy.

social_history.occupation_detail: International flight attendant, frequent long-haul flights (2-3 per month)

patient_scenario.family_history: Sister DVT age 35 in pregnancy, maternal grandmother PE age 72, no known thrombophilia

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated 6cm. Tachycardic, regular. Loud P2, right ventricular heave. No murmurs. Cool peripheries, delayed capillary refill.
examination_findings.respiratory: Tachypnoeic, using accessory muscles. Clear lung fields, no crackles or wheeze. Reduced air entry right base.
examination_findings.other_systems: Right calf 2cm larger than left, mild tenderness, no erythema. Alert but anxious, GCS 15.

investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 118 bpm, S1Q3T3 pattern, T wave inversions V1-V4, incomplete RBBB, right axis deviation
investigations.chest_xray: Hampton's hump right lower zone (wedge-shaped opacity), prominent pulmonary artery, otherwise clear
investigations.bloods: D-dimer 4250 ng/mL (markedly elevated), Troponin I 145 ng/L (elevated), BNP 480 pg/mL, ABG (6L O2): pH 7.48, PaO2 68mmHg, PaCO2 28mmHg, HCO3 22, Lactate 3.2 mmol/L
investigations.echocardiogram: Bedside echo: Dilated RV with reduced function, RV:LV ratio 1.3, septal flattening, moderate TR, RVSP 55mmHg, McConnell's sign present (RV free wall hypokinesis with preserved apex)
investigations.other: CTPA: Large saddle PE with bilateral segmental emboli, RV:LV ratio 1.4, no contrast in right lower lobe artery. Doppler USS legs: Extensive right femoral and popliteal DVT

immediate: High-flow oxygen to maintain SaO2 >94%
IV fluid resuscitation 500mL crystalloid bolus
Urgent thrombolysis assessment - sPESI score 3 (high risk)
Alteplase 100mg IV over 2 hours after consent - not PBS listed
short_term: ICU admission for haemodynamic monitoring
Commence heparin infusion after thrombolysis completed
Transition to rivaroxaban 15mg BD for 21 days - PBS code 10293M
Cease oral contraceptive permanently
Serial echo to assess RV recovery
long_term: Continue rivaroxaban 20mg daily after initial 21 days
Duration minimum 6 months, consider indefinite (unprovoked + OCP)
Thrombophilia screening after anticoagulation completed
Alternative contraception counselling (Mirena IUD recommended)
Occupational assessment for flying fitness
discharge_planning: Discharge when RV function improved and stable on oral anticoagulation
Compression stockings for post-thrombotic syndrome prevention
Education on anticoagulation adherence and bleeding precautions
Respiratory physician follow-up for CTEPH surveillance

marking_criteria.item: Recognises submassive PE with RV strain on echo
Correctly calculates sPESI score indicating high risk
Recommends thrombolysis for haemodynamic instability
Screens for thrombolysis contraindications
Appropriate anticoagulation choice and dosing (rivaroxaban)
Identifies OCP as major risk factor requiring cessation
Plans appropriate anticoagulation duration (≥6 months)
Arranges ICU admission for monitoring
Considers thrombophilia testing after anticoagulation
Addresses occupational implications for flight attendant

learning_objectives: Risk stratify pulmonary embolism using sPESI score and RV dysfunction markers
Apply Australian guidelines for thrombolysis in submassive PE
Select appropriate anticoagulation regimen for PE treatment
Identify and modify risk factors for recurrent VTE
references: eTG - Cardiovascular: Pulmonary embolism management
Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand PE guidelines 2023
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care - VTE prevention guidelines

osces.title: Aortic Stenosis - Severity Assessment and Surgical Referral

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Syncopal episode while gardening this morning, with associated chest tightness lasting 10 minutes
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Mrs Thompson experienced sudden loss of consciousness while bending over in her garden at 9am today. Preceding symptoms included 5 minutes of central chest tightness (7/10 severity, pressure-like quality) and light-headedness. Regained consciousness after 30 seconds with no post-ictal confusion. Has noticed increasing exertional dyspnoea over 6 months, now occurring after walking 50 metres on flat ground (previously could walk 500m). Experiences chest pressure when climbing stairs, relieved by rest within 2-3 minutes. Orthopnoea requiring 3 pillows, no PND. Mild ankle swelling by evening.

social_history.exercise: Limited by dyspnoea to household activities
social_history.occupation_detail: Retired 13 years ago, previously active in garden club

patient_scenario.family_history: Father died age 82 from heart failure, mother had rheumatic fever as child

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP 6cm above sternal angle. Apex beat sustained and laterally displaced to 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line. Palpable systolic thrill at right 2nd intercostal space. S1 normal, S2 soft with absent A2 component. Grade 4/6 harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur loudest at right 2nd intercostal space, radiating to both carotids. Carotid pulse parvus et tardus bilaterally. No diastolic murmur. Bilateral ankle oedema to mid-shin.
examination_findings.respiratory: Bibasal fine inspiratory crepitations to mid-zones bilaterally. No wheeze or pleural rub.
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly or ascites. No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.

investigations.ecg: 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm rate 72bpm, PR interval 200ms, QRS 110ms with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria (SV1 + RV5 = 42mm) and strain pattern with ST depression 2mm and T wave inversion in leads V5-6, I and aVL
investigations.chest_xray: Cardiomegaly with cardiothoracic ratio 0.58, prominent ascending aorta with calcification visible, upper lobe blood diversion and Kerley B lines at both bases consistent with mild pulmonary venous congestion
investigations.bloods: FBC: Hb 118 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L, Plt 245 x10^9/L. UEC: Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, Cr 95 μmol/L, eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73m². LFT normal. Troponin I 45 ng/L (normal <26). BNP 580 pg/mL (normal <100)
investigations.echocardiogram: Severe aortic stenosis with peak velocity 4.8 m/s, mean gradient 58 mmHg, calculated valve area 0.7 cm². Bicuspid aortic valve with heavy calcification. LV ejection fraction 48% with concentric LV hypertrophy (septal thickness 14mm, posterior wall 13mm). Mild mitral regurgitation. LA dilated at 45mm. PASP 45mmHg. No vegetation seen.
investigations.other: Coronary angiography shows 30% stenosis LAD, 20% RCA, no flow-limiting disease

immediate: Frusemide 40mg IV stat - PBS code 2622B
Continuous cardiac monitoring and hourly observations
Fluid restriction to 1.5L/day
Daily weight monitoring
short_term: Urgent cardiothoracic surgical referral for aortic valve replacement assessment
Heart team discussion for SAVR vs TAVI given age and comorbidities
Dental review and clearance pre-operatively
Coronary angiography if not recently performed
long_term: Aortic valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter based on heart team assessment)
Endocarditis prophylaxis not routinely recommended per current guidelines
Cardiac rehabilitation post-procedure
Annual echo surveillance if conservative management chosen
discharge_planning: Discharge once euvolaemic and surgical plan established
Frusemide 40mg PO daily - PBS code 1909B
Avoid vigorous exertion pending valve replacement
Cardiothoracic clinic appointment within 2 weeks

marking_criteria.item: Recognises classical triad of severe AS (syncope, angina, dyspnoea)
Performs correct auscultation at right 2nd intercostal space
Identifies radiation of murmur to carotids
Checks for slow-rising carotid pulse (parvus et tardus)
Correctly grades murmur intensity and character
Orders appropriate investigations including echo and ECG
Interprets echo findings correctly (valve area <1.0cm² = severe)
Recognises indication for urgent valve replacement
Appropriately refers to cardiothoracic surgery
Discusses SAVR vs TAVI options based on patient factors
Initiates diuretic therapy for heart failure
Provides appropriate activity restriction advice

learning_objectives: Recognise clinical features of severe symptomatic aortic stenosis per CSANZ guidelines
Perform focused cardiovascular examination for valvular heart disease
Interpret echocardiographic severity criteria for aortic stenosis
Apply appropriate indications for aortic valve replacement per eTG Cardiovascular
references: eTG - Cardiovascular: Valvular heart disease
CSANZ Position Statement on Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation 2023
National Heart Foundation - Management of Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines

osces.title: Mitral Regurgitation - Acute vs Chronic Differentiation

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Sudden onset severe shortness of breath and pink frothy sputum since 3am this morning
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Mr Chen woke at 3am with severe dyspnoea (10/10 severity), unable to lie flat, coughing up pink frothy sputum. Associated with severe retrosternal chest pain (8/10, crushing quality) starting 2 hours prior. Pain radiating to left arm and jaw. Diaphoresis and nausea present. Had inferior STEMI 5 days ago treated with primary PCI to RCA with drug-eluting stent. Was recovering well until this morning. Now extremely breathless at rest, orthopnoeic, using accessory muscles. No fever or productive cough prior to this episode.
past_medical_history: Inferior STEMI 5 days ago - RCA occlusion treated with PCI

social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, quit 5 years ago, 30 pack-year history
social_history.exercise: Previously walked 30 minutes daily, inactive since MI
social_history.occupation_detail: Works from home, high stress job with long hours

patient_scenario.family_history: Father died of MI age 58, mother has AF

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 88% on room air, 92% on 15L/min via non-rebreather mask

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated to angle of jaw when sitting upright. Apex beat displaced to 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line, hyperdynamic. S1 soft, S2 normal with loud P2, S3 gallop present. Grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla and back, no thrill. Bilateral pitting oedema to knees. Cool peripheries with capillary refill 4 seconds.
examination_findings.respiratory: Using accessory muscles, unable to speak in full sentences. Widespread coarse crepitations to apex bilaterally with wheeze. Pink frothy sputum visible.
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen distended with tender hepatomegaly 4cm below costal margin. No ascites.

investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 115bpm, Q waves in II, III, aVF from recent inferior MI, new ST elevation 1mm in V5-6 with reciprocal depression in V1-3
investigations.chest_xray: Bilateral alveolar infiltrates in bat-wing distribution, Kerley B lines, enlarged cardiac silhouette CTR 0.62, bilateral pleural effusions, upper lobe blood diversion consistent with acute pulmonary oedema
investigations.bloods: FBC: Hb 132 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, Plt 189 x10^9/L. UEC: Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, Cr 145 μmol/L, eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73m². High-sensitivity troponin I 8500 ng/L (normal <26), rising from 250 ng/L on admission 5 days ago. BNP 2400 pg/mL. ABG on 15L O2: pH 7.32, pO2 72mmHg, pCO2 32mmHg, HCO3 18mmol/L, lactate 4.2mmol/L
investigations.echocardiogram: Severe mitral regurgitation with flail posterior leaflet due to complete rupture of posteromedial papillary muscle. Eccentric jet directed anteriorly. EROA 0.65cm², regurgitant volume 85mL. Normal LV size (LVEDD 52mm) with hyperdynamic function (EF 65%). Inferior wall akinesis. Moderate pulmonary hypertension with PASP 55mmHg. No LA or LV thrombus.
investigations.other: Urgent coronary angiography shows patent RCA stent, no new culprit lesion, confirmed papillary muscle rupture on ventriculography

immediate: GTN infusion 5-200 mcg/min titrated to BP - PBS code 1735N
Frusemide 80mg IV stat then 20mg/hr infusion - PBS code 2622B
Morphine 2.5-5mg IV for dyspnoea and anxiety - PBS code 2696N
CPAP/BiPAP if not improving with medical therapy
Intra-aortic balloon pump insertion for afterload reduction
Emergency cardiothoracic surgical consultation
short_term: Emergency mitral valve repair or replacement within 6 hours
ICU admission post-operatively
Inotropic support as required
Mechanical ventilation until stable
long_term: Cardiac rehabilitation program
Lifelong anticoagulation if mechanical valve
Regular echo surveillance
Heart failure management with ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker optimisation
discharge_planning: ICU/HDU care initially, ward when stable
Warfarin if mechanical valve with INR target 2.5-3.5
Continue dual antiplatelet therapy for recent stent
Frusemide 40mg BD PO - PBS code 1909B
Cardiology follow-up 2 weeks post-discharge

marking_criteria.item: Recognises acute severe MR post-MI (papillary muscle rupture)
Differentiates from chronic MR by normal LV size on echo
Identifies holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla
Recognises signs of acute pulmonary oedema
Orders urgent echo to confirm diagnosis
Initiates vasodilator therapy (GTN) for afterload reduction
Administers IV diuretics for pulmonary oedema
Recognises need for emergency surgery
Arranges IABP for haemodynamic support
Provides appropriate respiratory support (CPAP/BiPAP)
Manages cardiogenic shock appropriately
Coordinates with cardiothoracic team urgently

learning_objectives: Differentiate acute from chronic mitral regurgitation using clinical and echo findings
Recognise mechanical complications of myocardial infarction
Manage acute pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock per eTG guidelines
Understand indications for emergency cardiac surgery in acute MR
references: eTG - Cardiovascular: Acute heart failure management
CSANZ Guidelines for the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes 2023
National Heart Foundation - Mechanical Complications of MI

osces.title: Infective Endocarditis - Modified Duke Criteria Application

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Fever for 3 weeks with night sweats and new shortness of breath
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Ms O'Brien presents with 3 weeks of intermittent fever (up to 39.5°C), drenching night sweats requiring change of clothes, and 5kg unintentional weight loss. Progressive exertional dyspnoea over past week, now SOB after one flight of stairs. Developed painful red spots on fingers 3 days ago. Noticed small red spots under fingernails yesterday. Had mitral valve prolapse diagnosed age 20. Dental extraction 6 weeks ago for infected molar, given amoxycillin for 5 days. No chest pain, palpitations, or syncope. Generalised arthralgia and myalgia. Poor appetite, early satiety.
past_medical_history: Mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation diagnosed 2012

social_history.exercise: Usually runs 5km three times weekly, unable last 3 weeks
social_history.occupation_detail: Daily exposure to oral bacteria, excellent dental hygiene

patient_scenario.family_history: Mother has rheumatic heart disease, father healthy

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP 4cm above sternal angle. Apex beat 5th intercostal space mid-clavicular line. Grade 3/6 pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla (previously documented as 2/6). New early diastolic murmur grade 2/6 at left sternal edge. Peripheral pulses bounding. No clinical signs of heart failure.
examination_findings.respiratory: Bibasal fine crepitations. No wheeze or pleural rub.
examination_findings.other_systems: Osler nodes on 2nd and 3rd finger pads bilaterally (tender, raised, red). Janeway lesions on thenar eminence (non-tender, macular). Splinter haemorrhages under 3 fingernails. Roth spots on fundoscopy. Splenomegaly 2cm below costal margin. No focal neurology.

investigations.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 105bpm, normal axis, no conduction abnormalities, no ischaemic changes
investigations.chest_xray: Normal heart size, clear lung fields, no consolidation or effusion
investigations.bloods: FBC: Hb 102 g/L (normocytic), WCC 15.8 x10^9/L (neutrophilia 82%), Plt 142 x10^9/L. ESR 95 mm/hr, CRP 156 mg/L. UEC: Na 136 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, Cr 78 μmol/L, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73m². LFT: mild transaminitis ALT 65 U/L. Rheumatoid factor positive 45 IU/mL. Urinalysis: microscopic haematuria, proteinuria 2+, no casts
investigations.echocardiogram: Mobile vegetation 12mm x 8mm on anterior mitral valve leaflet. Moderate to severe mitral regurgitation (increased from mild). Mild aortic regurgitation (new). Normal LV size and function (EF 60%). No abscess or fistula. PASP 35mmHg.
investigations.other: Blood cultures (3 sets before antibiotics): All 6 bottles positive for Streptococcus viridans, sensitive to benzylpenicillin (MIC 0.06 mg/L) and gentamicin

immediate: Take 3 sets of blood cultures from different sites before antibiotics
Start empirical therapy: Benzylpenicillin 1.8g IV 4-hourly - PBS code 8137L
Plus Gentamicin 1mg/kg IV BD (adjust for levels) - PBS code 2314R
Continuous cardiac monitoring
Daily examination for new murmurs or embolic phenomena
short_term: Continue IV antibiotics for 4 weeks (native valve endocarditis)
Monitor gentamicin levels (trough <1mg/L, peak 3-5mg/L)
Weekly inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR)
Weekly echo to monitor vegetation size and valve function
Cardiothoracic surgical consultation for valve assessment
long_term: Complete 4-week IV antibiotic course
Consider surgery if vegetation >10mm with embolic event or severe valve dysfunction
Dental review and treatment of any oral infection source
Echo at completion of therapy and 3 months later
Lifelong endocarditis prophylaxis education
discharge_planning: Hospital-in-the-home for IV antibiotics if stable
Daily temperature monitoring
Education on signs of complications (emboli, heart failure)
Infectious diseases and cardiology follow-up in 2 weeks

marking_criteria.item: Takes 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
Correctly applies Modified Duke Criteria
Identifies major criteria (positive blood cultures, vegetation on echo)
Identifies minor criteria (fever, predisposition, vascular/immunologic phenomena)
Recognises Osler nodes and Janeway lesions
Starts appropriate empirical antibiotics per eTG
Orders gentamicin levels and adjusts dosing
Monitors for complications with serial echo
Considers surgical indications (vegetation size, emboli)
Plans 4-week IV antibiotic course for native valve
Arranges appropriate follow-up and monitoring

learning_objectives: Apply Modified Duke Criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis
Recognise peripheral stigmata of endocarditis (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter haemorrhages)
Select appropriate empirical antibiotics according to eTG Antibiotic guidelines
Understand indications for surgical intervention in endocarditis per CSANZ guidelines
references: eTG - Antibiotic: Infective endocarditis
CSANZ Position Statement on Infective Endocarditis 2021
National Heart Foundation - Prevention of Endocarditis Guidelines

osces.title: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy vs Constrictive Pericarditis Differentiation

patient_scenario.chief_complaint: Progressive abdominal swelling and leg oedema over 6 months
patient_scenario.history_presenting_illness: Mr Papadopoulos presents with 6 months of progressive abdominal distension, now requiring paracentesis monthly (4-5L removed each time). Bilateral leg oedema to thighs, scrotal oedema developed 2 months ago. Exertional dyspnoea limiting him to 20 metres on flat ground. Orthopnoea requiring 4 pillows. Early satiety, 10kg weight gain despite poor appetite. No chest pain or palpitations. Had tuberculosis age 25 while working in PNG, treated with 6 months therapy. Recently returned from 2-year construction project in Darwin. Noticed prominent neck veins that worsen with inspiration.
past_medical_history: Chronic back pain from work injury 2015

social_history.alcohol: Previous heavy drinker (60 standard drinks/week), abstinent 5 years
social_history.exercise: Previously very active at work, now limited by symptoms
social_history.occupation_detail: Heavy manual labour, dust exposure, worked in tropical areas

patient_scenario.family_history: No cardiac disease, father had cirrhosis

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated to ear lobe when sitting at 45 degrees with prominent x and y descents. Kussmaul's sign positive (JVP rises with inspiration). No apex beat palpable. Heart sounds distant, pericardial knock present (high-pitched sound after S2). No murmurs. Peripheral oedema to sacrum.
examination_findings.respiratory: Reduced air entry bibasally with dullness to percussion (bilateral pleural effusions). No crepitations.
examination_findings.other_systems: Abdomen grossly distended with shifting dullness (ascites). Hepatomegaly 6cm below costal margin, pulsatile. Splenomegaly 3cm. Prominent abdominal wall veins.

investigations.ecg: Low voltage QRS complexes (<5mm in limb leads), widespread non-specific T wave changes, no electrical alternans
investigations.chest_xray: Normal heart size, pericardial calcification visible along left heart border and diaphragmatic surface (rim-like), bilateral pleural effusions, clear lung fields
investigations.bloods: FBC: Hb 108 g/L, WCC 6.8 x10^9/L, Plt 165 x10^9/L. UEC: Na 132 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L, Cr 125 μmol/L, eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m². LFT: Albumin 28 g/L, bilirubin 45 μmol/L (conjugated), ALT 85 U/L, ALP 180 U/L, INR 1.4. BNP 250 pg/mL (lower than expected for degree of symptoms)
investigations.echocardiogram: Normal LV size and systolic function (EF 55%). Thickened, echogenic pericardium with respiratory septal shift (ventricular interdependence). Inferior vena cava dilated (25mm) with <50% respiratory variation. Tissue Doppler: Annulus reversus (septal e' > lateral e' = 12 vs 8 cm/s). Hepatic vein flow shows prominent diastolic flow reversal with expiration.
investigations.other: Cardiac catheterisation: Equalisation of diastolic pressures (RA = RV = PA diastolic = PCWP = 18mmHg). Ventricular pressure tracings show square root sign (dip-and-plateau pattern). Discordant RV and LV systolic pressures with respiration. CT chest: Pericardial thickness 8mm (normal <4mm) with extensive calcification

immediate: Cautious diuresis - Frusemide 40mg IV BD (monitor for hypotension) - PBS code 2622B
Fluid restriction to 1L/day
Salt restriction <2g/day
Daily weights and fluid balance
Consider therapeutic paracentesis if tense ascites
short_term: Cardiac MRI to further assess pericardial thickness and inflammation
Cardiothoracic surgical consultation for pericardiectomy evaluation

tasks.task: Explain the diagnosis of peripartum cardiomyopathy to Sarah
tasks.expected_response: Sarah, you have developed a condition called peripartum cardiomyopathy, which is heart failure that develops in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months after delivery. Your heart muscle has become weakened and isn't pumping blood effectively, causing fluid to build up in your lungs and legs. This is a serious condition that needs immediate treatment, but many women recover their heart function with proper management.

tasks.task: Outline immediate management plan
tasks.expected_response: Immediate admission to high-dependency unit for cardiac monitoring. Start frusemide 40mg IV for diuresis with strict fluid balance monitoring. Commence hydralazine 25mg TDS for afterload reduction as it's safe in pregnancy. Avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs as they're teratogenic. Continuous CTG monitoring for fetal wellbeing. Liaise with obstetric team for delivery planning - may need urgent caesarean section if maternal condition deteriorates.

tasks.task: Discuss delivery timing and mode
tasks.expected_response: Given your moderate-severe heart failure at 36 weeks, we need to plan for delivery soon as this will improve your cardiac function. The timing depends on your response to medical therapy over next 24-48 hours. If you stabilize, we may attempt vaginal delivery with epidural for pain relief and assisted second stage to minimize cardiac stress. If you deteriorate or don't respond to treatment, caesarean section under regional anaesthesia would be safer. The neonatal team will be present as baby may need special care nursery admission.

tasks.task: Counsel about breastfeeding considerations
tasks.expected_response: Breastfeeding with peripartum cardiomyopathy requires careful consideration. Many heart failure medications like ACE inhibitors, which you'll need postpartum, aren't compatible with breastfeeding. Bromocriptine, which can help cardiac recovery, completely suppresses lactation. The physical demands of breastfeeding may also strain your heart during recovery. We'll discuss formula feeding options and provide lactation suppression if needed. Your cardiac recovery is the priority to ensure you can care for your baby long-term.

tasks.task: Explain prognosis and follow-up requirements
tasks.expected_response: About 50% of women with peripartum cardiomyopathy recover normal heart function within 6 months with treatment. You'll need regular cardiology follow-up with repeat echocardiograms at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months postpartum. Long-term medications include ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and possibly spironolactone. Future pregnancies carry a 30-50% recurrence risk with higher mortality if heart function doesn't fully recover. We strongly recommend contraception counseling before discharge.

tasks.task: Address Sarah's concerns about caring for her toddler and newborn
tasks.expected_response: I understand this is overwhelming with a 3-year-old at home and a new baby coming. Your heart condition means you'll need significant help initially - consider family support or home help services through maternal child health. Limit physical activities like lifting your toddler or climbing stairs. Arrange baby equipment on one level of your home. Your husband or support person should handle night feeds initially to ensure you get adequate rest for cardiac recovery. Social work can help arrange practical supports through Centrelink carer payments.

He returned to work but has developed central chest pain over past 3 days, worse on deep inspiration and lying flat, partially relieved sitting forward. Associated with extreme fatigue, exertional dyspnoea and occasional palpitations. He tried ibuprofen which provided minimal relief. No syncope or pre-syncope. Previously very fit, runs 10km three times weekly but now can't climb stairs without stopping.

examination_findings.peripheral: No peripheral oedema, Warm peripheries, Capillary refill 2 seconds

tasks.task: Explain the diagnosis of viral myocarditis to James
tasks.expected_response: James, you have developed viral myocarditis, which is inflammation of your heart muscle following your recent influenza infection. The virus has triggered an immune response that's causing inflammation in your heart, leading to your chest pain, fatigue and reduced heart pumping function. Your cardiac MRI confirms this diagnosis. Most people with viral myocarditis recover completely with supportive care, though recovery takes several months.

tasks.task: Outline immediate management plan
tasks.expected_response: Admit for cardiac monitoring given troponin elevation and reduced ejection fraction. Stop NSAIDs immediately as they can worsen myocarditis and increase risk of complications. Start colchicine 500 micrograms BD for anti-inflammatory effect without NSAID risks. Begin heart failure therapy with ramipril 2.5mg daily and bisoprolol 1.25mg daily, titrating up as tolerated. Monitor daily ECGs for arrhythmias. Bed rest initially with gradual mobilization. No specific antiviral therapy indicated.

tasks.task: Counsel about exercise restrictions
tasks.expected_response: Exercise restriction is critical for your recovery. You must avoid all competitive sports and moderate-high intensity exercise for at least 6 months from diagnosis. This includes your regular 10km runs. Exercise can trigger fatal arrhythmias in active myocarditis. After 3 months, we'll repeat cardiac MRI and exercise stress test. If these show recovery, you can gradually return to light exercise under supervision. Full return to competitive sports only after normal cardiac function confirmed at 6 months.

tasks.task: Discuss potential complications to monitor
tasks.expected_response: While most recover fully, we need to monitor for complications. These include arrhythmias - any palpitations, dizziness or fainting need urgent review. Progressive heart failure with worsening breathlessness or leg swelling requires immediate assessment. Rarely, fulminant myocarditis can develop requiring intensive care support or even mechanical circulatory support. About 20% develop dilated cardiomyopathy long-term. Warning signs include chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or worsening dyspnoea.

tasks.task: Explain follow-up investigations and monitoring
tasks.expected_response: You'll need regular cardiology follow-up at 2 weeks, 1 month, 3 months and 6 months. Serial echocardiograms will monitor your heart function recovery. Cardiac MRI at 3-6 months assesses myocardial inflammation resolution and scarring. 24-hour Holter monitoring checks for arrhythmias before exercise clearance. Blood tests including troponin and BNP track recovery. If ejection fraction doesn't improve by 3 months, we may consider endomyocardial biopsy to exclude giant cell myocarditis requiring immunosuppression.

tasks.task: Address return to work and lifestyle modifications
tasks.expected_response: You can return to sedentary work from home in 1-2 weeks if symptoms improve. Avoid physical stress and maintain regular sleep patterns to support recovery. No alcohol for at least 3 months as it can worsen myocarditis. Ensure adequate hydration but avoid excessive fluids. Get annual flu and COVID vaccines once recovered to prevent recurrence. Consider psychological support as the activity restrictions and uncertainty can cause anxiety. I'll provide a medical certificate for modified duties.

Associated with exertional dyspnoea - previously walked 5km daily, now breathless after 500m. Mild chest tightness on exertion, relieved by rest. No syncope or presyncope. Noticed irregular pulse when checking blood pressure at home. Fatigue has significantly worsened, requiring afternoon naps.

clinical_scenario.medications: Perindopril 8mg daily, Amlodipine 5mg daily, Metformin 1g BD, Atorvastatin 40mg daily
clinical_scenario.social_history: Ex-smoker quit 15 years ago (20 pack-years), Moderate alcohol 2-3 standard drinks daily, Retired 2 years ago, Lives with wife
clinical_scenario.family_history: Father had stroke age 75, Mother had atrial fibrillation, Brother has hypertension

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP 4cm above sternal angle, Regular tachycardia, Normal S1 S2, No murmurs, No signs of heart failure
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear lung fields bilaterally
examination_findings.peripheral: No peripheral oedema, All pulses palpable

investigations.interpretation: Typical atrial flutter with 2:1 AV block

investigations.interpretation: Structurally normal heart with mild left atrial enlargement

investigations.result: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, Free T4 15 pmol/L

tasks.task: Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc score and determine anticoagulation need
tasks.expected_response: Robert's CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 3: Hypertension (1 point), Diabetes (1 point), Age 62 (1 point). With a score of 3, his annual stroke risk is 3.2% without anticoagulation. According to CSANZ guidelines, anticoagulation is strongly recommended. Atrial flutter carries similar stroke risk to atrial fibrillation. Given no contraindications, I recommend starting a DOAC like apixaban 5mg BD or rivaroxaban 20mg daily, which are PBS-listed for this indication.

tasks.task: Explain immediate rate control strategy
tasks.expected_response: We need to slow your heart rate urgently to improve symptoms. I'll start metoprolol 25mg BD as you have no contraindications. This beta-blocker will slow AV node conduction, reducing ventricular rate to target 80-100 bpm at rest. If inadequate response, we can increase to 50mg BD or add digoxin 125 micrograms daily. Avoid calcium channel blockers like diltiazem while on amlodipine due to additive effects. Monitor BP and heart rate response.

tasks.task: Discuss cardioversion timing and preparation
tasks.expected_response: Since symptoms started 3 weeks ago, we cannot cardiovert immediately due to stroke risk. You need therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before elective cardioversion, or alternatively a transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) to exclude left atrial thrombus for earlier cardioversion. After starting apixaban today, schedule cardioversion in 4 weeks. Continue anticoagulation for minimum 4 weeks post-cardioversion regardless of rhythm, as atrial stunning persists. Success rate is 90% but recurrence common at 50% within one year.

tasks.task: Explain catheter ablation as definitive treatment
tasks.expected_response: Catheter ablation is highly effective for typical atrial flutter with 95% cure rate. It involves inserting catheters via groin veins to create a line of ablation across the cavotricuspid isthmus in your right atrium, blocking the flutter circuit. It's a day procedure under sedation, taking 1-2 hours. Major complications are rare (<1%) including cardiac tamponade or AV block. Given high success rate and low recurrence, CSANZ guidelines recommend ablation as first-line treatment for typical flutter rather than long-term medication.

tasks.task: Compare ablation versus cardioversion options
tasks.expected_response: Cardioversion offers immediate rhythm restoration but 50% recurrence within a year, requiring antiarrhythmic drugs long-term. Ablation has 95% long-term success, potentially eliminating need for rate control medications and reducing anticoagulation duration if you remain in sinus rhythm with low CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. Ablation prevents flutter recurrence but you may still develop atrial fibrillation (20-30% chance) requiring continued monitoring. Given your relatively young age and good health, ablation offers better long-term outcomes. I recommend ablation as definitive treatment.

tasks.task: Outline follow-up plan regardless of treatment choice
tasks.expected_response: Start apixaban 5mg BD today for stroke prevention. Begin metoprolol for rate control with BP and heart rate monitoring. Cardiology review in 2 weeks to assess rate control. If choosing cardioversion, book for 4 weeks post-anticoagulation. If choosing ablation, refer to electrophysiology - waiting list typically 6-8 weeks, continue rate control meanwhile. Post-procedure: ECG and Holter monitoring at 3 months, 6 months, then yearly. Continue anticoagulation based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc score even if successful ablation. Lifestyle: reduce alcohol, weight loss, treat sleep apnoea if present.
