tasks.task: Identify this as hypertensive emergency and explain immediate management priorities
tasks.expected_response: This is a hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage - PRES, acute kidney injury, and cardiac injury. Immediate priorities: Transfer to ICU for arterial line monitoring. Target BP reduction of 20-25% in first hour, so aim for 180-190/110-115 mmHg initially. Too rapid lowering can cause cerebral hypoperfusion. Start IV labetalol infusion 2mg/min with titration every 10 minutes. Alternative is nicardipine infusion. Avoid pure vasodilators like hydralazine which increase intracranial pressure. Continuous neurological monitoring for seizure recurrence.

tasks.task: Explain PRES diagnosis and pathophysiology to medical team
tasks.expected_response: PRES is caused by severe hypertension overwhelming cerebral autoregulation, leading to hyperperfusion, blood-brain barrier breakdown and vasogenic oedema, predominantly in posterior circulation. MRI shows characteristic parieto-occipital white matter oedema without infarction. It's reversible with prompt BP control, hence 'reversible' in the name. Untreated, it can progress to intracranial haemorrhage or permanent infarction. Triggers include hypertensive crisis, pre-eclampsia, immunosuppressants, and renal failure - Margaret has both hypertension and CKD.

tasks.task: Outline specific blood pressure targets and timeline
tasks.expected_response: First hour: Reduce MAP by 20-25% (target 180-190/110-115 mmHg) using IV labetalol infusion. Hours 2-6: Gradually reduce to 160/100-110 mmHg if tolerating well and neurologically stable. Within 24-48 hours: Target 140-150/90-95 mmHg. Transition to oral agents when stable - restart irbesartan and amlodipine with dose adjustment for renal function. Long-term target <130/80 given CKD. Monitor for signs of hypoperfusion - worsening confusion, focal deficits, or oliguria indicate too rapid reduction.

tasks.task: Manage seizure risk and provide neuroprotection
tasks.expected_response: Start levetiracetam 1g IV loading then 500mg BD for seizure prophylaxis - renally adjusted dose given eGFR 18. Avoid phenytoin as it's less effective in PRES. Maintain magnesium >1.0 mmol/L as hypomagnesaemia lowers seizure threshold - give 10mmol IV if low. Continuous EEG monitoring for 24 hours to detect non-convulsive seizures. Avoid benzodiazepines unless active seizures. Most patients don't need long-term anticonvulsants - can wean after PRES resolves (typically 2-4 weeks).

tasks.task: Address acute kidney injury management
tasks.expected_response: Margaret has acute on chronic kidney disease - creatinine doubled from baseline. Likely acute tubular necrosis from malignant hypertension. Strict fluid balance with input/output charting. Daily weights. Avoid nephrotoxins - no NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides. May need temporary dialysis if develops oliguria, hyperkalaemia >6.0, acidosis, or fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics. Renal function should improve with BP control. Frusemide 80mg IV for pulmonary oedema if urine output adequate. Nephrology consultation for dialysis planning if no improvement in 24-48 hours.

tasks.task: Discuss prognosis and discharge planning
tasks.expected_response: PRES is reversible in 70-90% with prompt treatment - neurological symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks. MRI changes resolve over 2-4 weeks. Medication adherence is critical - arrange Webster packs and home BP monitoring. Nephrology follow-up for CKD management. Neurology review with repeat MRI in 4 weeks. Address psychosocial stressors - social work referral for workplace stress management. Education about hypertensive emergency warning signs: severe headache, visual changes, confusion need immediate ED presentation. Consider cardiac echo given troponin rise.

tasks.task: Calculate corrected QT interval and explain significance
tasks.expected_response: Using Bazett formula: QTc = QT/√RR interval. With QT 485ms at heart rate 65, the corrected QT is 485ms, which is prolonged (normal <460ms in females). This prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation causing sudden cardiac death. Your symptoms during stress suggest adrenergic-triggered arrhythmias, typical of long QT syndrome type 1. The risk is increased by QT-prolonging medications like azithromycin and escitalopram you're currently taking.

tasks.task: Identify and manage QT-prolonging medications
tasks.expected_response: Stop azithromycin immediately - macrolides significantly prolong QT. Replace with amoxicillin 500mg TDS for sinusitis. Escitalopram also prolongs QT - discuss with psychiatrist about switching to sertraline which has minimal QT effect. Avoid all high-risk medications: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine), antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antiemetics (ondansetron, domperidone). Check www.crediblemeds.org for comprehensive list. Always inform healthcare providers about your long QT syndrome before prescriptions.

tasks.task: Explain beta-blocker therapy for long QT syndrome
tasks.expected_response: Beta-blockers are first-line therapy for long QT syndrome, reducing cardiac events by 70%. Nadolol 40-80mg daily or propranolol 40mg TDS are preferred - better evidence than metoprolol. They prevent adrenergic-triggered arrhythmias by blunting sympathetic stimulation. Start nadolol 40mg daily, titrating to resting heart rate 50-60 bpm. Never miss doses as withdrawal increases arrhythmia risk. Continue even if asymptomatic. Contraindicated: asthma, severe bradycardia. Side effects: fatigue, cold peripheries, vivid dreams. Beta-blockers are lifelong therapy.

tasks.task: Discuss lifestyle modifications and trigger avoidance
tasks.expected_response: Avoid sudden loud noises (alarm clocks, phones) - use gradual wake alarms. No competitive sports or swimming alone - risk of drowning if arrhythmia occurs. Avoid strenuous exercise but moderate activity is safe. Maintain normal potassium (>4.0) and magnesium (>0.85) - supplement if needed. Avoid energy drinks, excessive caffeine, and stimulants. Manage stress with counseling and relaxation techniques. Medical alert bracelet essential. Inform all healthcare providers, dentists about condition. Genetic counseling before pregnancy - 50% inheritance risk.

tasks.task: Explain indications for ICD implantation
tasks.expected_response: ICD indicated for: recurrent syncope despite beta-blockers, cardiac arrest survivors, torsades de pointes documented, QTc >500ms with symptoms. You meet criteria with QTc 485ms, exercise-induced VT, and syncope. ICD provides backup protection - detects and terminates ventricular arrhythmias. Doesn't replace beta-blockers, used together. Subcutaneous ICD option for young patients avoids transvenous leads. Complications: infection 1-2%, inappropriate shocks 20%, lead problems. MRI compatibility with newer models. Driving restrictions 6 months post-implant.

tasks.task: Arrange family screening and genetic testing
tasks.expected_response: First-degree relatives need ECG screening - your mother and brother already show QT prolongation and need cardiology assessment. Genetic testing can identify specific mutation in 75% of cases - helps risk stratification and guides therapy. LQT1 (swimming triggers), LQT2 (auditory triggers), LQT3 (sleep triggers) have different management. Positive genetic test allows predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives. PBS funds genetic testing with clinical long QT diagnosis. Family members with prolonged QT need beta-blockers even if asymptomatic. Genetic counseling helps understand inheritance pattern and reproductive options.

osces.title: Aortic Coarctation - Adult Presentation with Hypertension
osces.scenario: Timothy Walker, a 19-year-old university engineering student, presents to the GP after failing a pre-employment medical due to high blood pressure (165/95 mmHg). He has no symptoms and plays social basketball weekly without limitation. He mentions occasional mild headaches after studying and his calves sometimes ache after running, which he attributed to poor fitness. osces.title: Post-MI Complications - Left Ventricular Free Wall Rupture Recognition
osces.scenario: Maria Stavros, a 68-year-old retired café owner, is day 4 post anterior STEMI treated with delayed PCI (presented 18 hours after symptom onset). She had been recovering well but suddenly develops severe chest pain and dyspnoea at 0600 while getting up to use the bathroom. She appears shocked and distressed. Initial observations: BP 75/50 mmHg (was 125/75 yesterday), HR 125 weak and thready, SpO2 89% on 6L oxygen. JVP elevated to angle of jaw. Heart sounds are muffled. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans. Bedside echo shows large pericardial effusion with RV collapse during diastole.
